Introduction Visuomotor policies are increasingly capable of complex tasks from rich sensory observations~ open_vla, gemini_robotics_1_5, pi06_star , yet they remain brittle at deployment and can fail in ways they cannot recover from on their own. The dominant response is to scale policy learning itself, with more data, more compute, and larger architectures~ oxe_dataset, droid_dataset . While effective, these approaches are expensive and require access to the policy's parameters and training pipeline --- access a practitioner increasingly does not have, since strong policies are increasingly served as inference APIs or shipped with closed weights. When the weights are out of reach, deployment-time correction is a promising avenue. We therefore ask how a policy that has already been trained and deployed can be improved without modifying the policy itself. We assume only black-box access: the parameters, architecture, and action-generation procedure are unknown, and the policy can only be queried for actions. Fine-tuning and methods that steer the policy's internal sampling are therefore inapplicable, and improvement must come from an external wrapper that monitors execution and intervenes through actions alone. Two requirements make this demanding: policy rollouts are costly, so the wrapper must be learned from few labeled on-policy executions, and all monitoring and planning must keep pace with the control loop while the policy executes. Our approach is based on monitoring-and-intervention, or filtering~ ames_2016_cbf_qp, borquez2024safety , which in control theory most often enforces safety: a filter watches the nominal policy and overrides it only when a constraint would be violated~ bansalHamiltonJacobiReachabilityBrief2017b, wang_2024_coop_safe_perf . We instead filter for task completion. Rather than characterizing and avoiding every failure mode, an intervention seeks to return the system to a state from which the nominal policy can complete the task. The intuition is that a capable policy need not be replaced or retrained when it falters; a short corrective action is often enough to put it back in its basin of success. The framework has two components. A monitor tracks the nominal policy's execution and detects when it is no longer progressing toward task completion; we instantiate it with a policy-conditioned liveness value function~ wang2026_policy_eval , learned from on-policy rollouts with sparse episode-level outcome labels, that estimates how close the policy is to completing the task. When the value indicates a loss of progress, a planner briefly overrides the policy and searches a compact latent world model --- trained on the same rollouts plus auxiliary play data --- for a short corrective action sequence, then hands control back. Critically, the same value that triggers intervention also scores the futures the world model imagines, directing the planner toward states from which the nominal policy can recover. Methods that generate video futures report seconds-scale intervention times~ xu2026vlaintheloop, fan2026dreamavoid , forcing either a pause or a control rate too low for responsive manipulation. We therefore design around deployment latency: the world model is compact, candidate futures are evaluated in parallel, and planning emits an action chunk rather than a single action. In our hardware experiment a planning cycle takes , which, amortized over the chunk, keeps the monitor--planner loop above \,Hz. We summarize our contributions as follows. First, we formulate deployment-time improvement of visuomotor manipulation policies under a strict black-box access model and cast it as liveness filtering: an external wrapper intervenes briefly to return a fixed nominal policy to its basin of success. Second, we present a real-time instantiation in which a single policy-conditioned liveness value both monitors execution and guides corrective planning in a compact latent world model, with a data-informed action proposal that makes the search efficient. Third, we validate it across policy classes: on the ten-task LIBERO-Goal suite our method improves ~ pi05 from to , outperforming offline-RL and safety-filtering baselines, and on a Franka Panda manipulator it improves a diffusion policy~ diffusion_policy from to while operating within the policy's control loop. Related Work We group prior work by the access and supervision it assumes, noting in each case how our problem setting differs. One line of work intervenes inside the policy's action-generation process, requiring white-box access to the policy. Latent Policy Barrier~ latent_policy_barrier treats the latent embeddings of expert demonstrations as a barrier separating in- from out-of-distribution states, using a learned dynamics model to steer a diffusion policy's denoising noise back toward the expert distribution at inference, equating in-distribution behavior with task success. VLS~ liu2026vls steers a pretrained policy's denoising process with guidance from a vision-language model; and wagenmaker2025_steer_dp_latent_rl replaces a diffusion policy's Gaussian sampling noise with a distribution learned via reinforcement learning (RL). These methods intervene directly in action generation, but rely on the policy's internal representations or sampling procedure and so do not apply when the nominal policy is only a black box. A second class of methods treats the nominal policy as a black box and intervenes only through its inputs or outputs. RoboMonkey~ kwok2025robomonkey and Steer Your Generalists~ nakamoto2024_steer_generalist rerank action candidates sampled from the policy. This avoids modifying the policy's weights, but requires multiple policy queries at every decision point, which is prohibitive for real-time control: a single diffusion-policy query alone takes in our hardware setting. We instead query once per intervention and obtain candidate diversity from our own proposal distribution rather than from the policy's sampler. Most closely related to our work are methods that use a learned world model to improve a fixed policy at deployment. Latent Policy Steering~ wang2025latent continuously searches a latent world model for improved action sequences. In contrast, our monitor invokes planning selectively and returns control to the nominal policy after a short correction, limiting unnecessary computation and intervention when the nominal policy is progressing successfully. DreamAvoid~ fan2026dreamavoid ranks futures from a pretrained video world model at annotated critical phases, and VLA-in-the-Loop~ xu2026vlaintheloop specializes the paradigm to grasping, rolling back to an earlier state on a predicted grasp failure. Both are scoped to predefined critical events and to supervision we do not assume: access to the VLA's sampling procedure plus critical-phase, progress, and failure-boundary labels for the former, grasp-feasibility labels and state rollback for the latter. We assume only black-box access and learn a policy-conditioned liveness value from sparse episode-level outcomes; the same value both detects loss of progress and guides planning, so intervention is not confined to predefined events, such as the wrong-task behavior in Fig.~ fig:libero_t0_viz . Their video models are also slower at deployment, reporting \,s (DreamAvoid) and \,s (VLA-in-the-Loop) per intervention against our planning cycle. Monitoring-and-intervention filters have a principled basis in reachability analysis~ bansalHamiltonJacobiReachabilityBrief2017b , which formalizes intervention under known dynamics: a filter overrides the policy only when needed to keep the system within a desired set of states. This machinery supports the dual objectives of safety (avoiding a failure set) and liveness (reaching a goal set~ borquez2024safety ). We focus on the latter. Classical liveness filtering computes the reachable set exactly via dynamic programming~ borquez2024safety , but this is intractable for high-dimensional visual observations and the contact-rich dynamics of manipulation. We therefore build on the learned policy-conditioned liveness value of~ wang2026_policy_eval , which can be estimated from limited policy-rollout data with sparse, episode-level outcome labels. Whereas that prior work uses the liveness value for offline policy evaluation, we use it here both to detect loss of progress during execution and, critically, to guide corrective planning in a learned world model. World models differ in what they predict, and that choice sets the deployment cost. Video-generation models synthesize pixels, which is expensive enough to put them at seconds-scale latency; DreamerV3 predicts distributions over discrete latent codes~ hafnerMasteringDiverseDomains2024 ; feature-prediction models forecast the patch-level features of a pretrained visual encoder, as in DINO-WM~ dino_wm . We take the last approach and keep the model compact, since each intervention must evaluate many imagined action sequences within a real-time budget. title: RDCompGS: Rate-Distortion Optimization for Compression of 3D Gaussian Splatting with Image Codecs
comment: This manuscript has been submitted to IEEE Transactions on Multimedia (TMM)
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables high-quality, real-time novel view synthesis but requires significant storage and transmission resources. Mapping Gaussian attributes to 2D representations enables efficient compression using mature image codecs. However, Gaussian representations that achieve comparable rendering quality are generally treated similarly during optimization, despite substantial differences in coding rate, leading to limited rate-distortion (R-D) performance after compression. To address this limitation, we propose RDCompGS, a 3DGS compression method that enables overall R-D optimization of Gaussian representations with respect to subsequent coding. A differentiable estimate of the coding rate is incorporated into the R-D optimization with rendering distortion. The rate constraint adjustment model further regulates the R-D trade-off across different compression conditions. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that RDCompGS achieves average Bjøntegaard Delta Rate reductions of 37.84% and 49.31% with H.265/HEVC and JPEG XL, respectively. The estimated rate also shows a strong correlation with the actual bit-rate under different compression conditions.
full_text: RDCompGS: Rate–Distortion Optimization for Compression of 3D Gaussian Splatting with Image Codecs Huiping~Ren, Shuai~Wan, Luqian~Bai, Zhang~Chen, and~Fuzheng~Yang 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables high-quality, real-time novel view synthesis but requires significant storage and transmission resources. Mapping Gaussian attributes to 2D representations enables efficient compression using mature image codecs. However, Gaussian representations that achieve comparable rendering quality are generally treated similarly during optimization, despite substantial differences in coding rate, leading to limited rate-distortion (R-D) performance after compression. To address this limitation, we propose RDCompGS, a 3DGS compression method that enables overall R-D optimization of Gaussian representations with respect to subsequent coding. A differentiable estimate of the coding rate is incorporated into the R-D optimization with rendering distortion. The rate constraint adjustment model further regulates the R-D trade-off across different compression conditions. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that RDCompGS achieves average Bjøntegaard Delta Rate reductions of 37.84 and 49.31 with H.265/HEVC and JPEG XL, respectively. The estimated rate also shows a strong correlation with the actual bit-rate under different compression conditions. 3D Gaussian Splatting, 3DGS compression, rate-distortion optimization, image codecs. Introduction D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl20233d is an important approach for novel view synthesis. By representing scenes with explicit anisotropic 3D Gaussians and rendering them through -blending, 3DGS achieves high rendering quality and real-time performance. 3DGS is an active research topic and is relevant to areas such as autonomous driving, multimedia interaction, virtual reality, cultural heritage digitization, and digital twinning~ tian2026hfrs,shuai2026adversarial,Liang4DGS,zhao2026msa,FieldGS . However, representing a 3D scene with 3DGS typically requires millions of Gaussian primitives, leading to significant storage and memory overhead~ ali2026survey,chen2026survey . Existing studies on 3DGS compression mainly focus on two aspects. The first aspect directly compresses the native 3D Gaussian representation. We broadly classify current approaches into Gaussian parameter and attribute compression~ lee2024compact,niedermayr2024compressed,wang2024end,Girish2024EAGLES,chen2026pcgs,chen2025fast,huang2026entropygs,papantonakis2024reducing,fan2024lightgaussian , anchor-based compression~ lu2024scaffold,chen2024hac,chen2025hacpp,wang2024contextgs,zhan2025cat , and Gaussian primitive compactification~ hanson2025pup,fan2024lightgaussian,shuai2026adversarial,freitas2026visibility,chen2026refine,Chen2026SPAREGSSP . These strategies are not mutually exclusive and are often combined to reduce redundancy. The second aspect converts 3DGS into 2D representations and compresses them using mature image codecs~ yang2026lightweight,zhu2026Dual,wang20253dgcoding,lee2025compression,morgenstern2024compact,wang2024v . This direction enables 3DGS compression to directly leverage established coding standards and their existing software and hardware support, providing a practical solution for 3DGS storage and transmission. As shown in Fig.~ fig:codec_pipeline , the general pipeline consists of 3DGS generation and compression. The scene is first represented by Gaussian primitives and then mapped into 2D representations for coding. However, in 3DGS compression through image codecs, Gaussian optimization is usually separated from subsequent coding. Specifically, Gaussian optimization evaluates attributes according to their contribution to rendered views, while subsequent compression is performed considering both the coding distortion and the corresponding bit-rate as the cost. As the result, Gaussian representations with comparable rendering quality are generally treated similarly during optimization even when their coding rates differ substantially. Therefore, the rate-distortion (R-D) performance cannot be optimized for compression if reducing the rendering distortion is the optimization goal. Since the actual bit-rate produced by the codec is also not differentiable, it is not feasible to be directly incorporated into Gaussian optimization. Moreover, the balance between coding rate and rendering distortion changes across compression conditions. Therefore, applying a single rate constraint to all compression conditions cannot maintain an appropriate R-D trade-off, which limits the R-D performance after compression. To address the above issues, we propose RDCompGS, a 3DGS compression method that enables overall R-D optimization in which Gaussian generation and subsequent coding are treated as a whole. During Gaussian optimization, rendering distortion and the coding rate associated with subsequent compression are jointly optimized to improve the R-D performance after compression. To incorporate the coding rate into Gaussian optimization, RDCompGS introduces differentiable rate estimation based on the statistical distribution of transformed coefficients and their quantization probabilities. Different from prior approaches that optimize under a prescribed rate or distortion setting, the rate constraint adjustment model characterizes the relative strength of the estimated rate and rendering distortion and adjusts their balance across different compression conditions. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that RDCompGS achieves average BD-Rate reductions of 37.84 and 49.31 with H.265/HEVC and JPEG XL, respectively, while maintaining comparable rendering quality. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows. We consider Gaussian generation and subsequent coding as a whole for 3DGS compression and formulate the compression of Gaussian representations as an overall R-D optimization with respect to subsequent coding. Based on this formulation, we propose RDCompGS, which derives a differentiable estimate of the coding rate from transformed Gaussian attributes and introduces the rate constraint adjustment model to regulate the rate constraint under different coding conditions. We validate RDCompGS on three benchmark datasets using both H.265/HEVC and JPEG XL, showing consistent R-D improvements across different coding conditions. Additional experiments combining Gaussian pruning with image codec compression further confirm the effectiveness of RDCompGS. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section~ sec:related presents the related work. Section~ sec:method introduces the proposed method. Section~ sec:experiments reports the experimental results and analysis. Finally, Section~ sec:conclusion concludes this paper. Related Work sec:related Based on the Gaussian representation used during compression, we divide existing 3DGS compression methods into two types: compression of 3D Gaussian representations and compression of 3DGS with 2D representations. Compression of 3D Gaussian Representations subsec:compact_3d We broadly classify methods for compressing 3D Gaussian representations into Gaussian parameter and attribute compression, anchor-based compression, and Gaussian primitive compactification. Gaussian parameter and attribute compression reduces storage by making the representation of individual Gaussians more compact while retaining the native 3D Gaussian structure. Representative approaches include quantization, which reduces storage by lowering precision~ lee2024compact,niedermayr2024compressed,wang2024end,Girish2024EAGLES,chen2026pcgs , entropy coding based on symbol probabilities to reduce the coded length~ chen2025fast,huang2026entropygs , and spherical harmonics (SH) reduction~ fan2024lightgaussian,papantonakis2024reducing . Anchor-based methods reduce 3DGS redundancy by organizing local Gaussians around sparse anchors while exploiting relationships among anchors and their associated attributes. Representative methods include Scaffold-GS~ lu2024scaffold , HAC~ chen2024hac , HAC++~ chen2025hacpp , ContextGS~ wang2024contextgs , and CAT-3DGS~ zhan2025cat , which exploit attribute prediction, contextual dependencies, hierarchical relationships, and spatial correlations for compression. Gaussian primitive compactification reduces redundancy by controlling the number or distribution of Gaussians. Representative methods include PUP 3D-GS~ hanson2025pup , LightGaussian~ fan2024lightgaussian , APNet~ shuai2026adversarial , visibility-based geometry pruning~ freitas2026visibility , REFINE~ chen2026refine , and SPARE-GS~ Chen2026SPAREGSSP . These methods exploit spatial sensitivity scores, global significance scores, view-dependent masks and Rasterization Weight Sampling, multi-view visibility, rendering-aware importance, and global budget allocation to reduce redundant Gaussians or regulate their spatial distribution. Although these methods effectively reduce redundancy in native 3D Gaussian representations, they mainly compress Gaussian primitives in their original representation form. Another direction incorporates 2D representations into 3DGS compression, enabling the use of established image codecs for compression. Compression of 3DGS with 2D Representations subsec:codec_based We broadly divide existing 3DGS compression methods based on 2D representations according to when the 2D representation is introduced: during or after the Gaussian optimization process. Methods that introduce 2D representations after Gaussian optimization adopt different mapping strategies. LGSCV~ yang2026lightweight first applies a 3D Morton scan to order Gaussian primitives and then uses a 2D Morton scan to map them into blockwise 2D maps, which are compressed using H.265/HEVC. To improve performance at medium and low bit-rates, it further applies Principal Component Analysis to SH coefficients and introduces MiniPLAS for local primitive permutation. Zhu et al.~ zhu2026Dual propose a Dual-Hilbert scan algorithm that uses a 3D Hilbert curve to preserve spatial locality and a 2D Hilbert curve to map the ordered Gaussian primitives into 2D grids for subsequent H.265/HEVC compression. 3DGCoding~ wang20253dgcoding sorts Gaussian primitives in z-order according to their positions, maps the quantized attributes onto 2D planes, and compresses the attribute planes of static Gaussians using lossless PNG and those of dynamic Gaussians using H.265/HEVC. V ~ wang2024v sorts Gaussian primitives using Morton order, maps Gaussian attributes into video frames, and compresses them using H.264/AVC. For methods that introduce 2D representations during Gaussian optimization, CodecGS~ lee2025compression redesigns the explicit Gaussian representation using progressive tri-plane features and employs a multilayer perceptron to predict Gaussian attributes. The feature plane channels are then concatenated into frames and compressed using H.265/HEVC. Compared with CodecGS, SOG~ morgenstern2024compact retains explicit Gaussian attributes and directly organizes them into aligned 2D grids using Parallel Linear Assignment Sorting (PLAS). Specifically, PLAS improves the local smoothness of the grids by constructing a smoothed target with a Gaussian filter and performing parallel blockwise assignments to update the arrangement of Gaussian primitives. The optimized Gaussian parameters are then quantized and compressed using JPEG XL. To summarize, organizing Gaussian parameters into 2D representations provides a structured form that can be compressed using image codecs. However, Gaussian optimization remains separated from subsequent coding, which limits the overall R-D performance. title: Cracking Mobile Manipulation: From Failure Diagnosis to Agentic Robot System
summary: Recent vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong performance on local robot manipulation, yet their success does not readily translate to long-horizon mobile manipulation. In our experiments, a pretrained subtask VLA achieves 80% success rate on atomic manipulation tasks but only 19% when these skills are composed into mobile manipulation. We argue that this gap stems from failures across the execution process rather than from local manipulation capability alone. To uncover these bottlenecks, we systematically diagnose failures in long-horizon mobile manipulation and identify three dominant regimes: task planning, navigation and base positioning, and local manipulation. Based on this diagnosis, we develop failure-guided agentic intervention that augments a fixed subtask VLA with demonstration-based planning guidance, adaptive visual memory, accessibility-aware base adjustment, and local end-effector adjustment. On RoboCasa365, these interventions progressively improve task success from 19% to 47%, with the finalized system reaching 49% on held-out episode seeds, compared with 18% for the baseline. The same design improves performance from 14% to 37% on BEHAVIOR-1K and from 5/20 to 13/20 on real-robot tasks. These results suggest that reliable mobile manipulation can be advanced by diagnosing and intervening on the current bottleneck, rather than uniformly scaling the underlying policy. Our code will be released at https://github.com/PKU-VaLuE-Lab/Cracking-Mobile-Manipulation.git.
full_text: [1] #1 [1] [To report: #1] > X [1] #1 [1] #1 Introduction Recent vision-language-action (VLA) models have achieved strong performance on robot manipulation, particularly for the tasks that can be completed within a local tabletop brohan2023rt2,black2024pi0,black2025pi05,wen2025dexvla . Agentic systems further extend these capabilities to long-horizon mobile manipulation, through high-level planning, execution feedback, and tool use ichter2023saycan,zhang2026harnessvla,fu2026capx . Yet mobile manipulation exposes a striking gap between solving individual subtasks and reliably composing them over time. Unlike tabletop manipulation, a mobile robot is required to move across workspaces while maintaining task progress, and every movement changes the viewpoint and base configuration from which the next manipulation is executed yenamandra2023homerobot,fu2024mobilealoha,liu2024okrobot,wu2025momanipvla . As a result, strong local manipulation do not necessarily translate into reliable long-horizon mobile manipulation. The gap is surprisingly large. As shown in Figure~ fig:figure1 , a pretrained subtask VLA achieves 80 success rate on atomic manipulation tasks, yet the corresponding agentic baseline achieves only 19 on long-horizon mobile manipulation tasks. This discrepancy suggests that the central challenge is not simply whether the robot knows how to manipulate, but whether it can reliably carry a manipulation skill through the sequence of decisions and physical states required by mobile manipulation tasks. Specifically, a long-horizon task can fail even before manipulation begins: the planner may select the wrong target or lose track of task progress; navigation may reach the correct workspace but leave the robot in an unusable base pose; and even from a seemingly appropriate configuration, small errors in localization or end-effector alignment can derail the final interaction~ yenamandra2023homerobot,liu2024okrobot,huang2023voxposer . In this sense, what reliable mobile manipulation requires is not simply making a local skill stronger, but identifying where the execution pipeline breaks down. This leads to a fundamental question: We answer this question by cracking the failure structure of mobile manipulation. Starting from a pretrained VLA that already performs individual tabletop subtasks well, we systematically analyze its failures when these subtasks are composed together. Our analysis reveals three dominant failure regimes that form a natural progression through the execution: task planning, navigation and base positioning, and local manipulation. Planning errors prevent the robot from pursuing the correct subtask, while navigation errors prevent it from reaching an executable configuration. And manipulation errors remain after the robot has successfully reached the intended workspace. This diagnosis motivates a simple but powerful principle: intervene where the current system breaks, rather than uniformly increasing the capability of the underlying policy. Guided by this principle, we develop a failure-guided agentic framework that progressively adds targeted interventions around a fixed subtask VLA. For planning, in-context guidance from video demonstrations provides explicit task procedures~ zhong2023procedure,wang2023mimicplay , while adaptive visual memory retains what has already been accomplished and what remains to complete~ yoneda2024statler,sridhar2026memer . For navigation, an accessibility check evaluates whether the current robot configuration is suitable for the upcoming manipulation, followed by base adjustment when the approach is geometrically inadequate. Finally, for local execution, end-effector adjustment refines the interaction pose to compensate for residual spatial misalignment. These components are not independent add-ons: each is directly motivated by a diagnosed failure mode, transforming failure analysis into targeted agentic intervention. We evaluate the resulting agentic system on all mobile manipulation composite tasks in RoboCasa365 nasiriany2026robocasa365 . Despite 80 success rates on atomic tasks, the agentic baseline achieves only 19 task success in the long-horizon tasks. Progressively introducing the proposed interventions raises success rate to 47 . This remarkable gain generalizes to held-out episode seeds, improving baseline from 18 to 49 success rate. The same design also improves performance beyond RoboCasa365, raising the task success rate from 14 to 37 on five BEHAVIOR-1K tasks li2023behavior and from 5/20 to 13/20 on two real-robot tasks. Taken together, these results suggest a different way to approach long-horizon mobile manipulation. Rather than treating the robot as a monolithic policy whose capability must be scaled uniformly, we view it as an agentic system whose reliability can be improved by diagnosing bottleneck and intervening it precisely. Our contributions are summarized as follows: A systematic failure diagnosis of mobile manipulation. We analyze the gap between strong subtask-level manipulation and long-horizon mobile manipulation, identifying three dominant failure regimes: task planning, navigation and base positioning, and local manipulation. The analysis turns overall success gap into a concrete, stage-wise failure structure. A failure-guided agentic intervention framework. Based on the diagnosed bottlenecks, we introduce targeted interventions around a fixed subtask VLA, including demonstration-based planning guidance, adaptive visual memory, accessibility-aware base adjustment, and local end-effector adjustment. Agentic intervention consistently improves the performance of mobile manipulation. The proposed interventions improve the success rate from 19.0 to 47.0 on RoboCasa365. Our experiments further demonstrate consistent gains on held-out RoboCasa365 episodes, BEHAVIOR-1K tasks, and a real dual-arm mobile manipulator. Related Work Mobile Manipulation Systems and Policies Mobile manipulation requires coordinating base motion and manipulation over long-horizon tasks. Existing approaches span modular systems that separate perception, navigation, and manipulation~ yenamandra2023homerobot,liu2024okrobot , and learned policies that couple mobility and manipulation through teleoperated demonstrations, scene representations, whole-body control, or trajectory models~ fu2024mobilealoha,uppal2024spin,qiu2024geff,yan2024m2diffuser,sundaresan2025homer . With larger robot datasets and pretrained models~ ye2026data , generalist policies have scaled toward multi-task and cross-embodiment control~ brohan2022rt1,openx2023rtx,ghosh2024octo,liu2024rdt1b,li2024robovlms . Vision-language-action models further extend this paradigm to general robot control~ brohan2023rt2,black2024pi0,black2025pi05,wen2025dexvla,gemini2025robotics,nvidia2025grootn1,nvidia2025grootn15,nvidia2025grootn16,zheng2025xvla,wu2026lingbotvla,yu2026walloss,xiaomi2026robotics1,yuan2026qwenrobotmanip,kim2026rldx1 , while recent work targets mobile manipulation through fixed-base VLA transfer, whole-body action prediction, spatially enriched observations, and action-conditioned world models~ wu2025momanipvla,tu2026sgvla,yang2026panovla,kim2026cosmospolicy,yuan2026fastwam,chen2026abotm05,ma2026decowam . System-level approaches additionally incorporate structured planning, manipulation-aware base positioning, and recovery~ li2026momastage,lim2026anchorvla . Our focus is complementary: we study how failures are distributed across task planning, navigation and base positioning, and local manipulation in an agentic system, and how the dominant bottlenecks can be addressed by agentic intervention. Robot Failure Diagnosis and Recovery Task success rate alone provides limited information about why a robot fails. Recent benchmarks evaluate policies along fine-grained capability and failure dimensions~ gao2026ebench,yu2026so101failure , while diagnosis methods use multimodal execution traces or collected failure data to identify failure causes and generate corrective feedback~ liu2023reflect,duan2025aha,lin2025failsafe,lu2025robofac,zeng2026vifailback . Other methods integrate failure handling directly into execution through VLM supervisors, failure detectors, recovery policies, or world-model-based verification~ chen2024failure_recovery_vlm,yang2026fpcvla,zhao2026flare,luo2026fdec,seligmann2026vlafail,liu2026checkvla,zhang2026robustexecution . Rather than focusing on failure detection or recovery itself, we analyze where failures arise in an agentic mobile manipulation system, use this diagnosis to guide interventions, and track how the remaining failure distribution shifts as the system improves. Agentic Robots, Demonstrations, and Memory Language and vision-language models have been widely used for robot task planning, semantic grounding, and closed-loop execution~ ichter2023saycan,huang2023innermonologue,wang2025karma,driess2023palme,huang2023voxposer,rana2023sayplan,chen2024autotamp,sun2026dadu . Programmatic and coding-agent-based systems further compose perception, planning, and control tools through executable programs, iterative feedback, debugging, and skill refinement~ liang2023code,singh2023progprompt,huang2023instruct2act,fu2026capx,lu2026aspire,xiao2026enpire,zhang2026harnessvla , with recent work also exploring tighter integration between VLAs, external tools, and specialized robot policies~ lei2026towards,shi2026memoryvla . Video demonstrations can provide task specifications or procedure planning for long-horizon manipulation~ zhong2023procedure,wang2023mimicplay,jain2024vid2robot,wake2023gpt4vrobot , while memory and reusable skills help agents retain task progress and reuse prior experience~ yoneda2024statler,zhang2026harnessvla,shi2026memoryvla,sridhar2026memer,shah2026halo . In our agentic framework, video-based demonstrations are leveraged to build a skill library for task planning, while visual memory is maintained for long-horizon tasks. They serve as the targeted interventions on top of a fixed subtask VLA. Failure Diagnosis of Agentic Mobile Manipulation sec:diagnosis We analyze where the agentic baseline fails during long-horizon mobile manipulation. We first describe the evaluation tasks and baselines, then define the failure attribution procedure and summarize the main failure patterns. Diagnostic Setting sec:diagnostic_setting Benchmark and tasks. We study all 20 composite tasks in RoboCasa365~ nasiriany2026robocasa365 that require mobile manipulation. These tasks contain 2--15 subtasks and require the robot to move between workspaces while performing object transport, pick-and-place, and articulated-object interaction. Additional task details are provided in Appendix~ app:task-set . Baseline. Our baseline follows a hierarchical agentic design adapted from Harness VLA~ zhang2026harnessvla . A high-level planner selects subtask instructions or tools, while a shared subtask VLA executes both navigation and manipulation. The subtask VLA is trained on RoboCasa365 atomic task demonstrations and subtask-level segments from the training split. Implementation and training details are provided in Appendix~ app:vla_training . Preliminary results. While the subtask VLA can achieve 80 success rate on the atomic tasks of RoboCasa365, the agentic system reaches only 19 success rate on the mobile manipulation tasks of RoboCasa365. This gap motivates a key question: where does this agentic system fails? Failure Attribution sec:failure_attribution We evaluate the baseline on the 20 mobile manipulation tasks with five rollouts per task, giving 100 episodes in total. The baseline succeeds in 19 episodes, leaving 81 failed episodes for failure analysis. For each failed episode, we review the recorded actions, observations and simulator's state to identify failed subtasks. We then check whether the agent recovers from each error within the next three replanning attempts. If the affected subtask is completed within this window, we consider the error recovere

title: ForceBench: Benchmarking Force Integration for Robotic Manipulation
summary: Force feedback provides vision-language-action (VLA) policies with physical observations that can guide action selection and execution. However, differences in tasks, demonstrations, and control settings across existing systems hinder reliable comparisons of force integration designs. We introduce ForceBench, a simulation benchmark for evaluating six-axis wrist-force integration under a unified protocol. ForceBench combines eight tasks spanning physical-property inference, resistance-dependent interaction, and contact-rich assembly with 1,600 synchronized demonstrations and task-specific success criteria. We compare one no-force baseline and six force integration designs on a shared $π_{0.5}$ backbone. Prompt Fusion achieves the highest observed mean simulation success of 35.31%, compared with 23.25% for the baseline, and improves success rates across all three task categories. Predictive and temporal gains in simulation concentrate on physical-property inference, while both temporal designs underperform the baseline on assembly. Real-world evaluation of eight systems across five tasks supports the main qualitative trends: Prompt Fusion and Dual-Path Fusion achieve 63.00% mean success, compared with 40.00% for the baseline, but only Prompt Fusion improves every task. These findings support ForceBench's practical value for identifying the benefits and limitations of force integration across manipulation demands. The project page is available at https://forcebench-platform.github.io/.

Vision-Language-Action Models; Robotic Manipulation; Force Sensing; Performance Evaluation and Benchmarking. Introduction sec:intro Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual and language pretraining to robotic action, enabling a shared backbone to learn diverse manipulation skills~ kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,intelligence2025pi05visionlanguageactionmodelopenworld,kim2025oft . Physical interaction additionally requires responding to properties and conditions revealed through action, such as object mass and resistance. Learning-based policies increasingly exploit such feedback, extending diffusion-based visuomotor policies~ chi2023diffusion with compliance- or force-aware learning~ hou2024acp,liu2025factr,xue2025rdp and incorporating force into VLA models. Wrist force provides a six-dimensional observation of these interactions, combining three force and three torque components. These measurements can refine a visually specified motion or inform decisions about conditions that appearance alone does not reveal, supporting both action selection and execution. Existing systems incorporate force into action generation through adaptive fusion of force tokens with vision--language features~ yu2025forcevlaenhancingvlamodels or temporal force encoding with high-frequency feedback~ li2026favla,wang2026phaforce . Force also supports reactive execution through contact prediction that regulates feedback usage~ he2024foar , while joint action--wrench modeling supports reinforcement-learning post-training~ deng2026facet . Other work removes the force sensor at deployment by distilling force knowledge into vision~ zhao2026fdvla . Although standardized data and benchmarks have matured for vision-based manipulation~ fang2026domino,lan2025autobio , differences in tasks, demonstrations, and control settings across force-aware systems hinder direct comparisons. Moreover, aggregate success rates can obscure differences across physical-property inference, resistance-dependent interaction, and contact-rich assembly. We therefore ask how force integration designs can be reliably compared under a unified protocol, and how their benefits vary across manipulation demands. To address this gap, we introduce , a simulation benchmark dedicated to comparing six-axis wrist-force integration in robotic manipulation (Fig.~ fig:pipeline ). combines parameterized physical conditions, 1,600 synchronized multimodal demonstrations, a shared observation--action interface, and evaluation on task instances initialized with shared seeds. Seven tasks vary physical properties and resistance conditions to examine behavior beyond object appearance; a complementary contact-rich assembly task tests geometrically constrained execution. Task-specific success criteria and category-level metrics support comparison across these manipulation demands. We further assess the practical relevance of the benchmark through real-world experiments. Using this framework, we compare a no-force baseline and six force integration designs on a shared backbone, using the same task demonstrations and training protocol. The six designs comprise three current-sample conditioning interfaces---Token Fusion, Prompt Fusion, and Cross-Attention---a Token Fusion variant with auxiliary future-force prediction, and two temporal reference systems, Temporal Prompt and Dual-Path Fusion. ForceVLA provides an external comparison. Prompt Fusion achieves the highest observed mean simulation success of 35.31 , compared with 23.25 for the no-force baseline, and provides the most consistent improvements across task categories. In simulation, predictive supervision and temporal representations provide task-dependent gains that concentrate on physical-property inference, while both temporal designs underperform the baseline on contact-rich assembly. Real-world evaluation of eight systems across five tasks supports the main qualitative trends. Prompt Fusion raises mean success from 40.00 to 63.00 , tying Dual-Path Fusion overall while exceeding the no-force baseline on every task. Both temporal designs achieve higher physical-property inference success than current-sample Prompt Fusion, but lower assembly success than the no-force baseline. These results show that similar overall success rates can conceal different tradeoffs across manipulation demands, supporting 's practical value for comparing force integration designs. Our contributions are threefold: A unified benchmark for force integration. provides eight tasks with parameterized physical conditions, 1,600 synchronized multimodal demonstrations, and shared evaluation with task- and category-level outcomes for six-axis wrist-force integration. A systematic comparative study. We evaluate observation conditioning, auxiliary predictive supervision, and temporal force representations on a shared VLA backbone, characterizing their benefits and limitations across physical-property inference, resistance-dependent interaction, and contact-rich assembly. Real-world evaluation of benchmark findings. We evaluate eight systems across five real-world tasks in 800 trials. The results support the main qualitative trends observed in simulation and reveal task-dependent tradeoffs that overall success rates alone can obscure. Related Work sec:related Force-Aware Policies for Robotic Manipulation. Token-based approaches incorporate force or tactile observations into policy representations~ yu2025forcevlaenhancingvlamodels,huang2025tactilevla . Text-based conditioning includes proprioceptive discretization in ~ intelligence2025pi05visionlanguageactionmodelopenworld and stage-specific force prompts in ForceVLA2~ li2026forcevla2 . ManipForce and FAVLA use cross-attention~ lee2025manipforce,li2026favla , while FoAR regulates visual--force fusion using predicted contact~ he2024foar . TA-VLA and ForceFlow incorporate future torque or force prediction~ zhang2025tavla,forceflow2026 , and MoSS combines sensory streams with cross-modal attention and predictive supervision~ lee2026moss . FAWAM couples action--force prediction with online residual correction~ he2026fawam ; our auxiliary prediction head is used only during training. ForceMimic links force-aware demonstration collection to hybrid force--position imitation learning~ liu2024forcemimic . Recent work extends tactile policies with predictive world models~ lou2026dreamtac , while ContactWorld examines their visuo-tactile representations~ zhang2026contactworld . Benchmarking and Evaluation of Robotic Manipulation. RLBench, Meta-World, CALVIN, and LIBERO provide task suites and evaluation protocols for vision-based manipulation~ james2019rlbenchrobotlearningbenchmark,yu2021metaworldbenchmarkevaluationmultitask,mees2022calvin,liu2023libero . RoboCasa, RoboTwin 2.0, DOMINO, and AutoBio extend coverage to household, bimanual, dynamic, and laboratory settings~ nasiriany2024robocasalargescalesimulationeveryday,chen2025robotwin20scalabledata,fang2026domino,lan2025autobio . SIMPLER studies correspondence between simulated and real-world policy evaluations~ li2024evaluatingrealworldrobotmanipulation , and UniVTAC benchmarks visuo-tactile perception and interaction~ chen2026univtac . ForceBench complements these resources with shared demonstrations and a unified protocol for comparing six-axis wrist-force integration across physical-property inference, resistance-dependent interaction, and contact-rich assembly. ForceBench sec:benchmark ForceBench evaluates six-axis wrist-force integration across physical-property inference, resistance-dependent interaction, and contact-rich assembly. Its workflow combines parameterized task instances, synchronized expert demonstrations, and seeded policy evaluation under a shared observation--action interface (Fig.~ fig:pipeline ). Task-specific decision and completion metrics distinguish physical decisions from subsequent execution. Assets and Physical Mechanisms Built on Isaac Lab / Isaac Sim mittal2023orbit , ForceBench uses a Franka arm with a parallel gripper in tabletop and household environments. Assets define geometry and articulation, while task parameters specify mass, center of mass, resistance, and initial poses. Resistance mechanisms couple force and moment profiles to articulation state, producing direction-dependent resistance, rotational transitions, and axial engagement before turning. A shared task interface provides seeded initialization, interaction dynamics, expert state access, and outcome evaluation. Task Design ForceBench comprises eight tasks across physical-property inference, resistance-dependent interaction, and contact-rich assembly (Fig.~ fig:task_overview ). The first two categories vary physical conditions without distinct visual appearances; assembly complements them with thread engagement and constrained rotational insertion. Physical-property inference requires identifying an object property through interaction and selecting the corresponding destination. 2pt 0pt Weight Sort. Visually identical parcels have different masses. The robot lifts each parcel and places it in the black container if light or the blue container if heavy. Success requires correct placement, release, and settling. CoM Sort. Parcels share the same appearance and total mass but have centered or offset centers of mass, producing different rotational loads about the grasp. The robot holds each parcel steadily, then places centered parcels on the conveyor and imbalanced parcels in the basket, with release and settling required. Resistance-dependent interaction requires adapting direction, engagement, or stopping to the load encountered during motion. 2pt 0pt Faucet Turn. The robot opens a valve against resistance that peaks and then drops, with the peak angle varying across instances. It must stop in the target region just beyond the transition, release, and withdraw, leaving the water on and the handle stationary. Faucet Direction. The low-resistance direction and peak location vary across instances. Success requires crossing the resistance peak in the lower-resistance direction and leaving the valve open, released, clear of the gripper, and stationary. title: PolyMorph: Learning Locomotion Policy for Cross-Embodiment Adaptation
summary: Reinforcement learning has enabled robust locomotion for legged robots, but learned policies are typically tied to a specific robot morphology and require additional engineering when the number of legs, actuators, or mechanical properties change. We present PolyMorph, a morphology-conditioned framework that learns a single locomotion policy for heterogeneous legged robots. PolyMorph converts each robot's URDF into joint-link modules and combines a recurrent encoder, graph-based Transformer, and per-joint decoder to generate actions across variable leg counts and joint configurations. To improve training stability, PolyMorph uses morphology-normalized rewards, adaptive robot sampling, and URDF-derived PD-gain initialization. We evaluate PolyMorph in simulation across bipedal, tripedal, and quadrupedal robots, including unseen morphology variants and platforms, and deploy the policy on real quadruped platforms operated in multiple configurations. The results show that a single PolyMorph policy generalizes across diverse robot morphologies without per-robot policy retraining.
full_text: PolyMorph: Learning Locomotion Policy for Cross-Embodiment Adaptation Hyunsik Oh, Seunghun Jeon, Donghoon Youm, Jungwoo Hur, Hyeongjun Kim, \ Hyun Lee, Moonkyu Jung, and Jemin Hwangbo Reinforcement learning has enabled robust locomotion for legged robots, but learned policies are typically tied to a specific robot morphology and require additional engineering when the number of legs, actuators, or mechanical properties change. We present PolyMorph, a morphology-conditioned framework that learns a single locomotion policy for heterogeneous legged robots. PolyMorph converts each robot's URDF into joint-link modules and combines a recurrent encoder, graph-based Transformer, and per-joint decoder to generate actions across variable leg counts and joint configurations. To improve training stability, PolyMorph uses morphology-normalized rewards, adaptive robot sampling, and URDF-derived PD-gain initialization. We evaluate PolyMorph in simulation across bipedal, tripedal, and quadrupedal robots, including unseen morphology variants and platforms, and deploy the policy on real quadruped platforms operated in multiple configurations. The results show that a single PolyMorph policy generalizes across diverse robot morphologies without per-robot policy retraining. Reinforcement Learning, Multi-Embodiment Learning, Legged Robots Introduction n the field of robotics, significant progress has been made through various control methodologies, including Model Predictive Control (MPC)~ youm2023imitating and learning-based approaches such as imitation learning (IL)~ peng2018deepmimic, zhao2023learning and reinforcement learning (RL)~ hwangbo2019learning, schulman2017proximal . Among these, model-free RL has become a powerful tool for legged robot control because it directly optimizes policies from environment interactions without requiring explicit dynamics models. This makes RL particularly effective for complex and underactuated systems, enabling robust locomotion over challenging terrains such as rough slopes, stairs, and deformable terrain~ miki2022learning, kumar2021rma . Most existing studies on legged locomotion focus on enabling a single platform to perform a specific task~ kim2025high, ma2025learning . However, policies trained for one robot often fail to transfer to another due to differences in morphology, including degrees of freedom, link masses, inertias, and kinematic configurations. Adapting a policy to a new robot typically requires redesigning the environment, observations, action space, and reward functions, which demands substantial engineering effort. This motivates the development of general controllers that can operate across diverse legged robots. In this work, we address the following question: Can we train a single locomotion policy that operates across legged robots with diverse morphologies, including different numbers of legs and actuators, and deploy it on real hardware without per-robot retraining? We argue that such a controller must not only observe the robot's current state but also reason about its morphology, and that achieving this in practice requires addressing training-level imbalances that arise when robots with very different reward magnitudes and learning difficulties are trained together. To this end, we propose PolyMorph, a cross-embodiment locomotion framework with a URDF-conditioned policy interface. As shown in Fig.~ fig:overall_description , the same policy is deployed across diverse legged morphologies on various rough terrains in both simulation and the real world. Each robot is represented as a sequence of joint-link modules parsed from its URDF, and padding with valid-action masking allows the same policy to handle variable leg counts, actuator numbers, and joint configurations without redesigning the action interface. The policy combines a recurrent state encoder that summarizes proprioceptive history, a Transformer that conditions on URDF-derived graph structure, and per-joint decoder heads that generate actions only for actuated joints. A unified locomotion policy across heterogeneous morphologies can shorten the robot design-test cycle by allowing new designs or modified configurations to be evaluated without retraining a separate controller for each platform, which is particularly useful for rapid robot design workflows~ lee2024robotsketch, belmonte2022meta . It also enables policy reuse across heterogeneous robot platforms and exposes the policy to broader morphology and dynamics variations. Beyond designing a policy that can process robots with different kinematic structures, we observe that jointly optimizing across morphologies introduces training-level obstacles: reward magnitudes can scale with the number of joints and legs, biasing optimization toward certain morphologies; easy-to-learn robots can dominate uniform sampling and reduce the learning signal for harder morphologies such as bipeds; and manually tuned PD gains reintroduce per-platform engineering effort. Complementary to prior multi-embodiment methods that emphasize morphology-conditioned policy architectures, PolyMorph addresses these training-level obstacles through morphology-normalized rewards, adaptive robot sampling, URDF-derived PD-gain initialization, together with curriculum learning and domain randomization for robust training. The same policy parameters are shared across all robots, and only morphology-dependent inputs are derived from each robot's URDF. In summary, the main contributions of this work are as follows: We identify and address training-level obstacles in cross-embodiment optimization, including reward-scale mismatch, sampling imbalance between easy and hard robots, and per-platform gain tuning, through morphology-normalized rewards, adaptive robot sampling, and URDF-derived PD-gain initialization. We adapt joint-link tokenization, embodiment-masked attention, recurrent proprioceptive encoding, and per-joint action decoding into a URDF-conditioned policy interface that handles variable leg counts, actuator numbers, and kinematic structures with shared parameters. We validate PolyMorph on heterogeneous legged robots in simulation and demonstrate cross-morphology hardware deployment on two real quadruped platforms operated in quadrupedal, tripedal, and bipedal configurations, with additional ablations and comparisons against multi-embodiment baselines. Related Work sect:related_work Transformer architectures for robot control In legged robot control, Transformer-based policies have been used to process observation histories or sensory inputs for locomotion~ radosavovic2024real . Beyond such temporal use, Transformers also model relationships among input tokens through self-attention~ vaswani2017attention , making them suitable for control problems where multiple body parts must interact. This spatial formulation is particularly attractive for multi-embodiment locomotion, since variable-length token sequences naturally correspond to robots with different numbers of joints. However, standard Transformers do not explicitly encode the physical structure of the robot and must infer morphology-dependent relationships only from data, which can be sample-inefficient when training across heterogeneous robots. Body Transformer~ sferrazza2024body uses the robot's adjacency graph as an attention mask to inject structural bias for a fixed morphology. PolyMorph adopts this structural prior in a policy shared across heterogeneous morphologies, where URDF-derived morphology inputs and attention masks vary across embodiments and are combined with recurrent state encoding. Cross-embodied policy learning Cross-embodied policy learning aims to train a single policy that can operate across different robot embodiments. In legged robotics, Metamorph~ gupta2022metamorph uses a Transformer to control modular robots but is evaluated only in simulation. GenLoco~ feng2023genloco achieves real-world transfer through morphology randomization but focuses on quadrupeds. URMA~ bohlinger2024one learns multi-embodiment locomotion across quadrupedal and bipedal robots with an attention-based encoder--decoder. Graph neural networks~ wang2018nervenet encode robot morphology as graphs. GCNT~ luo2025gcnt further combines graph-based morphology encoding with Transformer communication to learn controllers across different robot structures. LocoFormer~ liu2025locoformer takes a different approach, combining large-scale procedural training with long-context adaptation to generalize locomotion across unseen embodiments. While these works have advanced policy architectures, the training-level aspects of jointly optimizing heterogeneous legged robots have received less attention. PolyMorph also targets them directly. Beyond locomotion, Chen et al.~ chen2026cross and Gupta et al.~ gupta2026demonstrate study cross-robot transfer from demonstrations through intention-aligned representations and kinematics-aware policy synthesis, respectively. Method sect:framework We propose PolyMorph, a morphology-aware locomotion learning framework that controls legged robots with different morphologies using a single policy. For each robot , we formulate the control problem as a Markov decision process (MDP) . Given a set of robots with different morphologies, our objective is to learn one policy that maximizes the average expected return: We optimize the policy using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)~ schulman2017proximal . As shown in Fig.~ fig:learning_framework , PolyMorph consists of three components: a state context encoder, a morphology-aware Transformer, and a decoder. The state context encoder processes general proprioceptive observations over time. The morphology-aware Transformer represents each robot as a sequence of joint-link modules and extracts morphology-conditioned embeddings using graph-based attention. The decoder combines the state embedding, morphology embedding, and command input to generate target actions for each actuated joint. State Context Encoder The state context encoder uses a shared GRU to summarize proprioceptive history that is important for locomotion across robot morphologies. title: E2DRL: End-to-End Differentiable Reinforcement Learning for 3D Obstacle Avoidance in Quadruped Robots
summary: Differentiable reinforcement learning shows strong promise for robot policy learning, but its application to legged locomotion has remained limited to blind walking or simulated 2D tasks. Extending it to end-to-end visual obstacle avoidance is challenging because hard collision constraints and early termination upon contact corrupt first-order gradients, trapping optimizers in local minima. We present E2DRL, which addresses this with a soft differentiable obstacle-interaction formulation: penetration penalties across multiple body keypoints with velocity-conditioned stop-gradient shaping to provide the first-order training signals for 3D obstacle avoidance. To realize a deployable perception-control system, a privileged teacher trained via Soft Analytic Policy Optimization (SAPO) in a differentiable simulator is distilled into a recurrent depth-based student via DAgger, then blended with a base locomotion policy using a terrain-aware gating module for deployment. In simulation, E2DRL achieves higher sample efficiency than PPO and demonstrates superior velocity-tracking performance and 3D obstacle-avoidance capability compared with both PPO and Duality-based DCBF NMPC. We present the first sim-to-real validation of end-to-end differentiable RL for 3D obstacle avoidance on a Unitree Go2 in static and dynamic environments.

INTRODUCTION Quadruped robots have shown strong potential for operation in human-centered environments tranzatto2022cerberus,mattamala2022efficient , where obstacle avoidance often extends beyond planar navigation. In cluttered scenes, a velocity-commanded robot may encounter obstacles with diverse heights and geometries, such as tables, shelves, chairs, and suspended boards. To navigate such environments effectively, the robot must not only track commanded motion, but also adapt its body posture and locomotion strategy in three dimensions, e.g., bypassing obstacles laterally or lowering its body to crawl underneath them. Enabling such command-conditioned 3D obstacle avoidance is therefore important for the practical deployment of quadruped robots miki2024learning,cheng2024extreme,margolis2023walk,sun2020path,liao2023walking . Recent studies have explored quadrupedal locomotion in complex environments through both optimization-based and learning-based approaches liao2023walking,rudin2022learning,lee2020learning,miki2022learning,kumar2021rma,miki2024learning,cheng2024extreme . Traditional optimization-based methods, such as Duality-based DCBF NMPC liao2023walking , incorporate safety constraints into online trajectory optimization for safe quadrupedal locomotion in narrow spaces. However, their reliance on online constrained optimization and simplified model representations makes it difficult to simultaneously avoid challenging obstacles while maintaining responsive velocity tracking. Model-free reinforcement learning offers an alternative, but typically treats the simulator as a black box and estimates gradients only from sampled returns suh2022differentiable , requiring large amounts of interaction data in contact-rich obstacle-avoidance tasks. Differentiable simulation has recently emerged as a promising alternative for more efficient policy learning suh2022differentiable,freeman2021brax,howell2022dojo . Prior work has also shown that differentiable physics can improve motion performance. Notably, Zhang et al. zhang2024back demonstrate high-speed drone navigation through complex environments with both static and dynamic obstacles, achieving substantial gains in speed and success rate. In addition, Schwarke et al. schwarke2024learning achieve robust proprioceptive quadrupedal locomotion by proposing a novel differentiable contact model, enabling seamless sim-to-real transfer with remarkable sample efficiency. These results suggest that differentiable physics can improve both optimization efficiency and control performance. We therefore seek to bring these advantages to quadrupedal 3D obstacle avoidance. Nevertheless, applying differentiable RL to quadrupedal obstacle avoidance remains challenging. Intermittent contacts, hard collision constraints, and early termination induce severe non-smoothness and gradient discontinuities. Consequently, first-order optimization methods become highly susceptible to suboptimal local minima. Existing differentiable RL methods for quadruped robots mainly address blind locomotion or simulated 2D tasks song2024learning,luo2025residual , leaving the integration of differentiable learning into deployable visuomotor policies for 3D obstacle avoidance unexplored. In this setting, the central challenge is not simply to add an obstacle-avoidance cost, but to design a training surrogate that keeps obstacle interactions informative for first-order policy optimization while discouraging nonphysical penetration. In this letter, we present E2DRL, an end-to-end differentiable reinforcement learning framework for quadrupedal 3D obstacle avoidance under velocity commands. The framework trains a privileged teacher with SAPO in a differentiable simulator, distills it into a recurrent depth-based student via DAgger, and blends the student with a proprioception-based locomotion policy through a terrain-aware gating module. A key innovation of this work is a soft differentiable obstacle-interaction formulation, used as a training-time surrogate rather than a physical contact model, which allows simulated penetration and applies differentiable multi-keypoint penalties with velocity-conditioned stop-gradient shaping. The gating module preserves nominal locomotion in free space while triggering active avoidance near obstacles. Experiments show that E2DRL achieves higher sample efficiency than PPO during training, while outperforming both Duality-based DCBF NMPC and PPO in velocity tracking and traversal of challenging 3D obstacles. The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: We propose a soft differentiable obstacle-interaction formulation for contact-rich quadrupedal obstacle avoidance, which addresses the local-optima and gradient-truncation issues of hard obstacle formulations by penalizing continuous penetration of multiple body keypoints with velocity-conditioned stop-gradient shaping, enabling stable first-order optimization across overhanging and ground obstacle configurations. We propose a deployment-oriented differentiable end-to-end obstacle avoidance framework that transfers differentiable RL skills for crawling and bypassing to a recurrent depth-based student policy. Furthermore, to improve velocity tracking in obstacle-free regions, we introduce a gating module that seamlessly integrates the student policy with a nominal locomotion policy. We present the first sim-to-real validation of an end-to-end differentiable RL policy for overhanging and ground obstacle avoidance on a physical quadruped robot in both static and dynamic real-world environments. Related Work Learning-based Quadrupedal Locomotion Deep reinforcement learning has significantly improved quadrupedal locomotion over diverse terrains. Rudin et al. rudin2022learning demonstrated that basic walking skills can be acquired within minutes through massively parallel training, while Hwangbo et al. hwangbo2019learning showed that reinforcement learning can produce agile motor skills such as rapid direction changes and recovery from external disturbances. Building on these advances, recent studies have extended quadrupedal locomotion to more challenging navigation scenarios involving obstacles and confined spaces. Miki et al. miki2022learning enabled locomotion in the wild. He et al. he2024agile achieved high-speed locomotion with obstacle avoidance in cluttered environments. Zhuang et al. zhuang2023robot demonstrated parkour-style behaviors that require coordinated whole-body control. In contrast to these prior works, our work focuses on end-to-end 3D obstacle avoidance with velocity-command tracking. Differentiable Reinforcement Learning Gradient-based policy optimization through differentiable simulation enables analytical policy gradients with lower variance than sampling-based methods~ mozer2013focused,suh2022differentiable,freeman2021brax,howell2022dojo . However, discontinuous contact dynamics create non-smooth optimization landscapes that cause BPTT-based methods to converge to poor local optima. Xu et al.~ xu2022accelerated proposed SHAC to mitigate this via short-horizon differentiable rollouts combined with an actor-critic baseline, and Xing et al.~ xing2024stabilizing further introduced SAPO with maximum entropy regularization~ haarnoja2018soft to smooth the landscape. Although existing differentiable methods have demonstrated success in robust blind locomotion and simulated 2D tasks song2024learning,schwarke2024learning,luo2025residual , the application to 3D obstacle avoidance remains unexplored. This is primarily due to the highly non-smooth optimization landscapes induced by hard constraints, as well as gradient truncation resulting from early termination. We bridge this gap by extending SAPO with a soft differentiable obstacle-interaction formulation. PROBLEM FORMULATION We address vision-based 3D obstacle avoidance for a quadruped robot given desired velocity commands. The robot must traverse environments with overhanging obstacles that require body-height adaptation and lateral ground obstacles that require bypassing. Observation Space: The robot observation comprises two modalities. The proprioceptive state includes base angular velocity, projected gravity vector, base velocity commands, joint positions, joint velocities, and last actions. The privileged exteroceptive state includes base position, base linear velocity, Euler angles, obstacle configurations and geometric obstacle parameters (clearance height, lateral width and longitudinal depth). During training, the full privileged observation is available to the teacher policy. For deployment, the privileged exteroceptive component is replaced by a depth image from the onboard camera, yielding the student observation . Action Space: The action specifies target joint positions for the 12 actuated joints, tracked by PD controllers with gains and . Method System Overview Our approach is a two-stage learning framework for 3D obstacle avoidance using only onboard perception, as illustrated in Fig.~ fig:overview . It bridges the sample-efficient First-Order Policy Gradient (FoPG) method with vision-based real-world deployment. In the first stage (Sec.~ sec:teacher ), a privileged teacher policy is trained in a differentiable simulator via Soft Analytic Policy Optimization (SAPO). To improve optimization robustness in 3D obstacle avoidance scenarios, we incorporate a stable frictional contact model and introduce a soft differentiable obstacle-interaction formulation. In the second stage (Sec.~ sec:student ), DAgger~ ross2011reduction distills the teacher into a vision-based student policy that relies solely on onboard depth images and proprioception. For deployment (Sec.~ sec:deployment ), a terrain-aware gating module dynamically interpolates between the original proprioceptive locomotion policy and the obstacle-avoidance student policy. The gating module is trained separately and is also used during distillation data collection. This design preserves the student's end-to-end observation-to-action mapping while integrating it with the locomotion policy to preserve nominal locomotion capability. title: Accelerating VLA Inference with Perturbation Informed Execution
summary: Action-chunking vision-language-action (VLA) models predict sequences of future robot actions. Under fixed-horizon execution, the robot executes a fixedlength prefix of each predicted chunk before invoking the policy again, leaving the remaining predictions unused. For a given number of executed actions, short execution horizons require more policy calls. Extending the execution horizon amortizes policy inference cost over more actions. However, uniformly applying long horizons across episodes can limit opportunities for precise corrections. To address this limitation, we propose PICES (Perturbation-Informed Chunk and Execution Horizon Selection), a training-free method that jointly selects an action chunk and the number of actions executed before the next policy call. Within a single policy call, the action expert generates a batch of action chunks from multiple initial noise samples and their locally perturbed counterparts, using the same conditioning features across all samples. PICES exploits differences between corresponding actions in each nominal chunk and its counterpart to determine candidate-specific execution horizons and select a nominal chunk for execution. Experiments on simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that PICES achieves speedup by up to 2.3x in wall-clock policy inference time on Jetson Orin and Thor relative to fixed horizon baselines while improving the success rate.
