Within a single policy call, the action expert generates a batch of action chunks from multiple initial noise samples and their locally perturbed counterparts, using the same conditioning features across all samples. PICES exploits differences between corresponding actions in each nominal chunk and its counterpart to determine candidate-specific execution horizons and select a nominal chunk for execution. Experiments on simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that PICES achieves speedup by up to 2.3 in wall-clock policy inference time on Jetson Orin and Thor relative to fixed-horizon baselines while improving the success rate. The code is available at : Introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models generate robot actions conditioned on visual observations, proprioceptive states, and language instructions~ brohan2022rt, kim2024openvla, kim2025fine . Recent VLA architectures pair a vision-language backbone with a flow-matching action expert that transforms initial noise into an action chunk, a sequence of future actions~ bjorck2025gr00t, black2024pi_0, intelligence2025pi_, shukor2025smolvla . In conventional action chunking, the robot executes fixed-length actions of each predicted chunk before replanning as illustrated in Figure~ fig:Figure1 (a). The number of actions executed before update observations defines the execution horizon~ black2026real . The cumulative policy invocations across policy rollout makes task-completion time dependent on both per-call latency and the number of policy calls~ zhou2026characterizing, jing2025mixture . At comparable success rates, shorter task-completion times enable a robot to complete more tasks within a fixed time budget~ shukor2025smolvla, huang2025dadu . This makes cumulative inference latency as an important consideration for onboard VLA deployment, where edge platforms such as NVIDIA Jetson Orin and Thor operate under compute and memory-bandwidth constraints~ yang2026jetson,jiang2026fast . For example, GR00T N1.7 requires 80.4ms per policy call on Jetson Orin and 150.9 ms on Jetson Thor~ FluxVLA2026,bjorck2025gr00t , whereas observation acquisition and actuation can operate up to 60Hz and 1kHz, respectively~ jiang2026fast, ma2025running, zhang2020modular . In observation-inference-execution pipeline, reducing the number of policy calls lowers cumulative inference latency and shorten task-completion time~ jing2025mixture . For action chunking policies, executing only fraction of each predicted action chunk incurs inefficiency. However, applying long horizons uniformly across task phases delays the incorporation of updated observations when precise control is required. This motivates adapting execution horizons to reduce repeated inference while preserving task success. Prior works have explored diverse action-chunk execution strategies to balance temporal consistency and reactivity, including temporal ensembling, adaptive chunk updates, and guided candidate selection~ zhao2023learning,so2026improving,liu2025bidirectional . AAC estimates action entropy of action candidates to decide a shared exceuction horizon~ liang2026adaptive . AutoHorizon derives the execution horizon from self-attention within a predicted chunk~ wang2026vla . selects a representative trajectory from multiple candidates and then performs additional flow-matching verification to determine execution horizon~ zhao2026dynamic . Our objective is to reduce wall-clock inference time while achieving comparable success rate by jointly selecting an action chunk and its execution horizon. This raises our key question: Given a bounded set of candidate action chunks generated in a single policy call, how can we select the action chunk and execution horizon to reduce the wall-clock inference time? We propose PICES (Perturbation-Informed Chunk and Execution Horizon Selection), a training-free inference time method that jointly selects an action chunk and its execution horizon. For each initial-noise sample, PICES constructs a locally perturbed counterpart by adding a small Gaussian perturbation. A single batched policy call generates the corresponding nominal and auxiliary action chunks using shared conditioning features encoded by the vision-language-model (VLM). Based on the arithmetic intensity analysis of action expert and hardware ridge-point in our motivational analysis, we restrict total batch size to a range with negligible incremental latency. For each candidate, the stepwise differences between nominal and auxiliary action chunks yield a local sensitivity value. We exploit these values to retain candidates with low initial sensitivity and estimate execution horizon for each candidate. From the candidate pool, PICES selects and executes the nominal chunk with the longest execution horizon. Figure~ fig:Figure1 (b) illustrates the reduction in policy calls: two calls execute eight actions, compared with four calls with fixed horizon execution. Savings from fewer policy calls outweigh the additional cost of candidate generation, reducing cumulative inference time as shown in Figure~ fig:Figure1 (c). Our key contributions are as follows: Through an open-loop study, we show that oracle selection from multiple action chunks can yield lower reference-action error over a longer execution horizon than a single-candidate, short-horizon baseline. We also characterize the cost of generating candidates in a batch. We propose PICES, a training-free method to reduce cumulative wall-clock inference time. PICES uses sensitivity to initial-noise perturbations to guide the joint selection of an action chunk and its execution horizon. We evaluate PICES across multiple VLA models in simulation and on real-world robot tasks. Compared with fixed-horizon baselines, PICES reduces policy calls by 25.4--60.3 and achieves 1.2--2.3 speedups in wall-clock inference time on Jetson Orin and Thor, while maintaining higher success rates. Related Work Action Chunking in VLA Models. Recent VLAs such as CogACT, , and GR00T series execute only a fixed-length horizon of each predicted chunk~ li2024cogact,black2024pi_0,bjorck2025gr00t . Executing a long fixed-length actions reduces policy calls but limits the incorporation of new observations, motivating adaptive execution horizons~ liang2026adaptive, wang2026vla, chen2026dynamic (see Appendix~ app:related_action_chunk for full discussion). In contrast, our method instead estimates a horizon for each candidate and uses the estimated execution length to choose the reliable action chunk to shorten cumulative inference time without training. Acceleration for VLA Models. Efficient VLA inference seeks to reduce task completion time using various methods. To reduce inference overhead, previous work exploits redundancy in visual inputs and model computation through token pruning, channel pruning, and model scheduling~ chen2024image, shukor2025smolvla, xu2026vla, feng2026see (see Appendix ~ app:related_accel for full discussion). Our method is orthogonal to token pruning, which reduces computation within individual policy calls. PICES examines how candidate-specific horizon selection can reduce policy calls, while explicitly accounting for the additional cost of generating and assessing multiple action candidates. Test-Time Scaling for VLA Policies. Test-time scaling can improve the performance of stochastic generative policies by allocating additional inference compute to generate and evaluate multiple candidates. In diffusion-based reinforcement learning, IDQL draws multiple actions from a diffusion-parameterized behavior policy and resamples them using critic-derived importance weights~ hansen2023idql . Extending this generate-and-select paradigm to VLAs, RoboMonkey constructs an action proposal distribution using policy samples, Gaussian perturbations and majority voting, followed by a learned verifier to select an action~ kwok2025robomonkey . TACO samples multiple complete action chunks and executes the candidate with the highest pseudo-count estimated by an auxiliary model~ yang2025steering . Our selection criterion is the estimated length of the executable prefix for each candidate without auxiliary module and training. Proposed Approach Background Input Condition and Action Chunk. To limit the latency overhead of this additional sampling, we explore affordable batch size during chunk generation. This motivates two questions: (1) Can multiple sampled chunks provide a lower reference-action error at a longer fixed execution horizon candidate than a single sampled chunk? (2) Under consideration of action expert's arithmetic intensity, how many candidate chunks can we expect to be generated in a batch with modest additional latency? title: ACRO: Actor-Critic Rollout Orchestration
summary: Executing a vision-language-action (VLA) policy involves deciding when to continue an attempt and when to intervene to improve its chances of success. We introduce ACRO, an Actor--Critic rollout orchestration layer that makes these decisions for a fixed VLA. ACRO seeks interventions that offer a more promising continuation, are physically feasible, and leave sufficient time to complete the task. A Critic learned from policy rollouts estimates success prospects to decide when to intervene and select a re-entry target along the executed trajectory. Trajectory Retraction shortcuts the visited path to return the robot to that target, where the same VLA resumes execution from a fresh observation. We evaluate ACRO with GR00T N1.7 and $π_{0.5}$ across SimplerEnv, RoboCasa, and real-robot manipulation. Under the same physical execution budget, including all return motion, ACRO improves success by 10.4, 7.3, and 21.7 percentage points, respectively. It also completes additional tasks as the execution budget grows. These results show that controlling when and where a policy resumes can turn its existing capabilities into more successful task executions. Project page: https://junhoo.me/acro

title: One-shot Human Video-Guided Adaptation for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have recently achieved remarkable progress by leveraging large-scale robot datasets and foundation models for general-purpose robot manipulation. However, their ability to rapidly adapt to novel manipulation tasks beyond the training distribution remains limited. Existing approaches often require task-specific robot demonstrations and additional training, which are labor- and compute-intensive, limiting the scalability of VLA adaptation to open-world scenarios. To reduce this dependence on target-task robot data, we propose CapPro, a framework that enables a VLA policy to adapt to previously unseen manipulation tasks using only a single human demonstration video. CapPro consists of two components. First, a phase-aware human video representation module constructs a compact video representation through learned visual token selection and learns task-relevant query representations under phase-caption supervision. Second, a video-conditioned adaptation module jointly incorporates the compact video and query-derived representations into the action-conditioning context of the pretrained VLA policy. % This design introduces task-specific guidance while largely preserving the original VLA action-generation backbone. In this way, the human demonstration provides task-specific execution guidance rather than an embodiment-aligned trajectory to imitate, without requiring target-task robot demonstrations or target-task fine-tuning. Experiments across source and unseen target tasks show that CapPro improves average performance across unseen target groups while maintaining comparable performance on the source tasks. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of human-video guidance for cross-task VLA adaptation.
full_text: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have recently achieved remarkable progress by leveraging large-scale robot datasets and foundation models for general-purpose robot manipulation. However, their ability to rapidly adapt to novel manipulation tasks beyond the training distribution remains limited. Existing approaches often require task-specific robot demonstrations and additional training, which are labor- and compute-intensive, limiting the scalability of VLA adaptation to open-world scenarios. To reduce this dependence on target-task robot data, we propose CapPro, a framework that enables a VLA policy to adapt to previously unseen manipulation tasks using only a single human demonstration video. CapPro consists of two components. First, a phase-aware human video representation module constructs a compact video representation through learned visual token selection and learns task-relevant query representations under phase-caption supervision. Second, a video-conditioned adaptation module jointly incorporates the compact video and query-derived representations into the action-conditioning context of the pretrained VLA policy. In this way, the human demonstration provides task-specific execution guidance rather than an embodiment-aligned trajectory to imitate, without requiring target-task robot demonstrations or target-task fine-tuning. Experiments across source and unseen target tasks show that CapPro improves average performance across unseen target groups while maintaining comparable performance on the source tasks. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of human-video guidance for cross-task VLA adaptation. Introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models have recently emerged as a promising paradigm for developing general-purpose robot manipulation systems by integrating visual perception, language understanding, planning, and action generation~ rt2,openvla,pi0,pi05 . Leveraging large-scale robot datasets and foundation models, recent VLA approaches have demonstrated impressive capabilities across diverse manipulation tasks, including object rearrangement, pick-and-place, stacking, and tool-use tasks~ rt1,openx,octo,droid . These advances establish VLA models as a strong foundation for building versatile robot manipulation policies. Despite these advances, current VLA models still have limited ability to rapidly adapt to manipulation tasks beyond their training distributions~ ricl,controlvla,dynvla . Although large-scale pretraining equips these models with reusable manipulation skills, successful adaptation to a new task often still requires task-specific knowledge of interaction patterns and execution procedures that may not be fully specified by the current observation and language instruction. Existing adaptation methods therefore often rely on additional robot demonstrations and task-specific fine-tuning to provide the required task knowledge~ openvla_oft,foca,ttvla . These procedures introduce substantial data and computational requirements, making it difficult to efficiently extend VLA policies to new manipulation tasks encountered at deployment. Human demonstration videos provide a natural source of task-specific knowledge for adapting VLA policies to new manipulation tasks~ egovla,egomimic,mimicplay,vid2robot . By showing how a person interacts with objects and progresses through a task, they capture visual information about interaction patterns, execution procedures, and task goals that may not be fully conveyed by language instructions alone~ videodex,track2act,orion,gen2act . In addition, such demonstrations can be collected without executing the task on a specific robotic platform, making them easier to obtain for new manipulation tasks~ phantom,robopaint . Using human demonstration videos for VLA adaptation introduces two key challenges. First, human demonstrations contain substantial visual redundancy, while different stages of execution convey different task-relevant information, making it difficult to identify the information that is most useful for guiding robot execution. Second, substantial differences in embodiment, observation perspective, and action space create a substantial gap between human demonstrations and robot execution, making direct behavior transfer difficult~ dexmv,immimic,human2robot . Together, these challenges make it nontrivial to exploit human demonstrations for VLA adaptation. In this paper, we propose CapPro, a one-shot human-video-guided adaptation framework that enables a VLA policy to acquire task-specific execution guidance from a single human demonstration video. CapPro consists of two components. First, a phase-aware human video representation module learns a compact video representation and task-relevant query representations under phase-level supervision, allowing the model to focus on stage-dependent execution information in the demonstration. Second, a video-conditioned adaptation module incorporates these representations into the conditioning context of the pretrained VLA policy, enabling task-specific information from the human demonstration to guide robot action generation without requiring direct human-to-robot behavior transfer. In this way, CapPro uses the human demonstration as task-specific guidance while retaining the original action-generation structure of the base VLA policy. We evaluate CapPro on the RoboTwin benchmark~ robotwin under a one-shot adaptation setting across 26 unseen manipulation tasks organized into three groups with increasing levels of task shift, and further validate its cross-task adaptation capability on real-world manipulation tasks. CapPro improves the average success rate across all unseen target-task groups compared with the pretrained VLA baseline, while maintaining comparable performance on the source tasks. The real-world experiments further demonstrate that human-video guidance can support adaptation to new manipulation tasks beyond simulation. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We formulate one-shot human-video-guided adaptation for pretrained VLA models, where a single human demonstration provides task-specific execution guidance for an unseen manipulation task without requiring target-task robot demonstrations or target-task fine-tuning. We propose CapPro, which combines phase-aware human video representation with video-conditioned adaptation to capture stage-dependent task information from a single demonstration and incorporate it into robot action generation without direct human-to-robot behavior transfer. We evaluate CapPro on 26 unseen manipulation tasks in RoboTwin with different levels of task shift, together with real-world manipulation tasks. The results show improved adaptation across unseen target-task groups while maintaining comparable performance on source tasks. Related Work Vision-Language-Action Models Vision-language-action (VLA) models integrate visual and language representations with robot action generation to learn unified manipulation policies. Leveraging large-scale multi-task robot data~ bridgedatav2,hpt and increasingly expressive action-generation mechanisms~ gr1,rdt1b , recent VLA models have acquired strong and reusable manipulation capabilities across a broad range of tasks. These works primarily focus on expanding manipulation capabilities through large-scale pretraining, whereas our work studies how an existing pretrained VLA policy can acquire task-specific knowledge for previously unseen manipulation tasks at deployment. Specifically, we use a single human demonstration video to provide such guidance without requiring target-task robot demonstrations or target-task fine-tuning. Robot Adaptation Adapting pretrained robot policies to new tasks generally requires incorporating task-specific information beyond that acquired during pretraining. Conventional approaches use downstream robot demonstrations to update policy parameters through full or parameter-efficient fine-tuning~ coral . More recent methods seek lighter adaptation mechanisms by conditioning pretrained policies on demonstrations or retrieved trajectories, reusing structured skill representations, or introducing specialized modules and deployment-time adaptation ~ recap,mosvla,moira . These approaches reduce the need for repeatedly retraining the entire policy, but task-specific information is still commonly obtained from robot-side demonstrations, predefined skill structures, or additional optimization. In contrast, our work uses a single human demonstration video as task-specific execution guidance for a pretrained VLA policy, enabling adaptation to unseen manipulation tasks without target-task robot demonstrations or target-task fine-tuning. Learning from Human Videos Human videos provide a rich source of transferable task knowledge for robot manipulation. Existing approaches commonly exploit such videos by either translating human motion and interactions into robot-compatible trajectories or training data~ im2flow2act,mimicfunc,rsrd , or by extracting higher-level task and motion representations to condition robot behavior. These methods have demonstrated that useful manipulation knowledge can be transferred across the human--robot embodiment gap at different levels of abstraction. In contrast, our work focuses on adapting a pretrained VLA policy to an unseen manipulation task using a single human demonstration as task-specific execution guidance. CapPro does not require explicit human-to-robot trajectory conversion or target-task robot demonstrations, but instead incorporates the demonstrated task information into the action conditioning of the pretrained policy. At each execution step , the policy receives the current robot observation and a language instruction , and predicts an action chunk : We study one-shot adaptation to a target manipulation task that is unseen during source-task training. At deployment, the policy is provided with a single human demonstration video depicting the target task. The demonstration provides task-relevant execution information but contains neither robot actions nor embodiment-aligned trajectories. No target-task robot demonstrations or target-task fine-tuning are used. Conditioning the policy on the human demonstration, the resulting action generation can be formulated as where serves as task-specific execution guidance rather than a trajectory for direct imitation. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:overview , the framework consists of two components: a phase-aware human video representation module and a video-conditioned adaptation module. The former extracts task-relevant execution information from the human demonstration in the context of the current robot observation, while the latter incorporates the resulting representations into the conditioning context of the pretrained VLA policy for action generation. title: Coordi-pi: Coordination-Aware Dual-Hand Action Representation for Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong potential for general-purpose robotic manipulation, but extending them to bimanual dexterous manipulation introduces a high-dimensional and structured action space. Existing bimanual VLA policies commonly concatenate right- and left-side arm--hand actions at each control timestep, leaving cross-hand interactions implicit within a single action vector. We introduce Coordi-$π$, a structured action representation for bimanual dexterous manipulation. Coordi-$π$ represents the right- and left-side arm--hand actions as individual action tokens and organizes them into an interleaved sequence, explicitly exposing the two sides within the action sequence. To explicitly encode hand identity and temporal synchronization in this interleaved representation, a learnable hand-identity embedding distinguishes the two sides, while sequence--control-timestep factorized rotary positional encoding (RoPE) separates sequence position from control timestep, allowing actions at the same control timestep to share a temporal coordinate while retaining distinct sequence positions. Across all five bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks in DexJoCo, Coordi-$π$ achieves state-of-the-art performance under both \textit{rand-obj} and \textit{rand-full}, improving the average success rate over $π_{0.5}$ from 31.9\% to 51.3\% and from 18.3\% to 32.3\%, respectively. Coordi-$π$ also consistently outperforms $π_{0.5}$ across four real-world bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks.

INTRODUCTION =-1 Vision-language-action (VLA) models have recently shown strong progress in general-purpose robotic manipulation~ rt1,rt2,openx,octo,openvla,pi0,pi05 . While early generalist policies largely focused on single-arm manipulation with parallel-jaw grippers, recent work has extended VLA-based control to higher-DoF embodiments, including dexterous hands, humanoid robots, and dual-arm systems~ hpt,gr00tn1,dexvla,dexora,dexjoco . Bimanual dexterous manipulation further requires each side to control a high-DoF arm--hand system while coordinating actions across the two sides~ buds , substantially increasing both the dimensionality and structural complexity of the joint action space. Despite recent progress, action representation remains underexplored for bimanual dexterous manipulation. Conventional approaches typically concatenate the right- and left-side arm--hand actions at each control timestep, where and denote the corresponding arm--hand actions. Although this representation naturally preserves the joint action executed at each timestep, the two sides are distinguished only by the feature dimensions they occupy, leaving their identities and cross-hand structure implicit within a single action vector. In contrast, representing the two sides as individual action tokens in an interleaved sequence, makes the bimanual structure explicit and enables direct token-level interaction. However, interleaving breaks the one-to-one correspondence between sequence position and control timestep: adjacent token pairs may represent either synchronized or temporally consecutive actions. To address these representation issues, we introduce Coordi- , a structured action representation framework for bimanual dexterous manipulation, as illustrated in Fig.~ fig:action_representation . Coordi- first represents each bimanual action chunk as an interleaved sequence of right- and left-side arm--hand tokens. A learnable hand-identity embedding distinguishes the two sides within the shared action representation. We further introduce sequence--control-timestep factorized rotary positional encoding (RoPE), which assigns each action token both a sequence-position coordinate and a control-timestep coordinate. In this representation, and occupy different positions in the token sequence while sharing the same control-timestep coordinate, explicitly representing their temporal synchronization. We evaluate Coordi- on five bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks in DexJoCo~ dexjoco under both rand-obj and the more challenging rand-full setting, and further evaluate it on four real-world bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks. Coordi- achieves state-of-the-art performance on DexJoCo, improving the average success rate over from to under rand-obj and from to under rand-full. Coordi- also outperforms across all four real-world tasks. Ablation studies further show complementary contributions from the interleaved action representation, hand-identity embedding, and sequence--control-timestep factorized RoPE. In summary, the contributions of this paper are threefold: We propose Coordi- , a structured action representation for bimanual dexterous manipulation that represents right- and left-side arm--hand actions as individual tokens and organizes them in an interleaved sequence, explicitly exposing the two sides within the action sequence. We introduce a learnable hand-identity embedding and sequence--control-timestep factorized RoPE to represent hand identity and temporal synchronization in the interleaved action representation. We show that Coordi- achieves state-of-the-art performance across all five bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks in DexJoCo under both rand-obj and rand-full, and outperforms across all four real-world tasks. RELATED WORK Bimanual and Dexterous Manipulation. =-1 Recent work has advanced bimanual dexterous manipulation through improved teleoperation, data collection, policy learning, and evaluation. BiDex develops a high-DoF teleoperation system for collecting bimanual dexterous demonstrations~ bidex , while DexMimicGen generates large-scale demonstration data from a small number of human demonstrations~ dexmimicgen . Related systems such as Mobile ALOHA~ mobilealoha , ALOHA Unleashed~ alohaunleashed , and DexCap~ dexcap further explore scalable data collection and policy learning for complex bimanual or dexterous manipulation. BiDexHands studies high-DoF bimanual dexterous control in simulation~ bidexhands . On the policy side, InterACT captures inter-dependencies between two arms during action prediction~ interact , and KStar Diffuser incorporates spatial--temporal robot structure and kinematic constraints into bimanual control~ kstar . RDT-1B develops a diffusion foundation model for bimanual manipulation~ rdt1b , while Dexora targets high-DoF dual-arm dual-hand VLA control~ dexora . DexJoCo provides a benchmark covering bimanual coordination, tool use, and long-horizon dexterous manipulation~ dexjoco . Coordi- focuses specifically on action representation for bimanual dexterous VLA control, where each side controls a high-DoF arm--hand system. Vision-Language-Action Policies. =-1 Vision-language-action policies leverage large-scale visual, language, and robot data for general-purpose robot control. PaLM-E~ palme and VIMA~ vima demonstrate early forms of multimodal reasoning and prompting for embodied manipulation, while RT-2 transfers vision-language knowledge directly to robotic actions~ rt2 . OpenVLA provides an open-source VLA pretrained on diverse robot demonstrations~ openvla , alongside the broader development of large-scale robot datasets such as DROID~ droid . For continuous action generation, combines a pretrained vision-language backbone with a flow-matching action expert~ pi0 , and further extends this framework toward open-world manipulation~ pi05 . Recent work has also extended VLA policies to more diverse robot embodiments. DexVLA studies general robot control across single-arm, bimanual, and dexterous-hand settings through a diffusion-based action expert~ dexvla . Coordi- builds on this line of VLA policies but focuses on the action representation required for bimanual dexterous control. Action Representation and Sequence Modeling. =-1 Robot policies represent continuous actions in different forms. ACT predicts temporally extended action chunks~ act , while Diffusion Policy represents continuous action trajectories through conditional diffusion~ diffusionpolicy . Within VLA policies, OpenVLA-OFT adopts continuous action prediction together with parallel decoding and action chunking~ openvlaoft , while FAST and ActionCodec study tokenization of continuous robot actions~ fast,actioncodec . SpatialVLA introduces spatially structured representations for robot actions~ spatialvla , and Ego-Pi adopts an interleaved action formulation for high-dimensional dexterous action prediction within a -based policy~ egopi . Positional structure in sequence models is commonly represented with RoPE~ rope , while multimodal extensions such as M-RoPE and VideoRoPE factor positional coordinates across spatial and temporal dimensions~ qwen2vl,videorope . Coordi- focuses on structured action representation for bimanual control, combining interleaved arm--hand tokens with explicit hand identity and control-timestep structure. title: SPECTRA-VLA: Base-Fine Hyperspectral Token Transfer at Frozen Vision-Language-Action Interfaces

summary: Hyperspectral imaging distinguishes RGB-similar objects, but a pretrained vision-language-action model needs a state its frozen decoder can use. SPECTRA-VLA provides a native-width spectral upgrade without retraining the visual encoder or action decoder. A learned continuous residual enriches each target token through its own normalized false-color reference; projection, norm control and validation-calibrated injection regulate the change. Across 86 held-out acquisitions, category balanced accuracy rises from 0.812 to 0.883. With identical residuals and scale, own-token addition improves reuse of an external category-derived probe on frozen decoder logits: 0.701 versus 0.590 with pooled replacement, at similar image-disjoint recognition. Five grouped tests covering the same 86 acquisitions recover within-category spectral shape with $R^2=0.802/0.337$ from continuous and posterior-code states. Category-matched spectral swaps further show that own-token composition approximately doubles the target-specific recovery increment after frozen decoding. Spectral enrichment and receiving-token preservation thus work together at the pretrained interface.

Hyperspectral imaging (HSI) supplies additional measurements, but replacing the visual representation can discard the token structure that the pretrained decoder expects. title: Refine Actions If Needed: Adaptive Action Chunk Refinement for Robot Manipulation
summary: Computationally lightweight manipulation policies predict executable actions with low inference latency, but prediction errors can limit task success. Iterative generative policies can achieve higher task success rates, but repeated network evaluations increase inference latency. Refining action proposals from computationally lightweight policies can combine these strengths, but the amount of refinement needed varies across states. We introduce RAIN (Refine Actions If Needed), a framework that predicts action errors at different refinement levels to decide whether and how much to refine each executable proposal, before performing any refinement. We train an ensemble to predict these errors by comparing action proposals and their refined versions with expert actions from offline demonstrations, without requiring explicit labels of refinement needs. Calibration balances uncertainty, computation, and temporal consistency. We evaluate RAIN on eight ManiSkill tasks and four real-robot tasks. In simulation, our policy achieves 66.6% success, approaching the best evaluated diffusion-policy success rate with 5.71 times lower policy latency. On the real robot, success increases from 55.0% with Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) to 72.5%, with comparable average successful completion time. Matched controls show that dynamic routing maintains the strongest observed fixed-refinement success level with 26.6% fewer refiner evaluations. Project page: https://rain-policy.github.io/.
full_text: \@captype figure Comparison of action generation and refinement paradigms. (a) Direct ACT predicts an executable action chunk in a single forward pass. (b) Generative policies such as diffusion policy (DP) and flow matching (FM) generate action chunks through iterative network evaluations. (c) Fixed-budget refinement applies a fixed number of refinement steps to every action proposal. (d) RAIN predicts whether refinement is needed before invoking FM, directly executes proposals that require no refinement, and adaptively allocates additional refinement steps when necessary. The bottle-manipulation sequence illustrates how the computational budget varies across successive policy calls within a single episode. fig:paradigm-overview Computationally lightweight manipulation policies predict executable actions with low inference latency, but prediction errors can limit task success. Iterative generative policies can achieve higher task success rates, but repeated network evaluations increase inference latency. Refining action proposals from computationally lightweight policies can combine these strengths, but the amount of refinement needed varies across states. We introduce RAIN (Refine Actions If Needed), a framework that predicts action errors at different refinement levels to decide whether and how much to refine each executable proposal, before performing any refinement. We train an ensemble to predict these errors by comparing action proposals and their refined versions with expert actions from offline demonstrations, without requiring explicit labels of refinement needs. Calibration balances uncertainty, computation, and temporal consistency. We evaluate RAIN on eight ManiSkill tasks and four real-robot tasks. In simulation, our policy achieves 66.6 success, approaching the best evaluated diffusion-policy success rate with 5.71 lower policy latency. On the real robot, success increases from 55.0 with Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) to 72.5 , with comparable average successful completion time. Matched controls show that dynamic routing maintains the strongest observed fixed-refinement success level with 26.6 fewer refiner evaluations. Project page: . Introduction sec:introduction Closed-loop manipulation policies must generate effective actions quickly enough to replan as the environment changes. Diffusion Policy (DP) and flow-matching (FM) policies commonly generate these sequences by transforming an unstructured noise sample into an observation-conditioned action trajectory through repeated network evaluations~ chi2023diffusion,lipman2023flow . This iterative process can improve task success rates, but repeated network evaluations increase inference latency. To reduce inference latency, a computationally lightweight policy can first produce an executable action proposal for a generative model to refine. Instead of generating the entire action sequence from noise, the model can then focus on correcting errors in the proposal. BRIDGeR and Action-to-Action (A2A) flow matching explore related approaches by replacing noise with policy samples or action-history representations~ chen2024bridger,jia2026a2a . However, improving the starting point does not by itself determine how much refinement is needed. For an executable proposal, the appropriate choice may range from direct execution to additional correction, depending on the current state. Figure~ fig:paradigm-overview contrasts direct generation, iterative generation, fixed refinement, and our policy with adaptive refinement. The problem is therefore to determine whether the expected improvement over direct execution justifies additional computation, before invoking the refiner. Making this decision before refinement presents two challenges. First, predicting how much refinement will improve action quality requires assessing refined actions before they are generated. Proposal uncertainty alone does not establish whether the refiner can improve a proposal or how much correction is worthwhile, while evaluating alternative refinements online consumes the computation we seek to save. Second, offline demonstrations provide expert actions, but no direct labels for refinement needs or the benefit of each allocation. The router must therefore learn from demonstrations to predict action errors at different refinement levels, including no refinement. These predictions allow it to decide whether and how much to refine by weighing the expected reduction in error against the additional computation. We introduce RAIN (Refine Actions If Needed) to address these challenges through offline comparative supervision and pre-refinement risk prediction. Here, risk refers to the predicted deviation of an action chunk from expert actions. At demonstration states, frozen proposal and refiner models generate candidates whose deviations from the same expert action chunk provide continuous surrogate targets for a risk ensemble. Offline calibration balances predicted risk, uncertainty, computation, and temporal consistency. The router then selects direct execution or only the chosen refinement, without online reward optimization or refinement probes. We instantiate this framework with Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT)~ zhao2023act as the proposal policy and flow matching as the refiner. We evaluate the framework on eight ManiSkill tasks~ tao2024maniskill3 and four real-robot tasks. In simulation, our policy achieves 66.6 success at 0.322\,ms/action of amortized policy latency, approaching the best evaluated diffusion-policy success rate. On the real robot, it improves success over ACT by 17.5 percentage points with comparable average successful completion time. Matched controls further show that dynamic routing maintains the strongest observed fixed-refinement success level while reducing policy latency by 15.7 . The paper makes three contributions: RAIN, an adaptive action-refinement framework that decides whether and how much to refine an executable action proposal before invoking a generative refiner, preserving a direct-execution path. A demonstration-only learning procedure that predicts continuous candidate risks from expert-action deviations, with offline calibration of uncertainty, computation cost, and temporal consistency. Evaluation on eight ManiSkill tasks and four real-robot tasks demonstrating the success--efficiency benefits of executable-proposal refinement, with matched controls isolating the additional computation savings from dynamic routing. Related Work sec:related-work Action policies and generative efficiency. Imitation policies model robot actions through direct prediction, implicit models, or tokenized representations. ACT predicts executable action chunks in one forward pass~ zhao2023act , while implicit behavior cloning and behavior transformers offer alternative representations of complex action distributions~ florence2022ibc,shafiullah2022bet,lee2024vqbet . Diffusion and flow-matching policies instead construct action sequences through iterative denoising or vector-field integration~ chi2023diffusion,lipman2023flow,chisari2024pointflowmatch . This expressive generation process requires repeated network evaluations at each control decision, motivating efforts to reduce inference cost. Several approaches reduce this cost by shortening generation or reusing computation. Consistency Policy, One-Step Diffusion Policy, and FlowPolicy enable few-step or single-step prediction through distillation or consistency training~ prasad2024consistency,wang2024onedp,zhang2024flowpolicy . Warm-start methods exploit temporal continuity or predict informative initial actions~ chen2025falcon,duan2025rti,li2026step , while streaming generation and improved flow couplings offer complementary efficiency gains~ hoeg2025streaming,jiang2025streamingflow,sochopoulos2025cot . However, distillation can trade action accuracy or diversity for speed~ hoeg2025streaming , while temporal reuse alone may not ensure compatibility with the current state~ li2026step . These trade-offs motivate starting from an executable proposal and allocating correction according to its predicted value. Executable proposals and learned refinement. Informative starting points offer another route to efficient generation. BRIDGeR refines source-policy samples~ chen2024bridger , while A2A and Vision-to-Action (VITA) construct flow sources from action history and visual representations~ jia2026a2a,gao2026vita . These methods show that generation need not begin from unstructured noise, but an informative source alone does not determine whether further refinement justifies its cost. When the source is already executable, refinement becomes optional. RAIN explicitly compares the predicted value and cost of correction against direct execution, making the proposal both a refinement starting point and an executable alternative. Learning corrections to an existing policy is also central to residual-policy methods. Residual reinforcement learning, FISH, and ResiP improve base policies through environment interaction~ johannink2019residual,haldar2023fish,ankile2025resip , while TRANSIC obtains corrective supervision from human interventions during deployment~ jiang2024transic . These approaches improve existing behavior but require additional interaction or intervention data for correction learning. RAIN instead learns refinement and its allocation from offline demonstrations, using candidate deviations from expert actions to supervise relative correction value. This supports adaptive refinement without collecting online rewards or human corrections. Adaptive computation for generative policies. Adaptive computation allocates different generation effort to different control decisions. AdaFlow adjusts integration using conditional variance linked to discretization error~ hu2024adaflow , while ProbeFlow estimates trajectory complexity from initial and lookahead velocity vectors~ fang2026probeflow . Prefix-Optimal Generative Policies (POGP) instead learn intermediate denoising values to stop when further generation offers little benefit~ salla2026pogp . These criteria adapt computation within generation but do not directly compare refinement against an independently executable proposal. RAIN makes this comparison before the first refiner evaluation, allowing direct execution when the predicted correction benefit does not justify its cost. Other approaches learn computation allocation from observations. Dynamic Denoising Diffusion Policy (D3P) jointly trains a step adaptor and diffusion policy through reinforcement learning~ yu2025d3p , whereas RAIN learns refinement allocation from offline demonstrations. Difficulty-Aware Stochastic Interpolant Policy (DA-SIP) selects integration steps and solver configurations, while the Vision-Adaptive Diffusion Policy Framework (VADF) adjusts denoising schedules and execution lengths~ chun2025dasip,yu2026vadf . These methods adapt generation or execution; RAIN instead compares correction amounts for the same executable proposal, including no correction. Modality-Adaptive Robot Sampling (MARS) selectively invokes stochastic generation when behavioral diversity is needed~ jia2026mars . Yet even a single-modal action can require precise correction. RAIN therefore predicts continuous candidate risks, preserving correction differences that can be weighed against uncertainty and computation cost. Method sec:method As shown in Fig.~ fig:method-overview , RAIN starts from an executable action proposal and treats generative refinement as optional correction. We first train the proposal policy and refiner, then freeze them. Using offline demonstrations, we compare actions at different refinement levels, including no refinement, with expert actions to obtain error targets. title: What Matters for World Modeling in Vision-Language-Action Models?
summary: Integrating world models into Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) has emerged as a promising direction, enabling policies to anticipate future dynamics beyond reactive observation-to-action mapping. However, existing approaches vary simultaneously in their world representations, integration paradigms, and policy backbones, making it difficult to determine what truly matters for effective world model integration. To disentangle these factors, we categorize existing efforts into four representative paradigms, namely Implicit Future Alignment, Explicit Future Query, MoT Future Expert, and External World Predictor. We instantiate each within a unified framework and systematically evaluate these paradigms with diverse world representations and policy backbones across in-domain, out-of-domain, long-horizon, dynamic, few-shot, and real-world settings. Our study yields four main findings: 1) world representation effectiveness is paradigm-dependent, whereas 2D semantic representations offer robust, cross-paradigm gains; 2) no single paradigm is universally optimal, yet the decoupled MoT Future Expert offers competitive overall performance, particularly in OOD robustness; 3) world modeling consistently benefits policies built on standard VLMs, while decoupled designs exhibit greater compatibility with pretrained VLAs; and 4) world modeling improves performance over action-only baselines across multiple settings, with notable gains on long-horizon and dynamic tasks. Project page and video demonstrations are available at https://dylanmqs.github.io/WM-in-VLAs/.
full_text: Experiments Experimental Setup subsec:experimental_setup We evaluate on LIBERO~ liu2023libero for multi-task manipulation, LIBERO-Plus~ fei2025libero for OOD robustness, RoboTwin 2.0~ chen2025robotwin for bimanual manipulation across task horizons, and DOMINO~ fang2026towards for dynamic manipulation. The four paradigms are abbreviated as WM-Align, WM-Query, WM-MoT, and WM-Ext. Our primary comparisons share the Qwen3-VL-2B backbone and training protocol; experiments additionally examine transfer to a pretrained VLA. Across all paradigms, frozen encoders extract world supervision targets, and additionally provide current visual features to initialize generative tokens in WM-MoT and WM-Ext, following~ zhang2025unijepa, lv2025f1, chen2026lawam . Implementation details and disaggregated results appear in Appendix~ app:experimental_setup . World Representation Analysis across Paradigms subsec:world_representation_analysis Finding 1: World representation rankings reverse across integration paradigms. As shown in Figure~ fig:extractor_stability , no single world representation universally dominates across architectures; instead, their relative rankings reverse across paradigms. For example, V-JEPA~2.1 provides the strongest OOD gain for WM-MoT, yet falls below the baseline when paired with WM-Ext, where DINOv3 and SigLIP perform best. Similarly, VGGT benefits WM-Align but degrades WM-Ext. Furthermore, WM-Align is relatively insensitive to the representation choice, whereas WM-MoT and WM-Ext exhibit high variance, making encoder selection consequential for decoupled designs. Finding 2: 2D semantic representations offer robust, cross-paradigm gains. DINOv3 and SigLIP consistently improve both ID and OOD averages across all four paradigms. In contrast, pixel-level representations are generally vulnerable to visual distribution shifts, causing WanVAE to underperform OOD; however, ImageVAE retains comprehensive spatial details with minimal information loss, still providing modest gains across paradigms. Meanwhile, VGGT captures low-level spatial geometry rather than high-level task semantics, rendering its utility fragile and architecture-dependent. Between the two semantic representations, DINOv3 and SigLIP perform comparably in-domain, whereas DINOv3 attains both the higher average gain and the higher upper bound across paradigms out-of-domain (Figure~ fig:extractor_stability (a, c)). We therefore adopt DINOv3 as the default world representation for subsequent comparisons. Main Results across Manipulation Benchmarks subsec:main_manipulation_results Finding 3: World modeling improves overall performance and visual robustness. As shown in Table~ tab:vla-robustness , all four paradigms consistently improve success over the action-only baseline across in-domain LIBERO and out-of-domain LIBERO-Plus. Notably, while our action-only baseline already matches or exceeds competitive references like OpenVLA-OFT~ kim2025fine and 4D-WAM~ yang20264d out-of-domain, world modeling provides substantial further gains across all paradigms. In-domain, WM-Align reaches the highest score of 98.6 by enriching individual visual tokens with fine-grained local dynamics through patch-wise alignment. Across out-of-domain perturbations, performance gains are shared on camera shifts, sensor noise, and background variations, with WM-MoT providing the largest overall boost of 4.4 and improving across all seven categories. Controlled ablations confirm that future predictive supervision yields a larger gain than adding MoT capacity and generative token inputs alone, as detailed in Appendix~ app:mot_supervision_control . Meanwhile, under linguistic perturbations, the decoupled WM-MoT and WM-Ext avoid notable drops, whereas coupled paradigms degrade by up to 2.9 , suggesting that separating future prediction may mitigate interference with the VLM's pretrained language knowledge. Finding 4: World modeling yields substantial gains on long-horizon tasks. As reported in Table~ tab:robotwin-c2c-c2r , world modeling consistently enhances RoboTwin 2.0 manipulation performance, especially as task horizons extend. Under Clean2Clean, all paradigms achieve notable improvements that progressively increase with horizon length, yielding gains of 5.5 to 8.6 on short tasks, 7.4 to 12.8 on medium tasks, and 16.5 to 26.3 on long tasks. Under Clean2Random, all four paradigms improve long-horizon success by 1.3 to 3.7 . In contrast, on short tasks, only WM-Align improves by 1.9 , while the other three drop by 0.8 to 2.5 . This indicates that short tasks rely primarily on immediate visual feedback, where predicting future states offers little benefit and can even introduce slight noise under visual shifts. Performance under Dynamic Environments and Data Scarcity subsec:performance_dynamic_data_scarcity [r,width=0.46 ,type=table,abovesep=-0.6 ] Performance on DOMINO Level~1 dynamic manipulation. Scores report success rate (SR, ) and manipulation score (MS). tab:dynamic-environments 2pt 1.03 [2] #1\, ( \,#2) [2] #1\, ( \,#2) @ lcc@ Method & SR & MS \\ InternVLA-M1 & 5.4 & 27.6 \\ Isaac-GR00T & 6.1 & 28.6 \\ OpenVLA-OFT & 9.1 & 24.1 \\ & 9.6 & 26.2 \\ Baseline & 10.6 & 29.1 \\ WM-Align & 1.3 & 1.0 \\ WM-Query & 2.9 & 2.9 \\ WM-MoT & 4.9 & 3.8 \\ WM-Ext & 4.5 & 3.9 \\ Finding 5: Decoupled predictive designs achieve stronger gains in dynamic manipulation. Table~ tab:dynamic-environments reports DOMINO Level~1 results alongside representative VLAs, including InternVLA-M1~ chen2025internvla , Isaac-GR00T~ bjorck2025gr00t , OpenVLA-OFT~ kim2025fine , and ~ intelligence2025pi . While all four paradigms outperform prior models and the 10.6 action-only baseline, their gains vary across architectures. WM-Align and WM-Query achieve 11.9 and 13.5 success, respectively, whereas decoupled predictive designs such as WM-Ext and WM-MoT reach 15.1 and 15.5 success. One possible explanation is that enforcing token-wise patch alignment or bottleneck queries on shared representations provides limited capacity for dynamic modeling, whereas dedicated predictive modules can more flexibly capture continuous object motion. Finding 6: Decoupled paradigms retain stronger performance under data scarcity. We compare policies trained with 25 , 50 , and 100 demonstrations on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, as illustrated in Figure~ fig:data_scaling and detailed in Tables~ tab:data-scaling-id-details -- tab:data-scaling-ood-details . Overall, decoupled architectures such as WM-Ext and WM-MoT maintain strong performance under data scarcity. In contrast, WM-Query degrades sharply in low-data settings, likely because the added query tokens require sufficient demonstrations to learn compact and effective world representations. Between the two decoupled designs, their relative advantages differ across domains. Specifically, WM-Ext achieves the highest in-domain sample efficiency, reaching 96.5 success at 50 data, while WM-MoT provides the strongest out-of-distribution robustness, leading all alternatives with 62.4 success at 25 data. Compatibility with Pre-trained Foundation VLAs subsec:compatibility_pretrained_vla Finding 7: Decoupled designs show better compatibility with the pretrained VLA. To examine how world modeling integrates into foundation VLAs, we incorporate all four paradigms into and evaluate them on RoboTwin 2.0 under Clean2Clean and Clean2Random settings, as reported in Table~ tab:pi05-robotwin-c2c-c2r . Decoupled architectures transfer more favorably to the pretrained backbone, as both WM-MoT and WM-Ext improve overall success rates under in-domain and out-of-distribution conditions. Between the two, WM-Ext achieves the largest in-domain gain, while WM-MoT provides the strongest out-of-distribution robustness. In contrast, coupled designs do not exhibit consistent gains. Specifically, WM-Query performs slightly below the baseline, while WM-Align degrades policy performance, dropping success rates by over 5 across both settings. A plausible reason is that WM-Align imposes auxiliary predictive objectives directly onto the shared visual representations, which can distort the pretrained feature space and disrupt the manipulation priors established during pretraining. Real World Experiments subsec:real_world_experiments Finding 8: World modeling consistently improves real-world manipulation performance. Across the four real-world tasks illustrated in Figure~ fig:realworld , all four world modeling paradigms consistently outperform the action-only baseline, raising the average success rate from 45.0 to 56.3--73.8 , with detailed experimental setups provided in Appendix~ app:experimental_setup and full per-task numerical results in Table~ tab:app-real-robot-per-task (Appendix~ app:real_robot_details ). On static tasks, all paradigms achieve steady improvements over the baseline, with WM-Ext achieving 90.0 on box cover block and WM-Align reaching 85.0 on placing corn. On dynamic tasks, performance gains differ noticeably across architectures. While WM-Align yields modest improvements, decoupled designs such as WM-MoT and WM-Ext provide substantial gains. Specifically, WM-MoT reaches 75.0 on dynamic picking and 55.0 on tomato placement, achieving the highest overall average of 73.8 .

title: FOMI: A Force-Feedback Manipulation Interface for Teaching Contact-Rich Manipulation
summary: Robot-free collection with handheld interfaces enables scalable acquisition of human demonstrations for policy learning. However, existing handheld interfaces often provide limited intuitive force feedback, making contact-rich demonstration collection challenging for human operators. To address this, we present FOMI, a force-feedback manipulation interface with a scissor-shaped mechanism, which transmits object interaction forces directly to the operator's hands through actuation links without force sensors. This intuitive force feedback supports real-time action adjustment during robot-free collection of contact-rich demonstrations. Around FOMI, we build a demonstration collection system that integrates sensor calibration, data acquisition, and synchronization for robot-free collection. By further mapping pose changes and gripper opening of FOMI to robot end-effector poses and gripper commands, the system also supports teleoperation. Across four contact-rich tasks, FOMI improves collection efficiency by approximately 29% and 18% over the best baselines in robot-free collection and teleoperation, respectively. Demonstrations collected with FOMI in both modes enable policies to perform challenging contact-rich manipulation tasks with high success rates.
full_text: Yishu~Shen , Yiming~Luo , Ruilin~Wang , Bowen~Yang , Shuai~Yang , Fangyi~Xu , Yujun~Shen , Fu~Zhang , Boyu~Zhou , and Yinghao~Xu 0pt The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology The University of Hong Kong Robbyant Southern University of Science and Technology Project leader. Corresponding author (e-mail: justimyhxu@ust.hk). .15in Robot-free collection with handheld interfaces enables scalable acquisition of human demonstrations for policy learning. However, existing handheld interfaces often provide limited intuitive force feedback, making contact-rich demonstration collection challenging for human operators. To address this, we present FOMI, a force-feedback manipulation interface with a scissor-shaped mechanism, which transmits object interaction forces directly to the operator's hands through actuation links without force sensors. This intuitive force feedback supports real-time action adjustment during robot-free collection of contact-rich demonstrations. Around FOMI, we build a demonstration collection system that integrates sensor calibration, data acquisition, and synchronization for robot-free collection. By further mapping pose changes and gripper opening of FOMI to robot end-effector poses and gripper commands, the system also supports teleoperation. Across four contact-rich tasks, FOMI improves collection efficiency by approximately 29 and 18 over the best baselines in robot-free collection and teleoperation, respectively. Demonstrations collected with FOMI in both modes enable policies to perform challenging contact-rich manipulation tasks with high success rates. Project page:~ Introduction Human demonstrations provide behavioral supervision for manipulation policy learning. Teleoperation~ wu2024gello,zhao2023aloha collects demonstrations directly on the target robot but requires robot hardware, limiting data scale and diversity. Robot-free collection with handheld interfaces such as the Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI)~ chi2024umi,fastumi2024 has therefore been widely explored for scalable demonstration acquisition in diverse real-world environments. However, collecting contact-rich manipulation demonstrations with these handheld interfaces remains challenging because a lack of intuitive force feedback can limit human operators' ability to perceive object interaction forces and adjust actions in real time~ liu2025forcemimic , resulting in more failed attempts and lower collection efficiency~ wu2025freetacman . A key factor is the interface's mechanical design, which determines how directly interaction forces are transmitted to the human operator. Common handheld interfaces in robot-free demonstration collection employ trigger-driven rack-and-pinion mechanisms~ chi2024umi,choi2026umift . These mechanisms transmit object interaction forces through multiple intermediate components, where mechanical backlash weakens force feedback~ wu2025freetacman . Alternatively, interfaces with active force feedback~ zhang2025doglove,citron2026modpack combine force sensing with motorized actuation to convey interaction forces to operators, requiring additional sensing hardware, actuators, and feedback control. These limitations motivate a mechanical interface that provides intuitive force feedback for real-time action adjustment during contact-rich demonstration collection without additional force sensors or active feedback actuators. Inspired by the comfortable handling and intuitive force feedback of scissors, we design a scissor-shaped mechanism to support contact-rich demonstration collection. Each handle forms a rigid assembly with its sector gear and actuation link, preserving a direct mechanical path for force transmission without additional transmission stages between the handle and the actuation link. To match the target parallel gripper, the two identical sector gears mesh with each other, constraining the two branches to open and close symmetrically. Building on this mechanical design, we introduce FOMI, a force-feedback manipulation interface, together with a demonstration collection system that integrates sensor calibration, data acquisition, and synchronization for robot-free collection of contact-rich demonstrations. Through calibration and mapping, the system further converts sensor measurements of FOMI's pose changes and gripper opening into robot end-effector pose targets and gripper width commands, enabling teleoperated demonstration collection with the same interface. Our main contributions are as follows: Mechanical design for intuitive force feedback: We design a scissor-shaped interface in which each handle is rigidly integrated with its actuation link, providing a direct force path for intuitive force feedback during robot-free collection, with meshing sector gears matching the symmetric motion of parallel grippers. Demonstration collection system for teaching contact-rich manipulation: We build a collection system around FOMI that integrates sensor calibration, data acquisition, and synchronization for robot-free collection, and further supports teleoperation by mapping FOMI's motion and gripper opening to robot commands. Improved collection efficiency and policy evaluation: Compared with baseline interfaces in both collection modes, FOMI achieves the highest collection efficiency and improves completion rates. Policies fine-tuned on FOMI demonstrations achieve high success rates on four contact-rich tasks. Hardware designs, code, and datasets will be released. Related Work Demonstration Collection Interfaces Human demonstrations for policy learning are commonly collected through robot-free collection or teleoperation. In robot-free collection, UMI~ chi2024umi and its variants~ choi2026umift,fastumi2024 enable demonstration collection across diverse real-world environments. In teleoperation, leader-follower interfaces such as GELLO~ wu2024gello , ALOHA~ zhao2023aloha , and Mobile ALOHA~ fu2024mobile use joint-space mapping for arm control to collect demonstrations, whereas VR systems~ george2025openvr and smartphone systems~ wang2023mimicplay,agarwal2026cobalt provide end-effector pose control. Recent interfaces have been developed to support both robot-free collection and teleoperation~ seo2025legato,surendran2026bridge . Force Feedback for Demonstration Collection The interface's mechanical design can influence force feedback and action adjustment during demonstration collection~ georgadarellis2026gripper . Existing manipulation interfaces provide force feedback through mechanical transmission or active feedback. UMI~ chi2024umi and UMI-FT~ choi2026umift use trigger-driven rack-and-pinion mechanisms, while other handheld interfaces use trigger-driven linkages~ fang2026robopocket,liu2026rdt2,xu2025exumi . These mechanisms transmit interaction forces to the hand, but multiple transmission stages and backlash may obscure force feedback. In contrast, finger-driven interfaces~ ohkawa2026yubi,wu2025freetacman transmit interaction forces to the actuating fingers, but supporting the interface with the actuating fingers may affect force perception and action adjustment. Alternatively, interfaces with active force feedback provide bilateral gripper force feedback~ luo2026omniumi or reflect interaction forces from the follower robot~ liu2025factr,zhang2025doglove,citron2026modpack , requiring additional actuators and feedback control. FOMI integrates each handle with an actuation link to provide direct mechanical force feedback and handle support during robot-free collection. Contact Sensing for Policy Learning Recent manipulation interfaces incorporate additional tactile or force sensors to collect contact information for learning contact-rich manipulation. Some interfaces collect synchronized visual and tactile observations and use tactile representation learning to support visuo-tactile policies~ xu2025exumi,liu2025vitamin,zhu2026touch . title: MUCO: A Mani-Unit-Structured Manipulation Framework for Compositional Long-Horizon Robot Tasks
summary: Learning and executing long-horizon robot manipulation as complete task trajectories raises data-collection costs, lim?its capability reuse, and causes local failures to cascade into later task stages. We introduce manipulation units (MUs) as reusable operations, each defined by a local goal, an initi?ation condition, and observable success and failure criteria. MUs are learned and verified individually. During execution, consecutive MUs remain coupled through shared environ?ment dynamics. We formulate MU-Structured Manipulation (MUSM) and realize it through MU-Centric Orchestration (MUCO). Given language and vision, MUCO constructs an MU sequence, matches each MU to compatible policy models in a frozen capability registry, and dispatches the model with the highest calibrated success rate. Visual verification checks MU outcomes against success and failure criteria and governs transitions, enabling retry or fallback to another model from the current state without re-executing verified MUs. Canonical keys enable checkpoint reuse for equivalent MUs across tasks without new demonstrations or updates. We evaluate MUCO on RLBench, RoboTwin 2.0, and five real-world tasks. MUCO achieves higher complete-task success and verified progress, stronger failure containment, and lower error propagation than baselines. Results demonstrate cross-task MU reuse and het?erogeneous policy composition without joint training, shared backbones, or common action representations.
full_text: Learning and executing long-horizon robot manipulation as complete task trajectories raises data-collection costs, limits capability reuse, and causes local failures to cascade into later task stages. We introduce manipulation units (MUs) as reusable operations, each defined by a local goal, an initiation condition, and observable success and failure criteria. MUs are learned and verified individually. During execution, consecutive MUs remain coupled through shared environment dynamics. We formulate MU-Structured Manipulation (MUSM) and realize it through MU-Centric Orchestration (MUCO). Given language and vision, MUCO constructs an MU sequence, matches each MU to compatible policy models in a frozen capability registry, and dispatches the model with the highest calibrated success rate. Visual verification checks MU outcomes against success and failure criteria and governs transitions, enabling retry or fallback to another model from the current state without re-executing verified MUs. Canonical keys enable checkpoint reuse for equivalent MUs across tasks without new demonstrations or updates. We evaluate MUCO on RLBench, RoboTwin 2.0, and five real-world tasks. MUCO achieves higher complete-task success and verified progress, stronger failure containment, and lower error propagation than baselines. Results demonstrate cross-task MU reuse and heterogeneous policy composition without joint training, shared backbones, or common action representations. Introduction A robot that can grasp a container, open its lid, and pour its contents should be able to recombine those capabilities when asked to prepare a different drink. Under the dominant trajectory-centric paradigm, however, a new ordering or combination is still treated as a new end-to-end task, typically requiring another complete demonstration or another task-level policy. The limitation is not simply that current policies are too small or their action horizons too short. The deeper problem is that the trajectory is asked to play too many roles at once. It is the unit of data collection and policy learning, as well as the unit of execution, evaluation, and recovery. For long-horizon manipulation, however, that unit is too coarse-grained. Vision-language-action (VLA) models and related multimodal policies have substantially broadened the behaviors that robots can express by coupling perception, language, and continuous action generation brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,physicalintelligence2025pi05,driess2023palme,jiang2023vima,openx2024 . Yet greater policy capacity does not by itself delineate where one operation ends, whether its intended state change was achieved, or which existing controller should handle the next operation. These questions are of particular importance in laboratory procedures, household activities, and assembly tasks, where an early error changes the physical context faced by every later action mees2022calvin,jiang2023vima . Long-horizon competence therefore requires not only a policy that can act, but also an organization of operation that makes intermediate progress reusable and inspectable. The trajectory-centric formulation couples semantically distinct operations into one data collection, learning, and execution problem. At the data level, collecting demonstrations for a lengthy task requires complete successful rollouts, even when most constituent operations have already appeared in other tasks openx2024,khazatsky2024droid . A change in task order or final objective can therefore require collecting another full trajectory. At the capability level, the trajectory-level formulation does not expose the operations learned by a policy model as units that can be selected, verified, and recombined. Therefore, knowing how to grasp, pour, and insert does not by itself enable a robot to execute those operations in a new long-horizon ordering mees2022calvin,jiang2023vima . At execution time, an early failure changes the state encountered by all later operations. Without explicit Mani-Unit boundaries, it is difficult to check whether each operation succeeded or to retry only the failed operation hu2026matters,zhang2026visualverification . This problem arises because learning and execution are organized around complete trajectories rather than reusable Mani-Units. To address these problems, we introduce manipulation units (MUs) as reusable operations, each defined by a local goal, an initiation condition, and observable success and failure criteria. An MU specifies what state change should be achieved, while the selected policy model determines how to achieve it through continuous robot actions. Building on MUs, we formulate MU-Structured Manipulation (MUSM), which represents long-horizon tasks as ordered MU compositions. In MUSM, individually learned and verified MUs are recombined into different task sequences. During execution, the outcome of each MU determines the initial state of the next, so consecutive MUs remain coupled through shared environment dynamics. Data are collected and policy models are trained separately for each MU. The same MU can then be reused across different task sequences and executed by different compatible policy models.| Compared with language-guided planners that primarily organize execution through high-level skill selection or program generation ahn2022saycan,liang2023code,huang2022innermonologue , MUSM does more than generate an execution sequence. MUSM represents long-horizon tasks as ordered compositions of reusable and verifiable MUs, and different tasks are formed by recombining the same MUs. Each MU retains its own data provenance and observable success and failure criteria. MUSM therefore changes both how task sequences are constructed and the granularity at which data are collected, policies are trained, outcomes are verified, and learned capabilities are reused across tasks. We realize MUSM through MU-Centric Orchestration (MUCO), which comprises four components: an MU constructor that converts task instructions and visual observations into ordered MU records; a matcher backed by a frozen capability registry that identifies compatible policy models and ranks them using calibrated success rates; model-specific adapters that translate observations and MU records into each policy model's native input; and a visual verifier that evaluates success and failure criteria and governs MU transitions and recovery. During execution, MUCO dispatches the highest-ranked compatible model for the active MU. After verified success, MUCO advances to the next MU. After failure, MUCO retries the current model or falls back to another compatible model from the current environment state without re-executing verified MUs. Our experiments test whether this Mani-Unit-centric organization addresses the limitations of trajectory-centric learning described above. We first examine whether a learned Mani-Unit can be reused in a new task. We then test whether assigning different policy models to different Mani-Units improves task success. Finally, we evaluate whether Mani-Unit verification and retry prevent an early error from affecting the rest of a long-horizon task. Our contributions are: We identify trajectory granularity as a shared bottleneck in data collection, capability reuse, and failure handling, introduce manipulation units (MUs) as reusable and verifiable operations, and formulate MUSM to represent long-horizon tasks as ordered compositions of MUs that can be recombined across task sequences. We introduce MUCO, a concrete realization of MUSM that integrates an MU constructor, a matcher backed by a frozen capability registry, model-specific adapters, and a visual verifier for transition control and failure recovery, without jointly retraining the underlying policy models. We establish an evaluation protocol that separates individual policy-model competence from the central claims of cross-task MU reuse without additional demonstrations, heterogeneous policy composition, and robustness to MU-level failures. Related Work Vision-language-action models. VLA models and related multimodal policies learn language-conditioned visuomotor behavior from robot demonstrations and large-scale vision-language data brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,physicalintelligence2025pi05,driess2023palme,jiang2023vima,openx2024 . Scaling these models improves the breadth and generality of individual executors, but does not prescribe how a learned capability should be reused across task compositions or replaced after a local failure. MUSM is complementary to such scaling: a VLA can be registered once as an executor for every Mani-Unit it supports, reused across tasks without task-specific architectural changes, and replaced by a specialist only where calibrated evidence indicates that the specialist is more reliable. The contribution is therefore at the learning-and-deployment interface around policies, rather than in a new action decoder. Hierarchical VLA orchestration. Hierarchical VLA agents pair a high-level VLM with a low-level VLA and study planner choice, controller steerability, termination, observation representation, and memory hu2026matters . This line establishes that orchestration choices matter even when a strong controller is available. MUSM is complementary but changes the object being orchestrated. A conventional hierarchy typically issues transient subgoals to one low-level controller; MUSM maintains a Mani-Unit as a persistent entity with its own data provenance, admissibility and outcome criteria, and a set of independently trained compatible executors. MUCO can consequently assign different executors to different occurrences of the same Mani-Unit and reuse the Mani-Unit record across task compositions. Language-guided task organization. Language models have been used to select skills according to affordances, synthesize executable programs, and replan from environmental feedback ahn2022saycan,liang2023code,huang2022innermonologue . These approaches establish the value of semantic reasoning above robot control. MUSM focuses on the learning and deployment unit beneath that reasoning. Rather than treating a skill call as an atomic symbolic action whose implementation is hidden from the planner, MUSM retains each Mani-Unit as a stochastic feedback-control problem with Mani-Unit-level data, explicit outcome criteria, and multiple possible executors. The organizer sequences Mani-Units, but does not abstract away their continuous execution or its uncertainty. Task planning and hierarchical reinforcement learning. Classical task planners reason over symbolic action schemas, predicates, and precondition--effect structures kaelbling1998planning ; hierarchical reinforcement learning and options introduce temporal abstraction through initiation conditions, intra-option policies, and termination rules sutton1999between,dietterich2000hierarchical . MUSM can be embedded in this formalism by treating each Mani-Unit--executor pair as an option, so our claim is not a new temporal-abstraction calculus. The distinction is the factorization MUSM makes explicit. A semantic Mani-Unit is separated from the policy that executes it; one Mani-Unit may map to multiple heterogeneous executors; a shared observation-based verifier judges all of them; and Mani-Unit data and capability estimates are reused across tasks. Options provide a language for temporally extended control, but do not by themselves prescribe this Mani-Unit-level organization of data, verification, calibration, and cross-task deployment.
