title: Complementary Future Token Pruning for World Action Models
summary: World action models (WAMs) jointly predict future visual states and robot actions, but processing dense future-frame tokens incurs substantial inference latency. We propose CF-Prune, a training-free framework for pruning future-frame tokens in pretrained WAMs. Our key insight is that future visual predictions support action generation and therefore need not preserve every visual detail required for high-fidelity video synthesis. CF-Prune combines instruction and action attention to identify task-relevant tokens during the initial denoising forward pass, even when future-frame and action representations remain highly noisy. An entropy-based phase identification mechanism further retains dense computation during precision phases to mitigate pruning-induced performance degradation. Experiments on RoboLab, RoboCasa, and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate consistent inference speedups. At a 35% pruning ratio, CF-Prune achieves average speedups of 1.19-1.27x while improving task success rates. At a 50% pruning ratio, it achieves 1.29-1.33x average speedups on both simulation benchmarks, with overall success rates within 1.0 percentage point of the baseline.

Introduction sec:introduction r 0.34 Rethinking future-video generation for action prediction. fig:conceptual Extending foundation models to physical environments, particularly robotic manipulation, has recently attracted significant attention, due to their potential to enable robots to generalize across diverse tasks and environments. Vision-language-action (VLA) models represent a prominent approach brohan2023rt, kim2024openvla,black2024pi_0 , while world action models (WAMs) based on video diffusion models have emerged to better capture scene geometry, physical dynamics, and future state evolution kim2026cosmos,ye2026world . However, deploying these models on real robots requires not only high task performance but also low-latency inference black2026real . Since robotic manipulation requires repeated action generation throughout a task, inference latency accumulates across policy queries, delaying action execution and substantially increasing the overall task completion time. This problem is especially critical for WAMs due to the substantial computational overhead of video diffusion models, making efficient inference essential for their practical use in real-world manipulation. WAMs jointly generate robot actions and multiple future frames, introducing dense spatiotemporal token grids that account for a substantial portion of the computation in the video diffusion backbone. While VLAs address a similar bottleneck by pruning observation tokens yang2026efficientvla,li2025sp,wang2025specprune , directly pruning future-frame tokens is difficult because they constitute the model outputs in conventional video diffusion models and support action generation through future-state prediction in WAMs. Video diffusion acceleration therefore modifies attention masks xi2025sparse,xia2025training , but the cost of determining effective masks can offset the gains in few-step WAMs. Existing WAM methods instead reduce denoising steps ye2026world or redesign the model to bypass future generation yuan2026fast ; the former retains the per-step token burden, whereas the latter requires retraining. Consequently, existing WAM acceleration methods do not directly reduce future-frame tokens without additional training. We propose ( ), a training-free method for pruning future-frame tokens in WAMs. Our key insight is that, while video diffusion models are designed to generate high-fidelity videos, WAMs use future-frame prediction primarily as an intermediate reference for action generation. Therefore, as illustrated in Figure~ fig:conceptual , future representations must preserve task-relevant semantics and dynamics but need not retain every fine-grained visual detail. Allocating a dense grid of tokens to future frames is thus unnecessarily redundant for action prediction, motivating selective pruning that retains only the tokens needed for action generation without retraining. Realizing this potential requires identifying which future-frame tokens matter for action prediction early in denoising, when their representations remain highly noisy and their relevance is not yet explicit. Specifically, constructs an attention-based pruning criterion by analyzing the concentration of visual information with respect to action and instruction tokens, enabling effective token selection even when the action and future-frame latents remain highly noisy. Using only the initial forward pass, identifies redundant tokens early in the denoising process, thereby maximizing pruning efficiency while demonstrating that the internal representations available at the beginning of generation are sufficient to select future-frame tokens needed for action generation. Finally, introduces a phase identification mechanism that exploits entropy differences across camera views and temporal positions within the action sequence to identify precision phases and selectively relax pruning, mitigating performance degradation. Across RoboLab yang2026robolab , RoboCasa nasiriany2024robocasa , and real-world tasks, achieves consistent efficiency gains at a 35 pruning ratio: a speedup with a 1.3 percentage point success rate gain on RoboLab, a speedup with a 4.0 percentage point gain on RoboCasa, and a speedup with a 5.4 percentage point gain in real-world experiments. At a 50 pruning ratio, achieves at least a average inference speedup across both simulation benchmarks, while keeping success rates within 1.0 percentage point of the dense baseline. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We reconsider the auxiliary role of future frames in WAMs and formulate token pruning from the perspective of action prediction, exposing redundancy that is not considered in conventional video generation. We propose , a framework requiring no additional training that identifies redundant future frame tokens from noisy initial latents using their information concentration with respect to action and instruction tokens, while selectively relaxing pruning based on cross-view and temporal attention-entropy contrasts. We extensively evaluate on the RoboLab and RoboCasa simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks, demonstrating consistent improvements in inference efficiency while preserving manipulation performance. Related Work sec:relatedworks World Action Models World action models build upon video diffusion models to jointly predict robot actions and future visual states, transferring learned physical dynamics and predictive capabilities to robot control kim2026cosmos,ye2026world,agarwal2026cosmos . Existing approaches either adapt pretrained video diffusion models through post-training on robot demonstrations kim2026cosmos,ye2026world or jointly denoise video, action, and other multimodal tokens within a unified generator agarwal2026cosmos . Other methods predict compact latent future representations or decouple video and action decoding for efficient action inference zheng2025flare,li2025unifiedvideoactionmodel . More recent action-centered designs jointly train action prediction and future video generation ye2026gigaworld,yuan2026fast . Across these approaches, future-state prediction serves as a key source of supervision or predictive context for action generation. WAM Acceleration Although future prediction is a defining advantage of WAMs, it comes at substantial inference cost because generating numerous future-frame tokens significantly increases computation within the video diffusion backbone. Existing approaches reduce inference cost by using fewer denoising steps agarwal2026cosmos or enabling single-step inference through decoupled video and action noise schedules during training ye2026world . However, these methods accelerate inference by reducing denoising steps rather than making each step faster. Other approaches replace explicit future-frame prediction with compact future-state representations zheng2025flare or avoid explicit future-video generation during inference ye2026gigaworld,li2025unifiedvideoactionmodel,yuan2026fast . These methods require changes to the model architecture or training objective, making them difficult to apply directly to existing pretrained WAMs without additional training. In contrast, our approach directly reduces the future-frame token burden through token pruning, with no further training required. VLA Token Pruning Vision-language-action (VLA) models typically combine a pretrained VLM backbone with an action prediction module to generate robot actions from visual observations and language instructions. Because processing dense visual tokens through large VLM backbones incurs substantial inference costs, recent studies have adapted visual token pruning techniques chen2024image,zhang2024sparsevlm to VLA policies. Some methods select task-relevant and diverse visual tokens yang2026efficientvla or jointly consider spatial and semantic importance li2025sp , while others adjust pruning intensity across manipulation phases using recent robot motion pei2026action . Further approaches combine semantic and action-decoding attention liu2025bridging , incorporate historical context into current token selection wang2025specprune , or forecast deep-layer token importance from attention patterns stored at previous control steps ma2026safe . Overall, these methods extend VLM-based pruning to robotic policies, but are not directly applicable to noisy future-frame tokens, limiting their efficiency gains in WAMs where noisy future-frame tokens dominate computation. method sec:method Problem Formulation sec:problem_formulation WAM Architecture. Video-generative world action models extend video diffusion models with an action modality to jointly predict future visual states and robot action trajectories. Given a language instruction, visual observations, and the current robot state, a WAM denoises future-video and action representations through either modality-specific generation experts or a unified diffusion transformer ye2026world,bi2026motus,agarwal2026cosmos . The action prediction horizon denotes the number of future control steps generated by a single policy query. Since the complete action vector at each step is represented by one token, an action trajectory contains tokens regardless of the action dimensionality. In contrast, a future video is represented in the video VAE latent space as a spatiotemporal grid containing latent timesteps and spatial positions per timestep. Flattening this grid produces future-video tokens. Challenges. Even after spatiotemporal VAE compression, future-video tokens substantially outnumber action tokens, with , and dominate computation at every denoising step. Directly pruning these tokens, however, is challenging because they constitute the model output rather than observed visual inputs and are gradually denoised from Gaussian noise. Estimating their importance only after sufficient visual information emerges reduces the acceleration benefit, whereas pruning them too early may discard information required for accurate action prediction. We therefore aim to identify redundant future-video tokens early in denoising without further training, reducing inference cost while preserving manipulation performance. title: HyperLoop: Hyperspectral-Assisted Loop Closure Detection in 3D-SLAM for Planetary Exploration
comment: Paper accepted at International Astronautical Congress 2026, IAC-26,A3,IP,163,x107111
summary: Autonomous navigation of planetary rovers is challenged by visually repetitive, featureless terrain. SLAM systems based on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) offer dense mapping but rely on RGB appearance descriptors that degrade under perceptual aliasing - a common failure mode in extraterrestrial environments where physically distinct locations appear visually identical. This paper presents HyperLoop, the first framework integrating hyperspectral imaging (HSI) into the loop closure module of a 3DGS-based SLAM system. Hyperspectral descriptors encode material-level spectral signatures complementing RGB features, providing robustness to illumination changes and visual repetitiveness. Two HSI descriptor families are introduced: Bag-of-Spectral-Words (BoSW), encoding spectral material distributions via TF-IDF weighted histograms, and PCA-K VLAD (PCAK-VLAD), capturing first-order residual statistics of PCA-compressed spectral signatures. Both are evaluated with SIFT-VLAD and NetVLAD RGB descriptors under Strict-AND and Weighted fusion strategies on a custom dataset from the Moon-Mars Outdoor Test Site (MMOTS) at DLR, comprising synchronized RGB-D and hyperspectral sequences across four planetary analog traverses (65.5 m total). A key finding is that the sensor's Red-NIR range (600-860 nm) provides limited discriminability for rock terrain: the best HSI fusion (SIFT-VLAD + BoSW, Strict-AND) achieves 5.04 cm ATE RMSE, within 1.8% of SIFT-VLAD alone (4.95 cm). The gain over NetVLAD (8.81 cm) is attributable to SIFT-VLAD, not HSI fusion. This motivates future adoption of SWIR sensors capturing diagnostic mineral absorption features absent from the 600-860 nm range for planetary SLAM missions.

E-mail:~ 8pt plus 2pt minus 4pt 6pt plus 2pt minus 2pt 6pt plus 2pt minus 2pt Nomenclature ll & Pixel spectral signature \\ & PCA-projected pixel spectrum \\ & Local SIFT descriptor \\ & -th cluster centre (RGB or spectral codebook) \\ & Nearest-neighbour cluster assignment \\ & VLAD residual vector for cluster \\ & Codebook / vocabulary size \\ & Cosine similarity score \\ & Similarity threshold \\ & Set of detected loop closures \\ & Set of ground-truth loop closures \\ & 3DGS Gaussian opacity \\ & Weighted fusion coefficient \\ Acronyms/Abbreviations ll 3DGS & 3D Gaussian Splatting \\ ROS & Robot Operating System \\ ATE & Absolute Trajectory Error \\ BoSW & Bag-of-Spectral-Words \\ DLR & German Aerospace Center \\ FOV & Field of View \\ HSI & Hyperspectral Imaging \\ MMOTS & Moon-Mars Outdoor Test Site \\ NIR & Near-Infrared \\ PCAK-VLAD & PCA-K Vector of Locally Aggregated Descriptors \\ PGO & Pose Graph Optimisation \\ RMSE & Root Mean Square Error \\ SIFT & Scale-Invariant Feature Transform \\ SLAM & Simultaneous Localization and Mapping \\ SWIR & Shortwave Infrared \\ TF-IDF & Term Frequency--Inverse Document Frequency \\ VLAD & Vector of Locally Aggregated Descriptors \\ Introduction Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM)---the joint estimation of a robot's pose and a map of its surroundings from on-board sensor data---has reached remarkable maturity over the past two decades~ slam-handbook . Classical geometrically-grounded pipelines now achieve centimetre-level accuracy in structured environments, while recent semantic extensions such as 3D scene graph representations~ rotondi2026scenegraphs further enrich these maps with object-level and spatial reasoning. Yet this progress has been concentrated in information-rich, feature-dense settings: urban streets, indoor offices, and structured facilities where visual cues are abundant and predictable. Mapping in extreme environments---planetary surfaces dominated by featureless regolith, visually repetitive craters, and mineralogically diverse rocks---remains a frontier where classical SLAM assumptions break down. Autonomous navigation of planetary rovers must contend with exactly these conditions. Rovers must navigate unknown, unstructured terrain autonomously, performing in-situ scientific analysis while building consistent environmental representations. Unlike the structured, feature-rich urban environments common on Earth, extraterrestrial terrain is dominated by craters, regolith, rocks, and dust that create a visually repetitive landscape. This causes perceptual aliasing: distinct locations appear nearly identical to optical sensors. In SLAM, this directly impairs loop closure detection: the critical process of recognising a previously visited location to correct accumulated odometric drift. Failed loop closures produce corrupted maps and irrecoverable trajectory divergence, threatening mission success. Despite visual similarity, planetary terrain is often mineralogically diverse. Rocks of different composition, regolith with varying particle distributions, and exposed bedrock exhibit distinct spectral signatures in the infrared range, differences entirely invisible to conventional RGB cameras. Hyperspectral imaging (HSI) captures tens to hundreds of narrow spectral bands per pixel, encoding material composition and chemical properties as a high-dimensional fingerprint. These signatures reflect what a surface is made of rather than how it appears, and are inherently more robust to illumination changes. Recent advances in 3DGS~ kerbl2023 have transformed dense visual SLAM by enabling efficient, photorealistic scene representations. LoopSplat~ loopsplat2025 , the first 3DGS SLAM system with explicit loop closure, demonstrates compelling performance in structured indoor environments using NetVLAD~ netvlad2016 descriptors. However, its reliance on RGB appearance limits applicability to the visually uniform terrain of planetary environments. This paper introduces HyperLoop, extending LoopSplat by integrating hyperspectral sensing into its loop closure module. The key contributions are: [leftmargin=1.5em, noitemsep, topsep=2pt] A 3DGS-SLAM architecture integrating HSI loop closure detection, the first such combination, to the best of our knowledge. Two HSI descriptor families: BoSW and PCAK-VLAD, adapted from visual retrieval literature to spectral signatures. Evaluation of Strict-AND and Weighted decision-level fusion strategies combining RGB and HSI descriptors. The first empirical analysis of hyperspectral loop closure on a planetary analog dataset, yielding an empirically motivated spectral range hypothesis for future mission hardware selection. The remainder of this paper is organised as follows: Section~2 covers relevant background; Section~3 reviews related work; Section~4 describes the HyperLoop methodology; Section~5 presents the experimental setup; Section~6 analyses descriptor performance; Section~7 reports trajectory and loop closure results; Sections~8 and~9 discuss findings and conclude. Background SLAM and Loop Closure SLAM jointly estimates a robot's pose trajectory and map from on-board sensor data~ slam-handbook . Sensor noise causes odometric drift; loop closure corrects it by recognising a previously visited location, inserting a constraint, and triggering Pose Graph Optimisation (PGO)~ Grisetti2010ATO . The pipeline comprises (1)~place recognition via descriptor similarity and (2)~geometric verification via spatial consistency checks. In planetary terrain, both stages are challenged: perceptual aliasing degrades appearance-based retrieval, and surface planarity limits geometric filtering. 3D Gaussian Splatting and LoopSplat 3DGS~ kerbl2023 represents a scene as a collection of anisotropic 3D Gaussian primitives, each parameterised by position , covariance , opacity , and view-dependent colour encoded via spherical harmonics (SH, a basis for view-dependent appearance). Differentiable splatting projects each 3D Gaussian as a 2D Gaussian; overlapping splats are composited via depth-sorted alpha-blending, enabling gradient-based optimisation of all parameters. LoopSplat~ loopsplat2025 implements a real-time dense RGB-D SLAM system on 3DGS with explicit loop closure. It maintains submaps (groups of keyframes) for computational tractability. Tracking minimises photometric and geometric losses. Loop closure candidates are retrieved via NetVLAD cosine similarity and verified by computing the geometric overlap of Gaussian splats between candidate submaps. Confirmed loops trigger submap registration in Gaussian space followed by PGO. Hyperspectral Imaging A hyperspectral image is a data cube , where is the number of spectral bands. Each pixel stores a spectral signature: reflectance at wavelengths, encoding material composition. Raw measurements are converted to reflectance via calibration~ lihsi2019 : where and are white-reference and dark-reference frames respectively. This removes illumination intensity, making spectral measurements comparable across acquisitions. An additional spectral correction corrects for spectral cross-talk between mosaic filter elements. Multi-Modal Sensor Fusion Multi-modal sensor fusion combines information from heterogeneous sensors to improve robustness beyond what any single modality can achieve~ khaleghi2013 . Three levels of fusion are commonly distinguished. Early (data-level) fusion merges raw sensor measurements before any feature extraction, requiring tight spatial and temporal alignment between modalities. Feature-level fusion concatenates or projects intermediate representations into a shared embedding space, and is applicable when modalities share a common field of view. Decision-level (late) fusion combines independent per-modality decisions or scores, and is applicable even when modalities have mismatched resolutions, fields of view, or update rates--making it the most flexible strategy for heterogeneous sensor pairs. Related Work Visual SLAM in Unstructured Environments Classical visual SLAM systems including ORB-SLAM~ orbslam2015 and ORB-SLAM2~ orbslam2017 achieve strong performance in structured, feature-rich indoor and urban scenes; however, all RGB-based approaches degrade severely in texture-poor terrain where distinctive appearance cues are absent~ altawil2024 . Outdoor and planetary analog environments compound this by adding illumination variation, featureless regolith, and large-scale perceptual aliasing--distinct locations that appear visually identical. These conditions cause place recognition to fail systematically, leading to missed loop closures and unbounded trajectory drift. Recent work on 3DGS-based relocalization in planetary-analog terrain~ peribanez2026 independently confirms that RGB appearance alone is insufficient for reliable localization under these conditions. No existing RGB-only SLAM system reliably solves loop closure on planetary analog terrain. 3DGS-Based Dense SLAM Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF)~ nerf2020 introduced volumetric scene representations capable of photorealistic rendering but required slow offline optimisation incompatible with real-time robotics. 3DGS~ kerbl2023 replaced implicit networks with an explicit set of anisotropic Gaussian primitives, enabling real-time rendering. LoopSplat~ loopsplat2025 built the first loop-closed 3DGS SLAM system and serves as the direct baseline for this work. Concurrent work by Perib\' a n ez~et~al.~ peribanez2026 demonstrates 3DGS-based visual relocalization on planetary-analog terrain and confirms that standard 3DGS representations suffer from aliasing and sparse-view ambiguity under challenging outdoor conditions--precisely the failure mode HyperLoop targets at the loop closure stage. None of these systems incorporate non-visual sensing into their loop closure modules. Loop Closure Detection Classical place recognition uses visual vocabulary retrieval with hand-crafted features; a comprehensive overview is provided by~ arshad2021 . NetVLAD~ netvlad2016 improved robustness to viewpoint and illumination by training on large-scale urban datasets, but this introduces a domain gap for natural unstructured terrain where object-centric features are absent. VLAD aggregation~ jegou2010,netvlad2016 underpins both NetVLAD and the hand-crafted descriptor baselines evaluated in this work. To the best of our knowledge, all existing loop closure detectors in 3DGS-based dense SLAM operate on RGB appearance alone; under perceptual aliasing, appearance similarity provides no reliable signal. LiDAR-based and multimodal loop closure methods are well established in other SLAM frameworks~ arshad2021 , but none have been integrated into the 3DGS submap pipeline. Hyperspectral Imaging in Robotics and Remote Sensing HSI has been extensively used in remote sensing for material classification and mineral mapping~ lihsi2019 . Orbital instruments such as CRISM on the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter~ murchie2007 have successfully identified mineralogical diversity on planetary surfaces, and drone-based surveys have demonstrated discriminative rock spectral analysis at ground level~ lee2021 . Despite this maturity in remote sensing, integration of HSI into real-time robotic SLAM systems remains entirely unexplored. HyperLoop is, to the best of our knowledge, the first system to integrate hyperspectral sensing into the loop closure module of a 3DGS-based dense SLAM pipeline, closing the gap between orbital spectral mapping and ground-level autonomous navigation. title: VLRLA: Deployment-Time Adaptation of Vision-Language-Action Models through In-Context Reinforcement Learning
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual perception and language understanding with robot control, providing a foundation for instruction-conditioned manipulation. However, conventional pretrained VLA policies lack a mechanism for gradual adaptation through accumulated interaction experience during deployment. We therefore propose VLRLA, a general framework that equips existing VLA models with \textit{in-context reinforcement learning} capabilities for deployment-time adaptation. Our approach augments a VLA model with a reinforcement learning module that learns from historical observations, actions, rewards, and termination signals. During deployment, the policy gradually refines its action generation and progressively improves task success while keeping model parameters fixed. Our approach is also designed for general applicability and compatibility with diverse learning history construction strategies and model training pipelines. Finally, through extensive experiments, we systematically investigate the learning properties of VLRLA in simulation and demonstrate its ability to adapt to unseen scenarios during real-world deployment.
full_text: Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual perception and language understanding with robot control, providing a foundation for instruction-conditioned manipulation. However, conventional pretrained VLA policies lack a mechanism for gradual adaptation through accumulated interaction experience during deployment. We therefore propose VLRLA, a general framework that equips existing VLA models with in-context reinforcement learning capabilities for deployment-time adaptation. Our approach augments a VLA model with a reinforcement learning module that learns from historical observations, actions, rewards, and termination signals. During deployment, the policy gradually refines its action generation and progressively improves task success while keeping model parameters fixed. Our approach is also designed for general applicability and compatibility with diverse learning history construction strategies and model training pipelines. Finally, through extensive experiments, we systematically investigate the learning properties of VLRLA in simulation and demonstrate its ability to adapt to unseen scenarios during real-world deployment. Introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual observations and natural-language instructions to robot actions, enabling robots to interpret their surroundings and carry out user requests. Their potential applications span household assistance, warehouse logistics, and industrial manipulation collaborationOpenXEmbodimentRobotic2023,intelligence VisionLanguageActionModel2025,luoPreciseDexterousRobotic2025,aiP07SteerableGeneralist,xuRLTokenBootstrapping2026 . Conventional VLA methods learn from collected demonstrations and could generalize to new situations. However, demonstration-based training alone does not provide a mechanism for gradual adaptation after deployment. A robot may encounter an unfamiliar camera viewpoint, lighting condition, or instruction phrasing, each of which hinders task performance. The central limitation is therefore the inability to turn accumulated deployment experience into adaptive behavior. Online Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) or interactive Imitation Learning (IIL) provide routes to deployment-time adaptation through parameter updates, using reward feedback or corrective actions, respectively~ wagenmaker2025SteeringYourDiffusionPolicyLatentSpaceReinforcement,xuRLTokenBootstrapping2026,luoPreciseDexterousRobotic2025,intelligence VLAThat2025,panSOPScalableOnline2026 . However, these approaches have several drawbacks: 1) Collecting the samples needed for policy updates takes tens of minutes to hours and involves substantial human effort; 2) They typically require task-specific hyperparameter tuning; and 3) They update policy in each deployment environment, making it difficult to scale to multi-task settings. These motivate us to explore an adaptation mechanism that uses deployment feedback without parameter updates. In this work, we propose VLRLA, a framework for equipping VLA models with in-context Reinforcement Learning (RL) capabilities. The framework augments a VLA model with a RL module that learns to use past interactions for adaptation. During deployment, action generation is conditioned on a memory of previous interactions and reward feedback, while model parameters remain fixed. As experience accumulates, this memory informs refinements to subsequent behavior, helping policy adapt to the deployment environment. The intended result is gradual improvement in task success through continued interaction during deployment and no parameter updates. Existing VLA works vary across training datasets, policy architectures, and deployment tasks, we aim to develop a general VLRLA framework that accommodates various learning history construction strategies, policy instantiations, and integration strategies. Our contributions are as follows: [leftmargin=1em,topsep=0pt] We formulate deployment-time adaptation in VLA models as an in-context reinforcement learning problem, using accumulated interactions and reward feedback to inform subsequent decisions while keeping model parameters fixed. We propose a general framework that unifies learning history construction and adaptation-module integration to equip pretrained VLA models with in-context reinforcement learning capabilities across diverse data construction settings, model architectures, and deployment tasks. We conduct extensive experiments in simulation and on real-world robots to demonstrate the effectiveness of VLRLA. Our results show adaptation across multiple pretrained backbones and improved task success with accumulated experience, including on challenging unseen tasks. Related Work Vision-Language-Action Models. VLA models integrate visual and language representations with action prediction to support generalist robotic manipulation. Progress in this direction has centered on expanding the data and representations learning for training robot policies. The RT series~ RT1RoboticsTransformer2022,brohanRT2VisionLanguageActionModels2023,collaborationOpenXEmbodimentRobotic2023 advances generalist robot control through multi-task learning, web-scale vision-language knowledge transfer, and training across robot embodiments. OpenVLA~ kim2024OpenVLAOpenSourceVisionLanguageActionModela makes VLA modeling accessible through an open-source model trained on diverse robot demonstrations and designed to support efficient fine-tuning. ~ intelligence VisionLanguageActionModel2025 pursues open-world generalization by co-training on heterogeneous robot and web data, combining semantic subtask prediction with robot control. LingBot-VLA~ wuPragmaticVLAFoundation2026 further explores large-scale pretraining across multiple dual-arm robot configurations, releasing a model, training infrastructure, and evaluation data to support adaptation across tasks and platforms. In this work, we study how to equip existing VLA models with in-context Reinforcement Learning capabilities for deployment-time adaptation. Deep Reinforcement Learning. DRL enables policies to improve through trial-and-error. Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)~ schulmanProximalPolicyOptimization2017 uses a policy-gradient surrogate objective to learn from on-policy rollouts. Soft Actor-Critic (SAC)~ haarnojaSoftActorCriticAlgorithms2019 combines off-policy actor--critic learning with an entropy maximization framework for continuous control. Recent studies apply these policy optimization principles to finetune pretrained VLA models. Examining the generalization benefits of RL fine-tuning, liuWhatCanRL2026 report that PPO-based OpenVLA fine-tuning improves semantic and execution generalization over supervised fine-tuning. SimpleVLA-RL~ liSimpleVLARLScalingVLA2025 also combines parallel trajectory collection with VLA-specific training optimizations to scale reward-based RL for OpenVLA-OFT. Other methods focus on online DRL fine-tuning directly in real-world tasks: RLToken~ xuRLTokenBootstrapping2026 uses a compact representation from a pretrained VLA for sample-efficient online DRL fine-tuning. Similarly, DSRL~ wagenmaker2025SteeringYourDiffusionPolicyLatentSpaceReinforcement learns an RL policy over the latent-noise input of a frozen diffusion or flow policy. These methods require parameter updates during RL fine-tuning, whereas our work studies in-context adaptation with all parameters fixed. In-Context Learning. Recent robotics research explores how demonstrations, prompts, and interaction histories can guide action generation at inference time for VLA models. For adaptation from demonstrations, In-Context Robot Transformer (ICRT)~ fuInContextImitationLearning2024 predicts actions from sensorimotor trajectories, allowing new tasks to be specified through demonstration prompts without parameter fine-tuning. ~ aiP07SteerableGeneralist combines language, subgoal images, and episode metadata to steer task execution, highlighting the role of multimodal context in generalization. In concurrent work, RoboTTT~ jiangRoboTTTContextScaling2026 compresses visuomotor context into recurrent fast weights through test-time training, focusing on one-shot imitation from human videos and online corrections learned through DAgger~ rossReductionImitationLearning2011 distillation. Specifically, reward-driven adaptation is addressed by Algorithm Distillation (AD)~ laskinIncontextReinforcementLearning2022 which performs in-context RL in discrete simulation environments. In contrast, our work focuses on designing a general framework to equip existing VLA models with in-context RL capabilities across diverse learning history construction strategies and model settings with validated effectiveness in both simulation and real-world continuous robot control tasks. Preliminaries sec:preliminaries Vision-Language-Action Policy. At timestep , a VLA model receives a language instruction and an observation where is camera image and is robot proprioceptive state, then generates an action chunk where is the action-chunk length, is the dimension of each action, and contains the actions , excluding the endpoint . The robot controller then executes the action chunk before replanning. In-Context Reinforcement Learning. A trial is a sequence of interactions that may span multiple episodes of the same task. We define the available history as , with , where is the observed reward and marks an episode boundary. This history contains only completed interactions before step . An in-context RL policy performs action generation while keeping fixed. For tasks and a discount factor , the learning objective is to optimize the task return: Algorithm Distillation (AD). Algorithm Distillation (AD), introduced by laskinIncontextReinforcementLearning2022 , trains a causal sequence model on ordered learning histories collected from a source RL algorithm: Preserving the order of learning across episodes helps the model learn how action generation changes with experience. At deployment, the model could perform in-context RL and gradually improve the task return by conditioning on its own interaction history in unseen tasks, without parameter updates. Training Adaptive Vision-Language-Action Models sec:method Algorithm Distillation (AD) provides a principled approach to distilling RL algorithms into causal sequence models, but its integration with existing pretrained VLA models remains unexplored. VLA methods differ in their data collection procedures, training pipelines, and deployment settings. We therefore design VLRLA as a general framework and demonstrate its effectiveness across multiple settings. This section presents the VLRLA framework, illustrated in . Model Design Deployment-time adaptation requires a robotic policy to integrate visual and language information with interaction feedback, retain experience over long horizons, and generate continuous actions. Our design addresses these requirements through recurrent memory, pretrained visual-language representations, and two policy instantiations that connect these representations to action generation. Recurrent Memory. In robotic tasks, a trial can span multiple episodes and thousands of tokens. To reduce the substantial memory and computation costs of dot-product causal attention~ vaswaniAttentionAllYou2017 , we use recurrent memory similar to Transformer-XL~ daiTransformerXLAttentiveLanguage2019 . This mechanism combines causal attention within a local window of timesteps with attention to cached representations from earlier windows. The policy forward pass is expressed as where denotes the full policy with parameters , denotes memory from the preceding step, and the outputs are the updated memory and generated action chunk . Memory retains information across episodes within a trial, and model parameters remain fixed during deployment. Visual and Language Preprocessing. sec:method-architecture We reuse representations from a pretrained VLA model to avoid training a visual-language encoder from scratch.

title: MorphAct: Robot Policies Morphing with the Worlds They Act In
summary: Progress toward general intelligence in the physical world requires scaling robot learning across diverse environments and interactions. However, existing robot policies use shared parameters that remain fixed across interaction contexts. When different operations favor competing parameter adjustments, fitting their mixture can leave individual operations insufficiently adapted. Our atomic-task diagnostics reveal competing update directions in both vision-language and action parameters, with source-improving updates increasing loss on other tasks. This motivates MorphAct, a contextual parameterization framework that dynamically adjusts robot policy parameters as interaction contexts change. Two coupled generators produce context-dependent low-rank updates for the vision-language and action modules. Their coupling follows the policy's computational dependency: vision-language updates shape the representations that condition action-side parameter generation. Both generators are trained jointly through the native action objective, without operation labels or expert-adapter targets. MorphAct improves performance across three VLA backbones on LIBERO and Meta-World, with gains of up to 16.30%. In real-world evaluation, it achieves gains of up to 14% over $π_{0.5}$. Ablations support the benefits of contextual parameter generation and representation coupling.
full_text: Progress toward general intelligence in the physical world requires scaling robot learning across diverse environments and interactions. However, existing robot policies use shared parameters that remain fixed across interaction contexts. When different operations favor competing parameter adjustments, fitting their mixture can leave individual operations insufficiently adapted. Our atomic-task diagnostics reveal competing update directions in both vision--language and action parameters, with source-improving updates increasing loss on other tasks. This motivates MorphAct ``Morph,'' rooted in Greek morph\= e (``form''), means ``to transform.'' , a contextual parameterization framework that dynamically adjusts robot policy parameters as interaction contexts change. Their coupling follows the policy's computational dependency: vision--language updates shape the representations that condition action-side parameter generation. Ablations support the benefits of contextual parameter generation and representation coupling. Introduction Progress toward general intelligence in the physical world requires scaling robot learning across diverse environments, operations, and interactions driess2023palme,black2025pi0 . This expansion brings together heterogeneous perceptual and control demands within a shared model. Such diversity arises not only across tasks but also within a single interaction: placing an object in a tray involves approaching it, establishing contact, transporting it, and positioning it precisely. These operations require different visual cues and control behaviors, often under an unchanged instruction. As environmental and operational coverage expands, a central challenge is how a shared model can effectively accommodate these heterogeneous demands. Vision--language--action (VLA) models provide a promising foundation by combining pretrained multimodal representations with action prediction brohan2023rt2,kim2025openvla,black2025pi0,liu2025bridging . However, conventional VLA policies execute diverse interactions using a shared, static parameter configuration. Context changes their activations and predicted actions, but their effective weights remain fixed, including after full fine-tuning or low-rank adaptation hu2022lora,kim2025oft . Different operations must therefore be learned through shared parameters, even when their training signals favor competing updates---a source of interference in joint optimization yu2020pcgrad . This raises the question of how effectively shared parameters reconcile the demands of different operations. We investigate this question through operation-level diagnostics using demonstrations from the 65 atomic tasks in RoboCasa365 nasiriany2026robocasa365 . At a common policy checkpoint, we examine gradient alignment, the effect of a single update on other tasks, and the contributions of individual parameter groups. The diagnostics reveal competing update directions in both the vision--language and action modules. Every measured source-improving update also increases loss on batches from other tasks, while opposing parameter-group contributions can cancel within a module. These findings expose local adaptation trade-offs in shared parameter space. They motivate a shared parameter-generation mechanism whose outputs vary with the interaction context. To address this challenge, we introduce MorphAct, a contextual parameterization framework that enables robot policies to morph with changing interaction contexts (Figure~ fig:morphact-teaser ). MorphAct generates context-dependent low-rank parameter updates for the vision--language and action modules, allowing a shared policy to adjust its effective weights to the current interaction. Because vision--language adaptation changes the representations used for control, MorphAct couples the two generators by conditioning action-side parameter generation on the adapted representations. Both generators learn jointly through the native action objective, without operation labels or expert-adapter targets. Low-rank factors provide an efficient implementation of these contextual updates. We evaluate MorphAct on X-VLA, , and zheng2026xvla,black2025pi0,intelligence2025pi05 using LIBERO liu2023libero and Meta-World yu2020metaworld , comparing each backbone's baseline with MorphAct. Across the three backbones, MorphAct improves Meta-World average success by 7.57--16.30 ; on LIBERO, X-VLA, , and gain 4.15 , 2.50 , and 1.75 , respectively. Real-world evaluation with further yields gains of 8.00--14.00 across four manipulation tasks. Controlled X-VLA ablations on LIBERO show that fixed generation conditions, single-module adaptation, and action-side generation conditioned on pre-adaptation features each reduce mean success. These results support contextual parameterization and representation coupling for accommodating diverse manipulation demands. Our contributions are threefold: (1)~We identify parameter conflicts as a challenge to scaling robot learning across diverse environments and interactions through operation-level diagnostic experiments. (2)~We introduce MorphAct, whose representation-coupled generators produce context-dependent vision--language and action parameter updates and learn jointly through the native action objective. (3)~We demonstrate success gains on three VLA backbones, two simulation benchmarks, and four real-world tasks, with ablations supporting contextual generation and representation coupling. Parameter Conflicts Across Operations sec:diagnosis As robot learning expands across environments and interactions, static-parameter policies must reconcile diverse operational demands through the same weights. We examine whether different operations favor compatible changes to these parameters. Our diagnostics measure gradient alignment, one-step cross-task loss changes, and parameter-group contributions in both vision--language and action modules at a common checkpoint. Setup. We use demonstrations from the 65 atomic tasks in RoboCasa365 nasiriany2026robocasa365 , grouped by native task ID. All measurements use a fixed RoboCasa-pretrained checkpoint and the native action loss over the full vision--language (VLM) and action parameter sets. Each sampling round draws batches and from disjoint episodes of task . Gradient comparisons use across tasks and as a within-task reference. For one-step transfer, supplies the update and the target evaluation. Appendix~ app:diagnostics details sampling, numerical settings, and metrics. Conflicting Directions in Both Modules sec:module-interference We first ask whether different tasks favor compatible parameter changes. At the common checkpoint, we compute task-batch gradients separately for the VLM and action modules and compare their cosine similarity. A negative cosine indicates competing local descent directions yu2020pcgrad . Across 16 sampling rounds, negative alignment occurs in 47.80 of cross-task VLM comparisons and 48.28 of action comparisons, versus 38.94 and 42.69 within tasks (Figure~ fig:adaptation-diagnostics (a)). The within-task reference shows that update directions also vary among episodes of the same task, while cross-task comparisons produce negative alignment more frequently. Competing adaptation demands therefore affect both the representations used for control and the action mapping. Cross-Task Interference from Parameter Updates sec:one-step-transfer Gradient alignment describes local update directions; we next measure the loss changes produced by an actual update. For each source batch , we take one full-parameter gradient step and evaluate the target batches , restarting from the common checkpoint for every source. Target observations, action targets, flow times, and noise remain fixed before and after the step. Across four rounds, all 260 updates reduce their source-batch loss, with a mean relative reduction of 2.38 . Yet each update increases loss on batches from 22--46 of the other 64 tasks, with a median of 32 (Figure~ fig:adaptation-diagnostics (b)). Every source-improving update thus has both helpful and harmful effects on other tasks: improving the source does not produce uniformly beneficial transfer across manipulation contexts. Conflicting Contributions Across Parameter Groups sec:contribution-cancellation The preceding comparisons summarize each module as a whole. To examine the interactions within these summaries, we decompose gradient alignment across 47 VLM groups and 19 action groups, including individual Transformer blocks shi2023recon . Each group's gradient inner product is normalized by the same full-module gradient norms, so the contributions sum to the module-level cosine. Positive and negative contributions can offset one another. We sum the absolute contribution mass canceled within each pair and divide by the total absolute contribution mass across comparisons. For cross-task pairs, cancellation reaches 36.13 in the VLM and 30.90 in the action module, compared with 23.51 and 22.70 within tasks (Figure~ fig:adaptation-diagnostics (c)). A small module-level cosine can therefore reflect opposing parameter-group contributions rather than uniformly weak interactions. Appendix~ app:diagnostic-groups reports the complete group definitions and decomposition. Implication for MorphAct. Together, these results show that adaptation demands differ across tasks and act on both representation and action parameters. An update that serves one context can work against another, with opposing contributions hidden by module-level summaries. This motivates sharing the adaptation mechanism while allowing its updates to depend on the current context. MorphAct uses two generators connected by the adapted visual--language representation. MorphAct: Morph with the Environment and Then Act sec:morphact MorphAct adjusts robot policy parameters to the current interaction context before predicting an action chunk (Figure~ fig:morphact-overview ). Two generators produce context-dependent updates for the vision--language and action modules, with action-side generation conditioned on the adapted vision--language representations. We describe this coupled generation process and its low-rank parameterization, then explain how both generators learn through the native action objective and how their outputs are reused within each action chunk. We denote the base policy parameters by , with vision--language and action modules parameterized by and . MorphAct generates for selected projections and predicts an action chunk as , suppressing sampling randomness. The generator weights are shared across contexts, while their outputs determine the context-dependent effective parameters. The two updates follow the policy's computational dependency: vision--language adaptation changes the representations used for control, so action-side generation conditions on the adapted features. Both are outputs of the same adapted VLM pass. In and , they correspond to final multimodal prefix tokens and layer-wise prefix key--value states, respectively. The constructor appends a robot-state token projected by to . Thus, the generators have separate parameters but are connected through the representation produced by upstream adaptation. title: FoveaVLA: Foveation Actions Replace the Wrist Camera in VLAs
summary: We present FoveaVLA, a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model that replaces the wrist camera with learned foveation actions. Wrist cameras provide close-up detail but restrict the view to the end-effector's surroundings. External cameras see the whole scene, but the policy receives them at low resolution, so the fine detail needed for manipulation is lost. FoveaVLA recovers this detail by predicting, alongside each action chunk, the interaction region to observe at the next policy query. The policy then receives crops of these regions, taken from the original-resolution images, together with the full views. We build FoveaVLA on $π_{0.5}$ in two configurations, Single and Dual, using one or two external stereo cameras with full and foveal RGB and depth inputs, and post-train both on DROID with RoboInter interaction annotations. Across four real-world task suites, FoveaVLA-Single achieves 70.8% success with one external RGB-D view, and FoveaVLA-Dual achieves 77.1%, versus 52.1% for the wrist-equipped $π_{0.5}$. Both match the baseline on plain pick-and-place and improve success with distractors, cloth manipulation, and far-away objects.
full_text: Experiments sec:experiments We evaluate learned foveation through five questions: (Q1) Can learned foveation replace the wrist camera? (Q2) What do foveal crops add beyond box supervision? (Q3) What do depth and a second view add? (Q4) Does the policy transfer to unseen environments? (Q5) Can the policy predict where to look next? Experimental Setup sec:exp:setup Data and training We post-train from the base checkpoint on DROID~ khazatsky2024droid , comprising K teleoperated Franka Panda episodes with a Robotiq 2F-85 gripper, two external stereo cameras, and a wrist camera. Our models use only external views and RoboInter interaction-box supervision~ li2026robointer (Sec.~ sec:training ), following the open-source training recipe~ openpi . All models are trained on eight NVIDIA H100 GPUs with a global batch size of . Appendix~ app:data details the data construction, and Appendix~ app:implementation gives the training and inference settings for Single and Dual. Tasks and protocol We evaluate on the real DROID setup across four suites: uncluttered, near-object Pick-and-Place; Pick-and-Place with Distractors; Fold/Unfold with near and far cloth placements; and Move with far objects. All methods share the same randomized object, placement, and prompt instances per suite ( trials total). The external cameras are placed by hand without extrinsic calibration. Appendix~ app:real_world lists the complete task instances and success criteria. Trials run at a target \,Hz for at most control steps, stopping early if continued execution risks robot damage. Success requires full task completion; we report mean success standard error of the mean (SEM), in percent, over trials per suite and pool all for Overall. Models and comparisons -Single and -Dual use one and two external RGB-D views, respectively, with full and foveal RGB and depth inputs (four images per view). We compare against wrist-equipped , which shares our base checkpoint and training data, and its deployment-time wrist blackout, ; -Single-External and -Dual-External variants, which were post-trained with one or two full external RGB views without a wrist view, box prediction, or crops; and -Single-External-RGB-D and -Dual-External-RGB-D, which add depth to the full views. ~ zawalski2024robotic uses two external RGB views and our box supervision but no crops. and retain foveation while removing depth from Single and Dual. The blackout tests how much relies on the wrist view at deployment, and the external-only baselines test how well a policy learns from external views alone. Replacing the Wrist Camera (Q1) sec:exp:real -Single achieves overall success using one external RGB-D view and -Dual , compared with for wrist-equipped . Both match the baseline's success on plain Pick-and-Place and achieve higher success on the other three suites (Fig.~ fig:main_task_results ). Table~ tab:results reports all baselines and ablations. Close-up detail across the workspace With a single external RGB-D view, success on Distractors rises from the wrist-equipped baseline's to , and success on Move rises from to . Dual achieves the strongest Fold/Unfold and Move results ( and ). Figure~ fig:attention suggests why: places almost all image attention on the wrist view and almost none on the external view, so it can miss a target outside the wrist view. keeps attending to the full external views, which cover the workspace, while the crops add close-up detail. Inference latency On an RTX 5080, -Single takes approximately \,ms per policy query (prefix encoding and action generation) and \,ms for cached-prefix box decoding. -Dual takes roughly twice as long. Box timing includes all camera views and coordinate conversion. title: Tactile-Guided Robot Learning: From Representation Learning to Foundation Models
summary: Tactile sensing is becoming central to robust, adaptive, and dexterous robotic manipulation. Beyond its traditional role in contact detection and reactive control, touch is increasingly used to learn transferable representations, condition manipulation policies, and support embodied physical reasoning. Yet existing surveys largely emphasize tactile hardware and perception, leaving the rapid shift toward learning-based tactile manipulation insufficiently synthesized. This paper reviews tactile-guided skill learning from a learning-centric perspective, organized by the functional role of touch across the learning and control pipeline. We examine tactile representation and policy learning, tactile foundation models, predictive and adaptive control, and generalization across objects, tasks, sensors, embodiments, and simulation-to-real transfer. Across these directions, we identify common design principles and remaining challenges in learning transferable physical representations, integrating semantic reasoning with contact-level control, and scaling tactile learning across heterogeneous data and hardware. Finally, we outline emerging directions toward tactile foundation and world models that can predict, reason about, and adapt physical interactions. Together, this review characterizes the transition of touch from a task-specific feedback signal toward a core modality for general-purpose embodied intelligence. An accompanying database of the reviewed literature and associated resources is available at https://sites.google.com/view/touch-in-robot-learning-review.

Yet existing surveys largely emphasize tactile hardware and perception, leaving the rapid shift toward learning-based tactile manipulation insufficiently synthesized. This paper reviews tactile-guided skill learning from a learning-centric perspective, organized by the functional role of touch across the learning and control pipeline. We examine tactile representation and policy learning, tactile foundation models, predictive and adaptive control, and generalization across objects, tasks, sensors, embodiments, and simulation-to-real transfer. Across these directions, we identify common design principles and remaining challenges in learning transferable physical representations, integrating semantic reasoning with contact-level control, and scaling tactile learning across heterogeneous data and hardware. Finally, we outline emerging directions toward tactile foundation and world models that can predict, reason about, and adapt physical interactions. Together, this review characterizes the transition of touch from a task-specific feedback signal toward a core modality for general-purpose embodied intelligence. An accompanying database of the reviewed literature and associated resources is available at paper web page . Tactile sensing, robot learning, robotic manipulation, tactile world models. Introduction Dexterous manipulation remains a major challenge in developing robots capable of human-level adaptability in unstructured environments lepora2024future . Despite substantial advances in perception, planning, control, locomotion, and embodied AI, robots still struggle with everyday contact-rich tasks such as precision insertion, deformable-object manipulation, and assembly under uncertainty billard2019trends . Unlike more structured robotic tasks, manipulation requires continuous regulation of physical interactions among the robot, objects, and environment cui2021toward . Successful manipulation therefore depends not only on detecting contact, but on estimating and regulating evolving contact locations, forces, friction, compliance, and interaction dynamics, often across multiple simultaneous contacts. These quantities are difficult to infer reliably from vision alone, particularly under occlusion and during fine manipulation, making tactile perception and tactile-guided control essential for robust and dexterous interaction li2025developments . Recent tactile sensors can capture high-resolution contact geometry, force distributions, deformation, and slip genesis2026gene265, zhao2025embedding , while advances in imitation learning tsuji2025survey , reinforcement learning kim2026robot , diffusion policies chi2025diffusion , Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models ma2026survey , and embodied AI feng2026multi have substantially expanded robots' ability to learn complex manipulation skills from data o2024open . Yet these developments remain only partially connected, where modern policies are still predominantly vision-centric and often treat touch as auxiliary information comanici2025gemini, black2024pi_0 . This limits their ability to reason about physical interactions in tasks where contact dynamics, rather than visual appearance alone, determine successful execution. The role of touch in robot learning is consequently shifting from estimating low-level quantities such as contact, slip, force, and object properties howe1993tactile toward providing physically grounded information throughout the learning and control pipeline. Tactile observations now support representation learning higuera2024sparsh , multimodal policy learning, physical reasoning huang2025tactile, morissette2026tactile, yang2024binding , adaptive decision making, and embodied world modeling cheng2026omnivtla . This shift reframes the central question from how robots can sense touch to how robots can learn from and act through touch. Despite rapidly growing work across tactile sensing, robot learning, computer vision, and embodied AI, this literature remains fragmented. Existing surveys largely emphasize sensor hardware, sensing principles, classical tactile perception, or earlier tactile-guided manipulation and control li2020review, kroemer2021review . Many also predate recent developments in foundation models and VLA systems and therefore do not capture the emerging role of touch within modern learning-based manipulation lepora2024future, jin2023progress, meribout2024tactile, mandil2023tactile, jahanshahi2025comprehensive, cho2024current, yu2025recent, zhang2022hardware, luo2025tactile, fang2025force, xie2025towards, hu2023machine, yao2024recent, xu2023recent, liu2023progress, huang2024recent, man2022recent, zhu2022recent, kroemer2021review . A unified learning-centric account of how tactile information contributes across representation, policy learning, embodied reasoning, and generalization is therefore still lacking. To address this gap, we organize the review according to the functional role of tactile information within learning-based manipulation (Fig.~ fig:scope ). We examine six research questions. RQ1 considers how tactile observations are represented, encoded, and fused with other modalities, covering self-supervised dave2024multimodal, xu2025unit , multimodal cheng2025touch100k, feng2026anytouch , and cross-modal representation learning fu2024a . RQ2 examines how touch conditions action generation through imitation learning 11455918 , reinforcement learning miller2026enhancing , diffusion policies xue2025reactive , and multimodal policy architectures. RQ3 investigates tactile-informed foundation and world models, including tactile-enhanced VLAs hao2026tla , multimodal world models zhang2026contactworld , and foundation controllers you2026tebi , where touch supports physically grounded reasoning and planning. RQ4 considers predictive and adaptive tactile control, where tactile feedback supports interaction-state estimation, feedback regulation, contact prediction, online optimization, and adaptation under uncertain physical interactions yin2025learning,xu2024letac,zhao2026tacman,nazari2025bioinspired,pmlr-v205-nazari23a . RQ5 evaluates generalization beyond training conditions across objects, tasks, sensors, robot embodiments, environments, and simulation-to-real transfer. Finally, RQ6 synthesizes these developments to identify the remaining challenges and research directions toward scalable tactile foundation models, general-purpose manipulation, and lifelong tactile learning. Tactile Representation Learning sec:representation Tactile sensing provides localized observations of physical interaction shaped by contact dynamics, sensor mechanics, and robot motion johansson2009coding . Raw tactile measurements, however, are often high-dimensional and sensor-dependent, with manipulation-relevant properties such as contact geometry, loading, deformation, and slip only implicitly encoded. Tactile representations bridge sensing and action by extracting compact, task-relevant features while preserving the spatial and temporal information required for perception, prediction, and control. While early approaches relied on physically motivated descriptors such as marker displacement, pressure distributions, and vibration spectra, recent work increasingly learns representations through supervised, self-supervised, multimodal, and multi-sensor training cao2026tactile , aiming for reusable features with reduced dependence on task-specific labels and sensor characteristics. This section examines four aspects of tactile representation learning, including learning informative features from unlabeled interaction data (Sec.~III-A); fusing touch with complementary sensing modalities (Sec.~III-B); aligning touch with pre-trained vision-language embedding spaces to exploit their semantic structure (Sec.~III-C); and, finally, assessing whether representations learned on particular sensors, tasks, or embodiments transfer beyond their training conditions (Sec.~III-D). Self-Supervised Tactile Representation Learning Self-supervised learning enables tactile representations to be learned from unlabeled interaction data gui2024survey, lee2018making , avoiding physically motivated preprocessing such as marker tracking li2023marker , finite-element modeling sferrazza2019ground , or task-specific descriptors. Unlike vision, where large-scale datasets and pretrained models are readily available russakovsky2015imagenet , tactile data require physical interaction and remain strongly sensor-dependent. Recent approaches therefore exploit data collected through robotic exploration, demonstration, or in-the-wild interaction yang2022touch , using reconstruction, contrastive learning, self-distillation, masked modeling, or action-conditioned prediction mandil2022action to learn reusable tactile features. Reconstruction-based methods require an encoded latent state to retain sufficient information for recovering the original observation, or components removed from it. Although scalable, this objective may preserve sensor-specific appearance rather than physically relevant interaction variables. Early work mura2020grasp used a recurrent conditional autoencoder to encode fingertip-force sequences for vision-free grasping, transferring the representation to material recognition and grasp-stability estimation. UniT xu2025unit instead introduces vector quantization van2017neural , using a VQGAN to encode tactile images as discrete tokens; despite pretraining on a single simple object, its structured latent space transfers zero-shot to unseen-object pose estimation and classification and to three real-world policy-learning tasks. Following masked modeling he2022masked , TacMAE cao2023mask reconstructs masked tactile-image regions, achieving 71.4 zero-shot and 85.8 fine-tuned accuracy on unseen YCB objects. For structured 3D tactile arrays, wu2025canonical reconstructs masked local forces from taxel coordinates, poses, and forces before transferring the encoder to a visuo-tactile Diffusion Policy. Finally, li2025tactile represents tactile observations as modulated neural implicit functions using a shared SIREN trunk, substantially reducing storage while retaining information for downstream pose estimation. Collectively, these methods progress from reconstructing raw sequences and pixels toward discrete tokens, physical force fields, and continuous functions, introducing stronger structural priors to encourage more transferable representations. Contrastive learning methods forgo reconstruction and instead enforce similarity between observations of the same interaction while separating distinct interactions.
