title: FPV-CRASH: A Dataset for Offline Crash Moment Localization in Drone First-Person-View Videos
summary: Crash Moment Localization aims to localize the major physical impact that interrupts controlled flight in an onboard first-person-view (FPV) video recorded by a drone, thereby providing a temporal reference for retrospective crash analysis in aerial robotics. However, existing crash-video datasets predominantly target surveillance or dash-camera footage, and their annotation schemes and task formulations are not designed for temporal localization of the major physical impact in UAV onboard FPV videos. To address this gap, we present FPV-CRASH, a dataset and fixed-protocol reference evaluation for offline Crash Moment Localization in drone FPV videos. FPV-CRASH contains 1,052 drone FPV clips (526 Crash and 526 Normal); each Crash clip has a single-frame reference annotation for the Crash Moment, and every clip is paired with four English captions automatically generated from sampled frames and the known Crash/Normal label. Normal clips carry no timestamp target and provide training-time background supervision. The captions support an auxiliary Text-to-Video Retrieval task, whereas localization inference remains video-only. We further provide a heatmap-based reference model that estimates a continuous Crash Moment timestamp from sparsely sampled frames. Under the fixed, non-source-disjoint clip-level protocol, the reference model reduces MAE from 1.12 s for the strongest fixed timing-prior baseline to 0.56 s (a 50% relative reduction) and achieves a median absolute error (MedAE) of 0.33 s; the fraction of clips localized within 0.5 s rises from 37.14% to 65.71%. The release includes annotations, available source video identifiers and URLs, clipping metadata, fixed split lists, and preprocessing code so that the reportable portion can be reconstructed without redistributing source footage. At submission time, all source-compilation URLs remained accessible.
full_text: Crash Moment Localization aims to localize the major physical impact that interrupts controlled flight in an onboard first-person-view (FPV) video recorded by a drone, thereby providing a temporal reference for retrospective crash analysis in aerial robotics. However, existing crash-video datasets predominantly target surveillance or dash-camera footage, and the corresponding annotation schemes and task formulations are not designed for temporal localization of the major physical impact in UAV onboard FPV videos. To address this gap, we present FPV-CRASH, a dataset and fixed-protocol reference evaluation for offline Crash Moment Localization in drone FPV videos. FPV-CRASH contains 1,052 drone FPV clips, with 526 Crash and 526 Normal clips; each Crash clip has a single-frame reference annotation for the Crash Moment, and every clip is paired with four automatically generated from sampled frames and the known Crash/Normal label English captions. Normal clips carry no timestamp target and contribute training-time background supervision only. The captions support an auxiliary Text-to-Video Retrieval task, whereas localization inference remains video-only. We further provide a heatmap-based reference model that estimates a continuous Crash Moment timestamp from sparsely sampled frames. Under the fixed clip-level protocol, the reference model reduces MAE from 1.12s for the strongest fixed timing-prior baseline to 0.56s (a 50 relative reduction) and achieves a median absolute error (MedAE) of 0.33s; the fraction of clips localized within 0.5s rises from 37.14 to 65.71 . The release contains the annotations, available source video identifiers and URLs, temporal clipping information, fixed split lists, and preprocessing code so that the reportable portion can be reconstructed without redistributing the original source footage. At submission time, all recorded source-compilation URLs remained accessible. Introduction Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are increasingly used for visual data capture~ zheng2023uavm . Their first-person-view (FPV) videos record flight motion and environmental contact, but a Crash/Normal label does not identify when controlled flight is interrupted. Localizing the major physical impact provides a temporal anchor for retrospective FPV crash analysis.The resulting timestamp provides a boundary between pre-impact flight and post-impact evidence, supporting targeted review of variable-length crash clips. Prior UAV research addresses high-speed flight, collision-driven navigation, online collision response, and accident forensics~ delmerico2019uzhfpv,gandhi2017learning,wang2024air,editya2024visual . Much of this work targets online operation; we instead locate the major impact in a fully observed FPV video. At inference, the model receives only a complete video and returns one continuous Crash Moment timestamp without a text query. FPV-CRASH contains 1,052 class-balanced clips, 4,208 captions, and single-frame Crash Moment references for 526 Crash clips. It uses a fixed class-stratified 60/20/20 split; localization (Fig.~ fig:crash_moment_localization ) is evaluated on Crash clips, while Normal clips provide background supervision. Our reference model combines sparse sampling with temporal modeling to predict continuous timestamps; optional video--text alignment provides training-time supervision and auxiliary retrieval, while localization inference remains video-only. We evaluate positional encoding, training-time text supervision, and Normal background supervision. Our contributions are as follows: We construct FPV-CRASH: 1,052 class-balanced FPV clips from approximately 40 crash compilations and three normal-flight compilations, with single-frame Crash Moment references and four automatically generated captions per clip (4,208 captions in total). We define Crash Moment Localization and its fixed evaluation protocol, and provide a heatmap-based reference model for continuous timestamp prediction. We examine positional encoding, training-time text supervision, and Normal background supervision under the fixed protocol, with detailed results discussed in Experiments. Among the controlled component ablations, the largest observed degradations occur when all heatmap BCE terms or slot encoding are removed, increasing MAE from 0.5585s to 0.8508s and 1.4221s, respectively. Related Work Visual Data and Autonomous Flight. Onboard UAV datasets cover state estimation and localization (EuRoC, Zurich Urban MAV~ burri2016euroc,majdik2017zurich ), high-speed flight (UZH-FPV~ delmerico2019uzhfpv ), and varied sensing conditions (INSANE~ brommer2024insane ); Race Against the Machine covers autonomous and piloted racing~ bosello2024ratm and FWAF-VID aggressive flapping-wing flight~ jiang2025fwafvid , but none provides crash-centered frame-level annotations. UAV vision research instead studies drone--satellite matching~ wang2022eachpart , language-guided geo-localization~ chu2024geotext , tracking with semantic conditioning or hierarchical feature aggregation~ blei2025cloudtrack,li2025cgtrack , time-optimal trajectory planning~ qin2024time , and risk-aware UAV--UGV routing~ mondal2025risk ---objectives that differ from retrospective localization of a physical crash impact. Collision Avoidance, Detection, and Failure Understanding. Collision-oriented UAV research targets prevention or online response: Learning to Fly by Crashing learns navigation from collision experience~ gandhi2017learning , ColANet provides collision-avoidance data~ pedro2020colanet , and later methods use optical flow~ pedro2021collision , integrated perception, planning, and control~ liu2025dynamic , or vision-transformer policies~ bhattacharya2025vision . After-impact work includes Air Bumper's inertial collision detection, recovery, and mapping~ wang2024air and pre-/post-accident frame labels and explanations from FPV videos~ editya2024visual . Fault-detection methods flag anomalous states or component faults~ keipour2019automatic,keipour2021alfa,le2025rflymad , which need not coincide with physical impact. We instead localize the major impact interrupting controlled flight from a complete video, rather than predicting, avoiding, or diagnosing failures online. Event Localization. Temporal localization targets point or interval events: SoccerNet casts timestamp prediction as action spotting~ giancola2018soccernet , ActivityNet Captions associates events with described intervals~ krishna2017dense , and temporal action localization estimates action boundaries or intervals~ lin2019bmn,zhang2022actionformer . Natural-language moment retrieval conditions interval prediction on a query~ zhang2020tan,lei2021qvhighlights , with active learning reducing annotation cost~ ji2023binary . Ego4D introduces Moment Queries for activity-interval localization and a Point-of-No-Return task for state-change keyframe localization~ grauman2022ego4d . ACCIDENT localizes traffic impacts in fixed-view surveillance videos~ picek2026accident , while accident anticipation predicts events from partial observations~ chan2016anticipating . In contrast, our task returns one major physical-impact timestamp from a fully observed drone FPV video, without an inference-time query. Representation Alignment. Contrastive vision--language learning aligns visual and textual embeddings~ radford2021clip , and Frozen in Time extends this to video~ bain2021frozen ; CLIP4Clip studies temporal aggregation~ luo2022clip4clip , Align and Tell combines local alignment with captioning supervision~ wang2023align , and GRAM uses a Gramian-volume objective for multimodal alignment~ cicchetti2025gramian . Our implementation adapts the official GRAM codebase, retaining its encoder organization and contrastive projection heads but excluding GRAM's Gramian-volume and data--anchor objectives; we instead employ video--text alignment with a scalar temperature and add a Temporal Transformer, Gaussian heatmap target, temporal localization head, and masked-Softmax expectation decoder for Crash Moment prediction. FPV-CRASH Dataset FPV-CRASH provides continuous onboard FPV clips with Crash/Normal labels, single-frame Crash Moment annotations for Crash clips, and English captions. Crash Definition and Annotation Protocol A Crash requires visible or highly credible physical contact that causes a loss of controlled flight or terminates the flight. The Crash Moment is the major impact after which control is not recovered, not an earlier light contact. Crashes involving a briefly occluded impact, water contact, rebound, or short post-impact motion qualify when the collision and interruption remain highly credible. Uncontrolled descents, blackouts, frozen imagery, and abrupt endings without an observable or highly credible contact event are excluded. FPV-CRASH may therefore under-represent impacts with occluded, poorly illuminated, or missing contact evidence. A primary annotator assigns each Crash clip a single-frame reference timestamp through repeated playback and frame-level inspection; ambiguous samples are excluded. The annotation records a frame index and its 30-fps timestamp. Because an impact may span adjacent frames, this is a temporal reference rather than a uniquely precise physical instant. A second annotator independently re-annotated 53 Crash clips (10 of the Crash set); the two references fall within 0.5s on 85.7 and within 1s on 95.2 of these clips, and the two annotators agree on whether an annotatable impact is present with Cohen's = 0.88. Data Collection and Curation Publicly accessible YouTube compilations provide the source material: approximately 40 crash compilations and three longer normal-flight compilations. The dataset is class-balanced but not source-balanced. We retain continuous single-drone FPV sequences and discard mixed viewpoints, adjacent edits, duplicates, and severe visual defects. Crash compilations routinely re-upload the same underlying footage under different edits, so per-compilation deduplication cannot catch reuse across sources: we therefore add an all-pairs near-duplicate scan over all 1,052 clips (CLIP-feature cosine similarity plus a perceptual hash) and report 13 pairs above the duplicate threshold. Because the split is clip-disjoint but not source-disjoint, a reused clip that lands in both Train and Test would let a model read the timestamp off a memorized instance, so the scan is a precondition for the headline MAE rather than a housekeeping step. We use content-change detection and manual refinement to segment Crash clips, retaining continuous pre-impact flight, the major collision, and sufficient post-impact evidence. Individually selected boundaries produce variable clip and pre-impact durations. For Normal clips, visual-change-based scene detection generates candidates; we sample away from edits, select durations broadly comparable to Crash clips, and screen for continuous flight without collisions or severe defects. We standardize all 1,052 clips to 30 fps without audio while retaining their original spatial resolution, and manually review them for completeness and visual quality. Each clip has four English captions generated with qwen3.7-plus from Alibaba Cloud Model Studio using sampled frames and the known Crash/Normal class. Class-conditioned generation reduces gross class inconsistency but may make text-supervision effects partly reflect class separation. Captions contain no Crash Moment timestamp, provide only auxiliary training supervision, and are unnecessary for video-only localization inference. We check generation completion programmatically, but captions receive no formal human correctness audit and are not exhaustively reviewed or edited; therefore, they are excluded from semantic dataset statistics. All source footage is third-party, publicly accessible material. We do not redistribute video; we release identifiers, timestamps, and preprocessing code only, and we describe how removal requests are handled. Th

title: Atomic-WAM: Execution-Grounded Atomic-Motion Reasoning for World Action Models
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) typically adapt video foundation models to robotic control through joint video and action prediction. However, task-level instructions may leave the next physical interaction underspecified, requiring semantic grounding and state-dependent motion selection. To this end, we introduce Atomic-WAM, an understand-then-execute framework that connects task reasoning to action generation through atomic-motion descriptions. Specifically, a vision-language reasoner describes the next local motion from the task instruction and visual context, guiding a WAM to predict future video and an action chunk. Furthermore, an automatic annotation pipeline curates temporally aligned, contact-enriched supervision from multi-view DROID demonstrations. To make atomic-motion predictions executable by the WAM, we post-train the reasoner with Execution-Grounded GRPO (EG-GRPO). With the WAM fixed, EG-GRPO adapts the reasoner through rewards for motion appropriateness and execution success. Finally, Atomic-WAM achieves 39.6% task success under default instructions and 31.6% under vague instructions in a real-to-sim evaluation on RoboLab. However, task-level instructions may leave the next physical interaction underspecified, requiring semantic grounding and state-dependent motion selection. To this end, we introduce Atomic-WAM, an understand-then-execute framework that connects task reasoning to action generation through atomic-motion descriptions. Specifically, a vision-language reasoner describes the next local motion from the task instruction and visual context, guiding a WAM to predict future video and an action chunk. Furthermore, an automatic annotation pipeline curates temporally aligned, contact-enriched supervision from multi-view DROID demonstrations. To make atomic-motion predictions executable by the WAM, we post-train the reasoner with Execution-Grounded GRPO (EG-GRPO). With the WAM fixed, EG-GRPO adapts the reasoner through rewards for motion appropriateness and execution success. Finally, Atomic-WAM achieves 39.6 task success under default instructions and 31.6 under vague instructions in a real-to-sim evaluation on RoboLab. \\ Project page: https://ssj9596.github.io/Atomic-WAM-project Introduction sec:introduction World Action Models (WAMs) transfer visual and motion priors from video foundation models to robotic control by jointly predicting future visual states and actions~ pai2025mimic,ye2026world,li2026causal,kim2026cosmos,agarwal2026cosmos3 . Through video pretraining, these models acquire rich dynamic priors for modeling physically plausible future evolution. However, robot control further requires determining which local evolution is appropriate under the current task and state. Given a fixed task-level instruction, the object to manipulate, the current interaction phase, and the local motion to execute are often not explicitly specified. Such task-level conditioning leaves two related requirements to the executor. First, a semantic grounding gap arises when categories, relations, or desired outcomes must be translated into concrete object interactions. For example, Put the red things in the bin requires identifying the relevant objects and deciding how to manipulate them. Second, a temporal granularity gap arises because a task instruction can remain unchanged as execution progresses through approach, alignment, grasp, transport, and release~ wallwm . Descriptive video pretraining does not by itself establish how to resolve these decisions in closed-loop control. Figure~ fig:conditioning illustrates the sensitivity of video predictions to language specificity, motivating a more explicit interface between task reasoning and motion execution. To address these requirements, we introduce Atomic-WAM, an understand-then-execute framework that connects task reasoning to video--action generation through an atomic-motion language interface. Specifically, a vision-language model (VLM) reasoner uses the task instruction and visual context to describe the next local interaction, including its target and relevant spatial grounding. A WAM then predicts the corresponding future video and action chunk. The reasoner revises its description as execution changes the scene, while the task-level objective remains fixed. Learning such an interface requires temporally aligned atomic-motion supervision, which is rarely available in existing robot demonstrations. We therefore build an automatic pipeline that partitions the DROID dataset~ khazatsky2024droid into semantically coherent atomic motions. The interface further allows us to improve grasp learning. To this end, we enrich the corresponding descriptions with visible contact details. The resulting labels supervise both motion selection and execution at the same atomic-motion granularity. Nevertheless, supervised atomic-motion learning alone does not guarantee that the selected motion is compatible with the learned executor~ finevla,chen2026steerable . Existing works introduce intermediate commands, subgoals, or semantic events to decouple high-level reasoning from low-level control~ chen2026steerable,intelligence2026pi,wallwm , yet such intermediate decision policies are typically not optimized directly from the downstream executor. We therefore introduce execution-grounded reasoner adaptation through EG-GRPO, which closes the loop between the reasoner and the executor: the reasoner selects atomic motions, the executor produces physical outcomes, and these outcomes serve as the learning signal to improve atomic-motion selection. Building on these advances, Atomic-WAM achieves competitive performance in an out-of-distribution real-to-sim evaluation on RoboLab~ yang2026robolab , with 39.6 task success under default instructions and 31.6 under vague instructions. In summary, our contributions are threefold: We introduce Atomic-WAM, an understand-then-execute framework that connects high-level task reasoning to joint video--action generation through state-dependent atomic-motion descriptions. We develop a scalable atomic-motion annotation pipeline that integrates displacement and gripper cues, multi-view evidence, and visual verification to provide temporally aligned, contact-enriched supervision for both motion selection and execution. We introduce execution-grounded reasoner adaptation via EG-GRPO, using physical outcomes from a fixed executor to improve atomic-motion selection through closed-loop optimization. Related Work sec:related_work Embodied foundation models. Recent embodied policies have benefited from two forms of large-scale pretraining: vision--language pretraining for vision-language-action (VLA) models and video generative pretraining for world action models (WAMs). VLA models transfer pretrained vision--language representations to action prediction~ brohan2023rt,kim2024openvla,black2024pi_0,shukor2025smolvla,bjorck2025gr00t,team2025gemini,wen2025dexvla . Such models benefit from rich semantic priors for objects, scenes, and language-specified tasks, supporting generalization across diverse manipulation tasks. However, vision--language pretraining primarily emphasizes visual--semantic alignment rather than action-conditioned temporal dynamics. In contrast, WAMs leverage video generation to model environment dynamics and couple future visual prediction with robot action generation~ ye2026world,agarwal2026cosmos3,li2026causal,kim2026cosmos,bharadhwaj2024gen2act,won2025dual,zhou2025act2goal,liao2026genie,hu2024video,wang2026unified . Despite this strength, the textual supervision of video foundation models is largely descriptive and offers limited grounding for semantically specified robot tasks. Atomic-WAM integrates the strengths of both forms of pretraining: a VLM reasoner progressively translates high-level task semantics into atomic motions, while the WAM predicts the physical evolution and robot actions. Embodied reasoning for robot control. High-level embodied reasoning enables robots to decompose tasks, assess progress, reason about object affordances, and derive spatially grounded plans from multimodal observations. Recent VLMs have substantially advanced these capabilities~ sermanet2024robovqa,ji2025robobrain,gong2026ace,team2026ace , but translating high-level reasoning into controllable robot behavior remains challenging. A growing line of work therefore grounds reasoning into robot policies through richer intermediate representations. Embodied Chain-of-Thought (ECoT) augments action prediction with intermediate reasoning over plans, subtasks, motions, and visually grounded features~ zawalski2024robotic . Steerable Policies train VLAs to follow commands at multiple levels of abstraction, including subtasks, atomic motions, and spatially grounded instructions~ chen2026steerable . Similarly, conditions robot behavior on diverse language, metadata, and visual subgoals~ intelligence2026pi , while WALL-WM organizes video--action learning around semantically coherent action events~ wallwm . HarnessWAM further incorporates execution evidence into task management, using progress feedback to support replanning and failure recovery~ gu2026harnesswam . These approaches strengthen the interface between reasoning and execution, but execution outcomes are generally not used to directly optimize the high-level reasoner under a downstream policy. Atomic-WAM closes this learning loop by executing candidate atomic motions with a frozen WAM and updating the reasoner from group-relative rewards that capture both motion appropriateness and execution success. Robot simulation evaluation. Real-world robot evaluation is difficult to reproduce because physical resets and environmental conditions vary across trials~ li2024evaluating . By contrast, simulation offers repeatable task instances and controlled variations in scenes and instructions. While conventional simulation benchmarks support scalable evaluation across diverse manipulation tasks~ liu2023libero,fei2025libero,chen2025robotwin,nasiriany2024robocasa , substantial training--evaluation overlap can lead to benchmark saturation and provide limited evidence of out-of-distribution generalization. Recent real-to-sim benchmarks instead evaluate policies trained on real-world data directly in simulation, providing a controlled setting for policy evaluation~ li2024evaluating,yang2026robolab . Within this setting, SIMPLER studies whether simulated evaluation reflects real-world policy behavior, while RoboLab further targets out-of-distribution task generalization with 120 novel tasks spanning visual, relational, and procedural competencies In this work, we adopt RoboLab to evaluate Atomic-WAM under this out-of-distribution real-to-sim setting. Method sec:approach Atomic-WAM connects task reasoning to video-action generation through state-dependent atomic-motion descriptions. We first construct the supervised data from robot demonstrations (Sec.~ sec:atomic_annotation ). Next, we present the “understand-then-execute” framework and training process (Sec.~ sec:exam_training ). Finally, we introduce a closed-loop optimization stage that leverages execution feedback to further improve atomic-motion selection (Sec.~ sec:execution_rl ). Atomic-Motion Data Curation sec:atomic_annotation Robot demonstrations typically provide only task-level instructions, leaving local motions unspecified. Collecting such supervision densely is expensive: neighboring observations often correspond to the same manipulation phase, making frame-wise annotation redundant. To reduce this redundancy, we curate atomic-motion annotations bottom-up from fine-grained physical clips, as shown in Fig.~ fig:exam_annotation . -grounded segmentation. Inspired by the speed-based segmentation of human hand trajectories in VITRA~ li2025scalable , we first derive candidate boundaries from changes in end-effector velocity. Additionally, we incorporate gripper-state transitions to capture interaction phases that are not evident from velocity changes alone. Together, these signals partition each demonstration into physical clips with locally consistent motion and gripper behavior. -motion labeling. We build a multi-stage annotation pipeline using models from Qwen family~ yang2025qwen3 . For each physical clip, we annotate the synchronized left, right, and wrist views separately. Each annotation records the visible action, manipulated object, source location, and destination. However, individual physical clips may fragment a complete action, while early clips can yield ambiguous source or destination labels. We therefore merge adjacent clips into atomic-motion segments using the three-view annotations, boundary observations, and temporal context. The atomic-motion granularity allows us to capture finer interaction details. For grasp-related segments, we further enrich the descriptions with visible grasp points and gripper positions. title: Investigating Behavior Cloning from Few Demonstrations for Autonomous Driving based on Bird's-Eye View in Simulated Cities
comment: 14 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables. Accepted manuscript (author version) of the paper published in the proceedings of BRACIS 2024 (34th Brazilian Conference on Intelligent Systems, Belém, Brazil, 17-21 November 2024). Project page: https://sites.google.com/view/weighted-bc
summary: This paper investigates the use of Behavior Cloning (BC) for autonomous driving from a bird's-eye view (BEV) perspective in simulated urban environments. BC uses supervised learning to mimic expert driving behaviors. Previous works have applied BC in the CARLA simulator but did not fully address the challenges of traffic light compliance. Our approach enhances BC by integrating a kernel density estimator to adjust training sample weights based on action density, thereby improving the learning of rare but critical actions such as stopping at red lights and accelerating at green lights, specially in scenarios of scarce number of expert demonstrations. Using BEV inputs, which provide an abstract top-down view of the driving environment, our method simplifies the policy learning process. The trained convolutional neural network (CNN) outputs steering and acceleration actions based on these BEV inputs and additional state variables. Experimental results in the CARLA simulator demonstrate that our weighted BC method significantly improves driving performance, achieving higher route completion compared to standard BC. This weighted approach proved to be crucial in learning correct driving behaviors, particularly in test environments not encountered during training, highlighting its potential for enhancing autonomous vehicle navigation.

Introduction Autonomous driving has traditionally been implemented using separate modules for perception, planning, and control, organized in a sequential pipeline juniordarpa,env_perception,surveypipeline,Parizotto2021 . However, learning-based approaches have been gaining popularity as they attempt to address the complexities of autonomous driving in various scenarios, whether in simulation or real-world environments. Most of these learning-based approaches rely on Behavior Cloning (BC), which employs supervised learning on a collection of expert demonstrations gathered offline nvidiabc,videobc,chauffernet,codevilla2018endtoend,codevilla2019exploring . For example, a human driver generates a set of input (observations) and corresponding desired output pairs. Codevilla codevilla2018endtoend,codevilla2019exploring employed BC for autonomous driving in the CARLA simulator. He collected a large dataset of human driving and augmented it using image processing techniques to train end-to-end policies conditioned on the desired route. Further improvements in BC were introduced in ral_prob_bc , where a large deep ResNet network was used for feature extraction. This approach combined data from cameras, LiDAR, and radar to create comprehensive feature maps. The work also incorporated a probabilistic motion planner to account for uncertainties in the trajectory. Couto Couto2021 has shown results on behavior cloning on the CARLA simulator, but the agent did not have to respect traffic lights. In this work, we investigate an approach where the agent is able to navigate the city while respecting traffic lights, i.e., breaking when the light is red, and crossing the traffic light when it is green. Only relying on regular BC to train an agent is not enough in a scenario with limited amount of training routes and where the agent needs to break at the red light and accelerate from stillness when light turns to green. To solve that, we employ a kernel density estimator Silverman2018density to estimate the actions density from the expert dataset. Then, the training samples are weighted in the BC loss function individually by setting the weight equal to the inverse of the actions' density. In this way, we can account for the underrepresented actions in the expert set, i.e., those happening at traffic light transitions. This weighting is needed because we are considering only eight routes as training data. Instead of learning directly from raw camera pixels as in Couto2021,cirl2018 , the agent in this work has structured image inputs that are more abstract and meaningful to the navigation task. To decouple feature representation from policy learning resnet_rl,Couto2023 has its advantages as potentially easing up the learning task. In our context, this decoupling is accomplished by using a mid-level representation of the vehicle's raw camera images. For example, Bird's-Eye View (BEV) representations of the road ahead have been used as mid-level inputs for trajectory generation and motor control networks in chauffernet and roach , respectively. In BEV representation, the camera scene is projected onto a top-down view, segmenting areas of interest, like vehicle lanes and sidewalks, into different colors env_perception . By using BEV as input for the control policy, the learning process can focus on the navigation problem, leveraging a more abstract and simplified view of the road ahead. The policy here is represented by convolutional neural networks, mapping the BEV image to control actuators such as steering and acceleration. Experimental results in the CARLA simulator demonstrate that our weighted BC method significantly improves driving performance, achieving higher route completion compared to standard BC. This weighted approach proved to be essential in learning correct driving behaviors, particularly in test environments not encountered during training. In Section~ sec:methods , we present the bird's-eye view representation employed as input to the convolutional neural network, the behavior cloning loss for the agent, and the kernel density estimation used to generate the weights per sample for the modified loss function. The agent architecture is presented in Section ~ sec:agent . Finally, the experiments and conclusions are shown in Sections sec:experiments and sec:conclusion . Methods sec:methods Bird's-Eye View - BEV representation The bird's-eye view of a vehicle represents its position and movement in a top-down coordinate system chauffernet . The vehicle's location, heading, and speed are represented by , , and respectively. The top-down view is defined so that the agent's starting position is always at a fixed point within an image (the center of it). Furthermore, it is represented by a set of images of size pixels, at a ground sampling resolution of meters/pixel. The BEV of the environment moves as the vehicle moves, allowing the agent to see a fixed range of meters in front of it. For instance, the BEV representation for the vehicle whose three frontal cameras are shown in Fig.~ fig:cameras is given in Fig.~ fig:bev , where the desired route, drivable area and lane boundaries are shown as three BEV channels. Besides, other three BEV channels for the traffic lights representing the state of the traffic lights (green or red) at different timesteps are shown in Fig.~ fig:bev_lights . Fig.~ fig:bev_final shows the integrated six-channel BEV image used as input to the agent. Behavior Cloning (BC) Behavior cloning is a supervised learning approach used in imitation learning, where the goal is to learn a policy that mimics the behavior of an expert. In this work, we want to learn a policy for an autonomous vehicle that outputs two actions (acceleration, steering) based on a Bird-Eye-View (BEV) representation of the environment and additional scalar state variables as input. For this reason we need to train a CNN to output these two continuous actions based on input from the BEV and the state variables. title: ObjDream: Guiding Vision-Language-Action Models with Object-Level Understanding and Future State Prediction
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for robotic manipulation, enabling robots to generate actions from visual observations and language instructions. However, most existing VLA models still operate on image-level visual representations inherited from pretrained vision-language backbones, while lacking fine-grained object understanding for manipulation. As a result, their robustness can degrade under out-of-distribution object layouts, clutter, and background variations. To address these limitations, we introduce ObjDream, an object-centric VLA framework centered on object-level understanding and future object state prediction. ObjDream uses a spatio-temporal object encoder to organize visual observations into temporal object slots, where persistent object identity and dynamic object state are represented through separate channels. These structured object representations are inserted into the token sequence of the vision-language model (VLM), where identity-guided routing modulates VLM attention to the corresponding object tokens. In addition, an action-conditioned object dynamics module predicts compact future object states relevant to manipulation during training, explicitly supervising object state evolution under robot actions without requiring future prediction at inference. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0 show that ObjDream improves generalization under diverse distribution shifts and scene perturbations. Real-world robot experiments further demonstrate that ObjDream transfers to physical manipulation settings with novel object arrangements and background changes.

However, most existing VLA models still operate on image-level visual representations inherited from pretrained vision-language backbones, while lacking fine-grained object understanding for manipulation. As a result, their robustness can degrade under out-of-distribution object layouts, clutter, and background variations. To address these limitations, we introduce , an object-centric VLA framework centered on object-level understanding and future object state prediction. uses a spatio-temporal object encoder to organize visual observations into temporal object slots, where persistent object identity and dynamic object state are represented through separate channels. These structured object representations are inserted into the token sequence of the vision-language model (VLM), where identity-guided routing modulates VLM attention to the corresponding object tokens. In addition, an action-conditioned object dynamics module predicts compact future object states relevant to manipulation during training, explicitly supervising object state evolution under robot actions without requiring future prediction at inference. Experiments on , -Plus, and RoboTwin~2.0 show that improves generalization under diverse distribution shifts and scene perturbations. Real-world robot experiments further demonstrate that transfers to physical manipulation settings with novel object arrangements and background changes. Project page . Introduction Robust robot policies must reliably manipulate objects in out-of-distribution environments, where their appearance, position, and surrounding context may differ from those in the training data. VLA models have made rapid progress in generalist robot control by scaling pretrained vision-language backbones, robot data, and action decoders~ brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,gr00t2025,wang2026qwen . To improve generalization, recent work has sought to preserve knowledge acquired during pretraining~ guo2026priorvla,hancock2026actions , use high-level plans to guide low-level control~ li2025hamster , or anticipate scene changes through future visual or latent-state prediction~ zhang2025dreamvla,sun2026vla . Although these approaches improve generalization to some extent, most VLA models still lack fine-grained object-level understanding. Their visual representations, inherited from VLMs, remain largely image-level, leaving the identity and spatial state of task-relevant objects entangled with appearance and surrounding context. This entanglement can weaken out-of-distribution robustness under shifts in object appearance, spatial layout, and background context. Object-centric approaches offer a natural way to strengthen object-level understanding by explicitly representing individual objects and their properties. Prior work incorporates object-aware visual representations to help policies focus on task-relevant regions~ zhu2023viola,li2025controlvla,liang2026pixelvla . Other methods extend object representations to relational reasoning~ hanyu2025slotvla , object-level memory~ chung2026rethinking , and long-horizon manipulation~ yang2026lilo . Although these approaches demonstrate the value of object-level representations, they often encode persistent object identity and time-varying object state in the same slot or token. As appearance and geometry change, this coupling can obscure persistent identity cues by mixing them with dynamic object state. Recent dual-state slot models show that separating identity from dynamic appearance can improve temporal consistency in video perception by keeping identity information distinct from time-varying visual content~ tran2026dual . Building on this insight, we investigate whether persistent identity references can be represented alongside dynamic object states and further used to guide VLM attention for language-conditioned manipulation. Beyond modeling the current visual observation, predictive models support manipulation by anticipating future observations or object states~ ferraro2025focus,chen2025goalvla,villar2025playslot . The choice of prediction target is important: reconstructing complete images requires modeling texture and background details that may be irrelevant to control~ zhang2025dreamvla , while goal-image methods such as Goal-VLA introduce an additional synthesis stage before estimating the target object pose~ chen2025goalvla . In contrast, object-centric world models show that scene evolution can be modeled using compact object representations~ jeong2025object . Motivated by this trade-off, we use action-conditioned prediction of compact future object states, including geometry and visibility, as auxiliary supervision for VLA training without requiring future object state prediction at inference. To this end, as illustrated in Fig.~ fig1_overview , we introduce , an object-centric vision-language-action framework for improving manipulation generalization. The architecture of builds on a pretrained VLM backbone and integrates a spatio-temporal object encoder, an object-level forward dynamics module, and a flow-matching action expert. Specifically, the spatio-temporal object encoder transforms visual observations into structured object slots, where persistent object identity and dynamic object state are represented through separate channels. These factorized object representations are mapped into the VLM hidden space and inserted into the token sequence, where identity-guided routing modulates attention to the corresponding object tokens. The forward dynamics module predicts future object states during training, providing auxiliary supervision for future object state evolution under robot actions without requiring future prediction at inference. The object encoder is pretrained with automatically generated offline object supervision and frozen during VLA training. We optimize with a joint objective combining action imitation with current and future object state supervision. Extensive evaluations on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin~2.0, and real-world robot experiments demonstrate competitive manipulation performance across diverse scene perturbations. The main contributions of this paper are listed below: [leftmargin=2em, topsep=0.25em, itemsep=0.25em, parsep=0pt] We present , an object-centric VLA framework centered on object-level understanding and future object state prediction to improve generalization under perturbations. introduces a spatio-temporal object encoder that explicitly represents persistent object identity and dynamic object state through separate channels. The resulting representations are integrated into the VLM hidden space with a novel identity-guided routing mechanism for robust language-conditioned manipulation. We introduce an action-conditioned object-level forward dynamics module for modeling object evolution during manipulation. It predicts compact future object states during training to provide direct auxiliary object-level supervision without requiring future object state prediction at inference. We further model inter-object relations from object features and pairwise geometry to provide structured context for action generation. Extensive evaluations on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin~2.0, and real-world robot experiments demonstrate competitive manipulation performance across diverse scene and environmental perturbations. Ablations further assess the effects of the key architectural components. Related Work Vision-language-action models. VLA models combine pretrained language or vision-language backbones with action decoders to learn general-purpose manipulation from large-scale robot demonstrations~ brohan2023rt1,brohan2023rt2,openx2023embodiment,octo2024,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,pi05 . Recent work improves VLA performance through stronger action decoders and fine-tuning strategies~ chi2023diffusionpolicy,zhao2023learning,kim2025fine,hou2025dita,gr00t2025,qu2025spatialvla , larger-scale cross-embodiment training~ cai2026xiaomi,team2026xiaomi,wu2026pragmatic,wu2026foundation,wang2026qwen , and better preservation or exploitation of pretrained visual-semantic and spatial priors~ guo2026priorvla,li2026spatial,wang2026lamp . Predictive objectives further use future images, video tokens, subgoal images, or latent states to provide temporal supervision for manipulation~ zhao2025cot,zhang2025dreamvla,cen2025worldvla,cen2025rynnvla,li2026fomovla . Despite these advances, existing VLA models still largely operate on dense image-level visual representations, where object-level structure is not explicitly organized for manipulation generalization. addresses this limitation by enhancing VLA policies with object-level understanding and future object state supervision. World models for robot control. World models learn action-conditioned environment dynamics and support robot control by planning or learning policies from predicted futures in observation or latent spaces~ hafner2019planet,wu2023daydreamer . Recent work extends this paradigm through language-conditioned video generation~ du2023learning,zhou2024robodreamer , pretrained visual latent dynamics~ zhou2024dino,assran2025v , and world-action or unified video-action models that couple future prediction with executable actions~ ye2026world,li2026latent . These approaches provide dynamics supervision by modeling anticipated scene evolution. However, prediction in pixel or video space requires modeling high-dimensional visual details and can introduce training or inference overhead. Recent approaches therefore explore more efficient formulations, including avoiding explicit future imagination at inference or exposing compact representations of scene changes~ yuan2026fast,bai2026bridge . follows this direction by using compact future object state prediction as supervision during training, while directly generating actions at inference without explicit future object state decoding. Object-centric representations for manipulation. Object-centric representation learning decomposes visual scenes into entity-level latent variables and has been widely studied in scene decomposition, temporal tracking, and structured dynamics~ locatello2020object,kipf2021conditional,wu2022slotformer . In robotic manipulation, object-level representations have been used to improve sample efficiency and enhance visuomotor attention and robust policy conditioning through object proposals, grounded geometry, object-centric prompting, and physically grounded object concepts~ zhu2023viola,vo2025clutter,li2025object,wei2026physically , enable efficient VLA learning through compact object-centric tokenization~ bendikas2025focusing , and support structured control through object-centric dynamics and relational representations~ ferraro2025focus,mosbach2024sold,hanyu2025slotvla,yang2026lilo . Complementary approaches use structured affordance representations to provide action-relevant object grounding, interaction localization, and geometric guidance for VLA policies~ yu2026affordancevla . Recent predictive approaches further incorporate object-aware future representations, masks, or addressable slot states into world-action learning~ wang2026oflow,yu2026maskwam,liu2026oa . Recent dual-state slot models separate per-frame appearance from persistent object identity, highlighting the value of disentangling identity from changing visual content in object-centric representations~ tran2026dual . From this perspective, combines persistent identity references with dynamic object states and uses identity-guided routing to provide object-specific context for language-conditioned manipulation. title: VisibilitySplat: Ray-Traced Occlusion for Relighting with 3D Gaussian Splatting
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables. Published at WSCG 2026
summary: We address inverse rendering with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by introducing explicit visibility modeling for relighting as well as material and light decomposition. Our approach augments the standard rasterized 3DGS pipeline with a sparse visibility oracle that estimates transmittance-weighted occlusion for Gaussian primitives from sampled lighting directions. This oracle is implemented using a point-based ray tracer accelerated by a bounding volume hierarchy (BVH) and queried sparsely within the inverse-rendering objectives, while the original 3DGS loop is retained for training efficiency, interactive visualization, and tooling compatibility. Shading follows a physically based rendering (PBR) formulation with a principled microfacet bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF) and low-resolution high-dynamic-range (HDR) environment maps. We evaluate our method on the TensoIR synthetic dataset against baselines based on neural radiance fields (NeRFs), tensor representations, and 3DGS. The results show competitive performance and improvements over several earlier baselines for novel-view synthesis (NVS), albedo reconstruction, and relighting. Ablations indicate that explicit visibility modeling is an important contributor to relighting and material-illumination disentanglement, while pure PBR supervision can favor appearance fitting in NVS. Overall, the findings suggest that sparse, point-based visibility queries effectively complement rasterized splatting for inverse rendering while preserving the practical advantages of the 3DGS ecosystem.
full_text: Introduction Inverse rendering (IR) seeks to recover geometry, reflectance, and illumination from images by inverting the image formation process. Neural radiance fields (NeRFs) mildenhall:2021:nerf enable high-fidelity novel-view synthesis (NVS) and have been extended toward relightable decompositions under unknown illumination (e.g., NeRFactor zhang:2021:nerfactor and TensoIR jin:2023:tensoir ), but their implicit volumetric formulation is costly to train and render. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) kerbl:2023:3dgs instead optimizes explicit point primitives via differentiable rasterization, enabling real-time rendering and practical tooling, and has recently been adopted for IR (e.g., 3D Gaussian Splatting for Inverse Rendering (GS-IR) liang:2024:gs-ir and Gaussian Inverse Rendering (GIR) shi:2025:gir ). A key challenge is visibility: screen-space alpha compositing provides limited information about cast shadows and mutual occlusion, which are crucial for stabilizing material-light disentanglement under unknown illumination. While 3DGS-based IR pipelines benefit from fast forward rendering, visibility signals derived from the rasterizer alone can be too weak or too view-dependent to constrain shadows robustly. Recent work, including Inter-Reflective Gaussian Splatting (IRGS), therefore augments splatting with ray-based visibility estimation gao:2024:relightable3dgaussians, gu:2025:irgs . We take a pragmatic step along this trajectory by adding a sparse visibility oracle that estimates transmittance-weighted occlusion from sampled lighting directions, while retaining the original 3DGS rasterization loop for training efficiency and interactive visualization. This lightweight division of labor injects physically meaningful visibility constraints without replacing the splatting renderer (Fig.~ fig:teaser ). Rather than proposing a highly specialized approximation or learned visibility model, we deliberately study a direct formulation based on explicit visibility queries. This provides a reference baseline for assessing how much transmittance-weighted visibility contributes to IR and relighting with 3DGS. Our contributions are as follows: (i) a sparse visibility oracle for 3DGS that estimates how much light reaches each Gaussian from sampled environment directions, implemented with a point-based ray tracer accelerated by a bounding volume hierarchy (BVH); (ii) a reference baseline on the TensoIR synthetic benchmark, including comparisons to NeRF-based, tensor-based, and 3DGS-based IR methods and ablations that isolate the effect of explicit visibility. Related Work Radiance Fields The original NeRF method mildenhall:2021:nerf introduced neural volumetric representations for NVS, with subsequent work improving anti-aliasing and efficiency via scale-aware integration and more explicit encodings barron:2021:mip, barron:2022:mip360, barron:2023:zip, muller:2022:instantngp, fridovich:2022:plenoxels,fridovich:2023:kplanes, chen:2022:tensorf . 3DGS kerbl:2023:3dgs further shifts computation to explicit anisotropic Gaussian primitives rendered by a custom rasterizer, enabling real-time performance. Geometry-oriented variants huang:2024:2dgs, yu:2024:gaussian and BVH-based Gaussian ray tracing loccoz:2024:3dgrt broaden the representation toward editing and secondary-ray effects. Inverse Rendering Neural fields for inverse rendering: IR aims to recover geometry, materials, and illumination from images and is intrinsically ill-posed. Early NeRF-based methods reduced ambiguity with simplifying assumptions: PhySG zhang:2021:physg represents bidirectional reflectance distribution functions (BRDFs) and lighting using spherical Gaussians (SGs) but omits complex visibility and indirect transport. NeRFactor zhang:2021:nerfactor factorizes shape and reflectance under unknown lighting. InvRender zhang:2022:invrender derives spatially varying indirect illumination directly from the learned radiance field to improve albedo recovery. Ref-NeRF verbin:2022:ref improves specular handling via a reflected-radiance parameterization that also yields better normals. To raise physical fidelity without losing efficiency, TensoIR jin:2023:tensoir builds on tensor-factorized fields to support on-the-fly visibility queries and second-bounce effects during reconstruction. Complementary surface-aligned fields stabilize geometry and normals for IR pipelines yariv:2021:volsdf, wang:2021:neus . More recent work targets illumination modeling itself: ENVIDR liang:2023:envidr learns a neural environment for shiny scenes. NeRF-as-Emitter ling:2024:nerf-as-emitter replaces the distant-light assumption with a near-field light NeRF, improving accuracy under spatially varying illumination, and NeILF++ zhang:2023:neilf++ jointly learns incident-light and outgoing-radiance fields with inter-reflections to better disentangle material and lighting. Gaussian splatting for inverse rendering: Adopting 3DGS for IR leverages real-time forward rendering but introduces new challenges: splats lack native surface normals, and forward splatting does not natively model occlusion or multi-bounce light. GS-IR liang:2024:gs-ir addresses these by regularizing per-Gaussian normals and baking visibility for secondary effects while recovering geometry, spatially varying bidirectional reflectance distribution functions (SVBRDFs), and environment lighting under unknown illumination. Subsequent work deepens physical correctness: GaussianShader jiang:2024:gaussianshader estimates robust normals and per-splat shading for reflective scenes. DeferredGS wu:2024:deferredgs decouples geometry from lighting and performs deferred shading for editable relighting and Ref-Gaussian yao:2024:reflective targets glossy reflections with a specialized deferred pipeline. Beyond perfect mirrors, SSS-GS dihlmann:2024:subsurface introduces subsurface scattering to a 3DGS framework using an explicit surface plus an implicit scattering component. To improve general relighting, RNG fan:2025:rng conditions radiance on view and light directions with shadow cues and depth refinement, while BiGS liu:2024:bigs unifies surface and volumetric materials via bidirectional spherical harmonics (SH), supporting near- and distant-light setups. Finally, GI-GS chen:2024:gi-gs explicitly decomposes direct/indirect components and uses lightweight path tracing on a G-buffer for multi-bounce global illumination, bringing 3DGS-based IR closer to physically faithful relighting at interactive rates. These efforts are complementary to geometry-focused 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) huang:2024:2dgs and surface extraction with Gaussian Opacity Fields (GOF) yu:2024:gaussian , as well as to BVH-accelerated Gaussian ray tracing for secondary-ray phenomena loccoz:2024:3dgrt . Overview Gaussian Splatting 3DGS~ kerbl:2023:3dgs is a method for rendering 3D scenes in real time, offering high visual quality and fast training. A scene is represented as a cloud of anisotropic 3D Gaussians: with mean and covariance . The complete parameter set for each Gaussian is defined as , where the mean specifies the position, the full covariance encodes the ellipsoidal footprint, denotes the opacity, and is the color, stored as a set of SH coefficients. The covariance matrix can be decomposed into a scaling matrix and a rotation matrix constructed from a unit quaternion , which results in . With the extrinsic camera matrix and intrinsic camera matrix , the screen-space mean and covariance matrix are defined as where is the Jacobian matrix of the affine approximation of the perspective projection~ zwicker:2002:ewa . The final color at pixel is obtained by depth-sorting Gaussians and accumulating color in a front-to-back manner: where denotes the accumulated transmittance, and for readability we use the shorthand . Physically Based Rendering We follow a physically based rendering (PBR) formulation similar to recent IR systems such as TensoIR jin:2023:tensoir , NeRFactor zhang:2021:nerfactor , and GS-IR liang:2024:gs-ir . Image formation is expressed by the surface rendering equation with geometric visibility and an energy-conserving microfacet BRDF, while geometry, reflectance, and illumination are represented by differentiable fields and optimized from multi-view images. For example, TensoIR introduces efficient online visibility and secondary shading, NeRFactor learns a visibility field, and GS-IR attaches BRDF parameters to Gaussians with an occlusion approximation. We model distant lighting as a high-dynamic-range (HDR) spherical environment map parameterized in equirectangular coordinates~ debevec:1998:rendering . title: TacClaw-Infinity: A Large-Scale Vision-Tactile-Language-Action Dataset for Dexterous Manipulation
summary: Large-scale robot learning increasingly relies on diverse human demonstrations, yet tactile manipulation data remain difficult to scale, and existing multimodal datasets often lack consistent quality control and structured supervision. We present TacClaw-Infinity, a large-scale structured Vision-Tactile-Language-Action (VTLA) dataset for contact-rich manipulation, collected with TacClaw, a tactile-enabled UMI-style handheld interface that records synchronized visual observations, fingertip tactile signals, and end-effector trajectories without requiring a target robot during data collection. TacClaw-Infinity is built through a distributed worldwide collection across homes, laboratories, industrial workplaces, retail stores, and outdoor environments including tasks contributed by academic and industrial collaborators. Together, these efforts yield over 10,000 hours, 1 million episodes, and 1 billion frames spanning more than 1,000 task types. We develop a scalable pipeline for trajectory reconstruction, multimodal quality control, embodiment-aware filtering, and structured annotation, covering contact-centric segmentation, subtask description, and spatial grounding. We validate TacClaw-Infinity at both the data and model levels: At the data level, we assess the collection interface, the action-space compatibility of the curated demonstrations, and the structured annotations, while for the model level, we demonstrate cross-embodiment transfer across three heterogeneous robots without robot-specific demonstrations.

title: Human Demonstrations as Post-Training Data for Any Robot Body: Retargeting the Object, Not the Hand
comment: 16 pages, 17 figures, 7 tables, 2 algorithms; 56-page supplement as ancillary file. A subset of episodes with their per-robot outcomes: https://playground.dxtr.co
summary: Human demonstrations are today used largely for pretraining vision-language-action models, with little ability to use the same data for target-embodiment or task-oriented training, which scalable deployment of robots in industrial and general environments depends on. A human demonstration recorded on a simple and scalable device such as a mobile phone can serve as post-training data for a robot whose body differs in structure and capability from the human who recorded it. This is made possible not by retargeting the hand's motion but the object's. A capture yields a body-free record: the object's pose over time, its contact intervals, and a reconstructed 3D object with provenance. Any robot, given as a URDF and a short descriptor, is solved against that record and scored in simulation against the demonstrated object motion as ground truth: the human-to-simulation leg of human-to-simulation-to-robot transfer, measured per robot. Each (robot, episode) pair gets one outcome: pass, failure with a named mode, or refusal, with its reason, before any motion. The method runs as a working system over a growing collection; the set analysed here is a sample of it: 42 captures solved on 8 robots, 157 pairs, of which 31.2% pass, 52.2% fail, 14.0% are refused and 2.5% are unauditable (kinematic feasibility, +/-50 mm / +/-15 deg, in simulation). Refusals held up: every pair the checks refuse on stored evidence yet ran anyway failed (13 of 13; 5 on a body whose public model welds its hand). A description file could not be shown to screen a robot: its outcomes were barely more predictable than guessing. No policy has yet been trained on the record. The record decides what a robot may post-train on; whether the policy then works on the real robot is the simulation-to-robot question, answered downstream.

Introduction sec:intro A human demonstration records what an object did, and a great deal about the body that did it. Any robot can use the first, but only a body built like the demonstrator's can use the second. Today, robot learning uses human demonstrations mostly for pretraining, where human video at internet scale is retargeted in bulk to teach a vision-language-action model what manipulation looks like~ luo2026beingh05,wang2026ego2robot . Deployment depends on the step after that (Fig.~ fig:enters ), in which a specific robot is post-trained on a specific task from tens to a few hundred episodes of its own body. Human demonstrations are hard to use there, because the robot's body decides which of them it can execute at all. Systems that do transfer a demonstration to a robot target one robot at a time~ li2024okami,huang2026physv2a,zhai2026psi,yu2025real2render2real , and they drop the demonstrations that robot cannot use. This paper turns a demonstration recorded on a simple and scalable device, such as a mobile phone with nothing attached to it, into post-training data for any robot (Fig.~ fig:teaser ). It does so by retargeting the object's motion. Throughout, the data is post-training data: a target-embodiment training set, the tens to a few hundred episodes of one robot on one task on which a pretrained policy is post-trained, or at that scale a task policy is trained from scratch. Nothing here is pretraining data. We write post-training set for short. Fig.~ fig:concept shows the design, and Table~ tab:glossary collects the terms. A capture is reduced to a body-free record: the object's pose over time in metres, the intervals over which it was held, and one reconstructed 3D object whose observed surface is kept apart from the completed one. The hand is treated as a witness to contact rather than copied: when and where it held the object are kept on the object, as the contact intervals and as a contact map on the mesh. Any robot, given as a URDF and the short descriptor of Table~ tab:descriptor , is solved against that record without rescaling it. Its kinematic replay is then scored against the demonstrated object motion as ground truth. This measures, for each robot, the human-to-simulation leg of human-to-simulation-to-robot transfer ( sec:why ). Each (robot, episode) pair receives one outcome. The pair passes at the declared tolerance or fails with a named mode, or the robot refuses the episode before any motion is generated. A refusal carries a reason from a fixed list and the measured quantity behind it. Every outcome goes to an append-only ledger in which the latest entry for a run supersedes the earlier ones. A pass that cannot meet a later check is therefore retracted by a dated entry, and the earlier row stays in the ledger. Every pipeline we know of that retargets human demonstrations already makes the refusal decision. A feasibility filter drops motions a humanoid cannot track~ he2024h2o,ji2024exbody2 . A grasp planner discards a trajectory when none of its sampled grasps survives a simulator check~ zhai2026psi , and a curation stage removes whatever a quality model dislikes~ wang2026ego2robot,ye2025video2policy . The decision stays inside the pipeline, and only what survives it is released. A reader then cannot tell whether an episode is missing because it was never captured, because one body could not reach it, or because a filter that no longer exists once rejected it. We keep the decision, with its reason, beside the record. The set analysed here holds captures solved on robots from body classes, (robot, episode) pairs in all, of which pass, fail, are refused and are unauditable. Every refused pair that ran anyway failed ( of , sec:refusalvalidity ). A robot's description predicts its outcomes barely better than guessing does ( sec:predictor ). Ranking grasps by sweep coverage passed of pairs where ranking by grasp quality passed ( sec:ablations ). Human2Sim2Robot~ lum2025human2sim2robot names the human-to-robot embodiment gap. It and Video2Sim2Real~ han2026video2sim2real cross that gap for one robot. They use the demonstrated object motion as a reward for reinforcement learning in simulation, then transfer the policy. We use the same object motion as ground truth, not as a reward. We measure the human-to-simulation leg for every robot, kinematically and with no learning in the loop, and we keep the measurement. The simulation-to-robot leg belongs to the policy post-trained on the result and is measured downstream. Contributions. 1pt 0pt 2pt The body-free demonstration record, and the per-robot human-to-simulation gap it makes measurable (Fig.~ fig:concept , Fig.~ fig:record , sec:record ). Refusal before motion, from a fixed vocabulary and kept with its certificate. Refused pairs that ran anyway all failed, and we could not screen a robot the model has not seen from its description ( sec:refusalvalidity , sec:predictor ). Grasp selection ranked by sweep coverage of the whole demonstrated path, with its ablation against ranking by grasp quality (Alg.~ alg:grasp , Table~ tab:ablations ). A worked corpus across embodiments in classes, with retractions on the record (Fig.~ fig:outcomes , Table~ tab:bodies , Table~ tab:retractions ). The object as ground truth sec:why Copying the hand has no ground truth once the body changes. A hand path scaled onto the jaw gripper of a low-cost arm is a guess about what that arm should do, and the guess differs for every body. Robots given the same demonstration then cannot be compared with each other, and none of them can be said to have reproduced it (Fig.~ fig:handobject ). The object's motion is different: it is what the task is about, it is the same for every body, and a robot either reproduces it within a stated tolerance or does not. We therefore take the ground truth from the object: its pose over time and the intervals over which it was held. Both are recovered once from the capture, in metres, and never rescaled to suit a workspace. This makes outcomes comparable across bodies, since every body is scored against the same reference motion with the same tolerance. It also makes the gap between the demonstration and the simulated robot a per-frame quantity, the object-path error, summarised by the fraction of scored frames inside the tube ( sec:solve ). Some episodes can be ruled out from a robot's description and the record alone: its end effector has no closing joint, its stroke is narrower than the object, or its reach is shorter than the sweep. An attempt that cannot pass spends solve time and, worse, would put a motion the body cannot execute into its post-training set. So the robot refuses before any motion, and the measured quantity goes on the record. The choice has costs, however. The object must be rigid, with a recoverable pose, so a deformable object or a hand-to-hand transfer is refused as object not rigid (Table~ tab:refusals ). Only the contact interval is scored, because the approach and the retreat are the least transferable part of a demonstration, and each body therefore gets its own synthesised approach and retreat. The demonstrated path is a tolerance target for reproducing the task, not an optimum, and a robot that finds a better path is scored as having missed this one. Other parts of a demonstration do not depend on the body either: the scene the object moved through, the demonstrator's path across it, the state changes the task caused and the sounds it made. The record in this paper holds the object's motion, its contact intervals, its reconstructed 3D object, and the support plane and scene bounds that the solver reads for collision and placement. The demonstrator's path is formulated for bodies that move but has no gated outcome yet. Environment state and audio are left as extensions of the same record. Fig.~ fig:record shows what is stored. Related work sec:related Object-centric transfer from human video. Transferring the object's motion instead of the hand's is an established line of work. Single-video systems replay a recovered object trajectory~ li2024okami,heppert2024ditto,kerr2024rsrd,zhu2024orion , and a policy can be trained to generate the object's pose trajectory from a few demonstrations~ hsu2024spot . Flow and track methods transfer point motion~ wen2024atm,bharadhwaj2024track2act,xu2024im2flow2act,yuan2024generalflow,chen2025ecflow , and real-to-sim-to-real systems use the demonstrated object motion as a reward~ dan2025xsim,lum2025human2sim2robot,han2026video2sim2real . Capture on a bare phone is not new either~ palanisamy2026mobileego , nor is retargeting a demonstration to a body given only as a URDF~ yin2026feasiblecap,wang2026ego2robot ; cross-embodiment policy transfer can also mask the end effector out of the policy's view instead of retargeting~ piseno2026cloak . A handheld gripper, with or without a phone on it~ chi2024umi,etukuru2024rum,xu2026hommi,patel2026bpp,fang2026robopocket , or a motion-capture glove~ wang2024dexcap records the end effector itself and so bypasses retargeting at the price of the device; a phone with nothing attached records the object and leaves the end effector to the descriptor. MimicGen and DexMimicGen~ mandlekar2023mimicgen,jiang2024dexmimicgen also cut demonstrations into object-centric segments, to generate robot data in simulation from a few robot demonstrations, and EgoMimic~ kareer2024egomimic co-trains on egocentric human video and robot data for one platform; the record keeps the segments as a measurement per body instead. The record itself is recovered with off-the-shelf components, named in Appendix~C~ lugaresi2019mediapipe,pavlakos2024hamer,ravi2024sam2,xiang2025trellis . Table~ tab:related lists no system that releases, per robot, the episodes it could not use and why. Grasp selection conditioned on the whole motion. Choosing a grasp because the motion after it stays feasible is an old idea. The grasp is a planning variable in~ simeon2004manipulation , filtered by reachability in~ xue2011reachability , chosen by post-grasp objectives in~ ghalamzan2016taskrelevant,ghalamzan2018postgrasp , optimised with the trajectory by~ wang2020manipulationtrajopt and ranked under predicted object motion by~ akinola2021dynamicgrasping . huang2026phy

title: When Do Discrete Actions Make Good Continuous Controllers?
comment: 53 pages (12 main text), 19 figures, 12 tables. Project page: https://iscoyizj.github.io/discrete-action-website/
summary: Though modern AI models like LLMs predict discrete tokens, today's robotic foundation models represent actions as continuous vectors. In this paper, we challenge this common consensus by asking if continuous action parametrizations are superior to their discrete counterparts. We conduct an extensive comparison of single-step regression and multi-step flow variants of both continuous and discrete policies in both from-scratch single-task and multi-task VLA training, in both simulation and on real hardware. In all regimes, we find that discrete action prediction, even the most naive, uniform-bin quantization, can match or even outperform continuous-action policies in task success rate. Moreover, we find that the challenge to discrete action policies is \emph{not} action precision, but rather factorization error introduced by product-distribution predictions across time and action dimensions. We show that, when paired with the correct interventions---iterative computation through discrete flows, or distribution sharpening through classifier-free guidance---discrete flow policies can turn this weakness into a strength, enabling more responsive action changes during a predicted action chunk. Lastly, we show that attempts to explicitly inject geometric information into discrete policies, e.g. through corruption processes that emulate continuous flow matching, do \emph{not} yield consistent improvements. Taken together, our findings question existing assumptions that robotic action prediction requires distinct design decisions compared to other AI domains, and motivates the possibility of discrete action prediction as a compelling alternative to today's continuous action parametrizations.
