Link for the webpage https://iscoyizj.github.io/discrete-action-website/ Introduction A major goal of modern robot learning is to perform complex and varied tasks to high precision. As a result, the community has devoted significant study to the question of how to parametrize the actions predicted by robotic policies and foundation models, such as vision-language-action models (VLAs)~ brohan2023rt,Kim2024OpenVLAAO,black2024pi0,nvidia2025gr00t and world action models (WAMs)~ li2025uva,ye2026worldaction,kim2026cosmospolicy,li2026causalworld . The common consensus is that robot models should predict continuous-valued actions during deployment, as these are lossless and therefore support high-precision behavior. For example, most of today's VLAs predict actions using continuous-space generative models, such as flow~ black2024pi0,physicalintelligence2025pi05 or diffusion models~ chi2023diffusion , which are believed to better capture training data diversity whilst enhancing the precision of action predictions. At the same time, modern robot learning is adopting increasingly more features from other AI domains, notably language modeling. These include test-time reasoning wei2022chain , on-task self-correction huang2022inner , future goal prediction du2023learning , and long-term memory Wang2023VoyagerAO . In fact, recent work has showcased the possibility that frontier language models can directly control robot embodiments through text generation brohan2023rt, Kim2024OpenVLAAO . Yet, today's frontier AI models, even ones that process multiple modalities such as text, images, and audio, both take as input and produce discretely quantized tokens. Whether robot actions should follow the same discrete format therefore raises a key question: Are robot actions unique among other AI modalities in that they must be predicted as continuous values, or can discrete action representations compete with, or even outperform, their continuous counterparts? Contributions In this work, we undertake a systematic comparison between the performance of continuous and discrete action parameterizations for both single-task robot policies and multi-task vision-language-action (VLA) models. In short, we show that discrete action parametrization can be competitive with, and even uniformly outperform, continuous action prediction, provided that correct design decisions are made. These findings provide a deeper understanding of the performance of recent discrete diffusion/flow VLA policies liang2025discrete,wen2025llada,chen2025udvla . In greater detail, we consider parametrizations of the action head, or part of a robot model responsible for action prediction. Our comparison builds on classical supervised control and imitation learning~ pomerleau1988alvinn,ross2011reduction,osa2018algorithmic . We focus our study on 4 representative parametrizations: (1) continuous regression (CR), which predicts continuous-valued actions in a single forward pass and is trained with a regression objective~ bojarski2016end,kim2025oft (2) continuous flow (CF), which generates continuous actions using flow matching, a family applied to robot control and motion planning~ hu2024adaflow,chisari2024pointflowmatch,black2024pi0,zhang2024flowpolicy,nguyen2025flowmp (3) discrete regression (DR), which predicts a quantized action via cross-entropy classification~ brohan2022rt1 and (4) discrete flow (DF), which predicts quantized actions in multiple steps via the discrete flow matching objective~ gat2024discrete . Hybrid methods such as Behavior Transformer~ shafiullah2022behavior combine discrete action-bin prediction with a continuous offset; in contrast, we study purely discrete and continuous action heads separately to isolate the effect of action representation. Recent work compares regression and flow policies under architecture-matched settings~ pan2025noising . We evaluate these parametrizations from single-task policies on RoboMimic~ robomimic2021 to multi-task VLA-scale policies using RoboCasa~ robocasa365 , DROID~ khazatsky2024droid , and LIBERO~ liu2023libero , as well as real-world robot experiments. All are evaluated using closed-loop task success, action prediction accuracy, and within-chunk temporal variation. We identify 3 key findings that upend prior beliefs about the relative performance of discrete and continuous action modalities, challenging the prevailing view that precise robot control requires predicting continuous action prediction: [leftmargin=8pt] Finding 1: Control Precision Contrary to prior belief, discrete action parametrizations, even discrete regression (DR) with the simplest bin discretization, can exhibit greater control precision than their continuous counterparts, despite the possibly lossy quantization of actions! We support this claim in both sim and real settings in . We show that this arises from greater policy reactivity, both to the action-chunk time index and the conditioning observation. Finding 2: Iterative Refinement and Guidance Mitigate Factorization Error ( ). Independently predicted tokens can combine incompatible choices across time and action dimensions, even when individual token distributions are accurate. DF solves this by iterative computation, while classifier-free guidance reduces ambiguity by changing token preferences. Both improve control significantly, supporting joint consistency as main explanation for their gains. In the RoboCasa comparison, guidance raises DR success from 27.1 to 49.2 , approaching DF's 53.9 and CF's 52.7 , largely ahead of CR's 38.8 . Encoding action distances or using alternative tokenizers improves some configurations, but none exceeds our best DF result with uniform bins and the standard mixture path. Adjacent bins also acquire similar output embeddings, suggesting that discrete heads can learn local geometry without encoding it explicitly. We discuss related work in . title: Towards Agentic Robots: Model, Data, Environment, and Harness
summary: Foundation models are driving a paradigm shift in robotic intelligence, moving beyond low-level action prediction to goal-directed orchestration of data collection, model training, task planning, and real-world execution. We characterize this emerging paradigm as an agentic robots, in which agents reason over human instructions, interact with robotic environments, rectify execution errors autonomously, and dynamically adjust operational strategies. Although this field develops fast, current studies are not well connected. Researchers have no consistent view of how to combine different agentic functions into a complete robot system. This paper provides a unified overview of existing research on agentic robots. We first trace the development from robot policies to agentic systems, covering vision-language-action models, world models, and world-action models. We then clarify the definition and scope of agentic robots and organize existing research into seventeen categories across four functional domains: Model, Data, Environment, and Harness. Across these domains, we examine how agents shape model learning and robot decisions, collect and curate robot data, construct worlds, tasks, and tests for learning and evaluation, and organize capabilities for robot use. Finally, we discuss open challenges and outline directions for future research. Looking forward, we hope this work contributes to a clearer understanding of agentic robots and supports new approaches to making them more capable, reliable, and adaptive.
full_text: Overview of agentic robots across Model, Data, Environment, and Harness. The four domains connect model decisions, robot execution, environmental interaction, and learning from experience. fig:four-domain-overview Introduction sec:introduction Over the past few years, foundation models including large language models (LLMs) and multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have greatly advanced robotic policy learning. They endow robots with novel capabilities that traditional task-specific models lack, especially in scene and task understanding and cross-scene generalization, by scaling robot datasets and model size~ survey_ax_2212_06817,survey_ax_2405_12213 . As a dominant technical solution in this field, vision-language-action (VLA) models utilize either discrete action tokens or diffusion- or flow-matching-based continuous action prediction strategies to connect robotic action prediction and the semantic knowledge embedded in pre-trained LLMs~ survey_ax_2307_15818,survey_ax_2410_24164,survey_ax_2504_16054 . Nevertheless, improved action prediction alone cannot guarantee reliable execution for long-horizon tasks. These tasks demand robots to track task progress, adjust plans amid environmental changes, and recover from failures. VLA policies by themselves cannot consistently deliver these capabilities. Recently, agentic robots are attracting surging attention in the research community, which represent a new generation of embodied intelligent systems that integrate foundation model reasoning with embodied agency and environmental interaction capabilities. General-purpose models such as GPT-6 Astra~ openai2026astra and Gemini 4 Argon~ google2026argon are opening new possibilities for such systems. For example, GPT-6 Astra demonstrates promising capabilities as a robot manipulation agent, using visual observations to generate end-effector commands and adjust its actions from execution feedback without task-specific fine-tuning~ survey_ax_2609_24170 . On RoboDojo, it achieves a 22.48 average success rate across 42 simulation tasks, outperforming the trained robot policy DM0.5 (19.34 )~ dexmal2026dm05 , GalaxeaVLA G0.5 (14.88 )~ galaxea2026g05 , Xiaomi-Robotics-1 (13.93 )~ survey_ax_2607_15330 , OpenWAM- (11.92 )~ survey_ax_2609_07398 and (6.91 )~ survey_ax_2504_16054 . Despite this progress, inference latency and resource costs highlight the importance of how foundation models are integrated into robotic systems. Beyond optimizing and scaling model parameters, agentic robots use foundation models to plan actions, monitor task progress, and revise decisions based on execution feedback. Their capabilities therefore depend on both the model and the tools, observations, and feedback available in the environment. The agentic robot paradigm addresses the “brain in a vat” limitation of previous robotic solutions, shifting robotic intelligence from static pattern matching toward adaptive autonomous operation. Despite growing interest, research on agentic robots remains fragmented across model learning, data acquisition, environment construction, and runtime system design. These directions are often studied separately, although their contributions interact within a robotic system. Related terms such as embodied agents, autonomous robots, and self-improving robotic systems further blur the scope of the field by emphasizing different capabilities without consistently clarifying their boundaries. Together, these issues make it difficult to identify where agents make decisions and how those decisions contribute to the overall system. A unified taxonomy should therefore distinguish the roles of individual components while explaining how they work together. To this end, we organize agentic robotics into four functional domains: Model, Data, Environment, and Harness, tracing the agent’s decisions within each domain and their effects across the system. Figure~ fig:four-domain-overview shows how these four domains work together in agentic robot systems. The four questions above guide our discussion of how agents contribute to robotic systems. Section~ sec:model examines how agents support model learning and robot decision-making, while Section~ sec:data explains how they collect, annotate, and refine robot data. Section~ sec:environment considers the worlds, tasks, and tests agents construct for learning and evaluation. Section~ sec:harness examines how agents coordinate executable capabilities, monitor execution, recover from failures, and retain useful knowledge for subsequent tasks. This paper makes three main contributions: A Unified Illustration for Agentic Robotics. We trace the evolution from robot policies to agentic systems and clarify the role of agents in robot task execution and capability development. We introduce a taxonomy spanning Model, Data, Environment, and Harness, bringing these research directions into a common framework. A Systematic Analysis of Agentic Methods. We synthesize the mechanisms through which agents acquire, coordinate, and improve robotic capabilities. By comparing representative approaches across the taxonomy, we explain how agent decisions depend on available tools, robot executors, and interaction feedback, and examine the strengths and limitations of these approaches. A Research Agenda for Practical Agentic Robots. Drawing on this analysis, we outline research directions for establishing agents' contributions and translating current advances into reliable, efficient robot operation. The agenda connects fair evaluation with the challenges of physical deployment and generalization across robotic platforms. Evolution of Robot Learning sec:policies-to-systems Robot learning spans four connected stages: learning executable behavior, integrating multimodal knowledge, predicting physical outcomes, and coordinating execution and improvement. (1) Conventional Robot Policies: Learning Executable Behavior. Reinforcement and imitation learning map observations to actions, while generalist policies share experience across tasks and embodiments. Their capabilities depend largely on the robot experience available during training. (2) Vision-Language-Action Models: Connecting Knowledge to Action. VLAs bring the visual and linguistic knowledge of pretrained foundation models into control, connecting the interpretation of scenes, instructions, and semantic relationships to action generation. (3) World Models and World-Action Models: Anticipating Physical Outcomes. These models connect action selection and generation to predictions of environmental change, using representations of future states, observations, and their relation to actions. (4) Agentic Robots: Organizing Execution and Improvement. Agentic systems extend model-mediated decisions to selecting and coordinating capabilities, acquiring experience, and using feedback to guide subsequent execution and capability improvement. These stages describe overlapping research traditions and complementary capabilities that can coexist in one system. Conventional Robot Policies sec:conventional-policy-learning Conventional robot policies learn from demonstrations or reward-based experience. We group visual policies by scene representation: image-based policies use image features, while 3D-aware policies introduce geometric structure for action prediction. This distinction concerns scene representation, not action dimensionality. Early policies learn actions from camera images. Guided policy search~ survey_ax_1504_00702 maps images and robot state to motor torques, while QT-Opt~ survey_ax_1806_10293 learns an image-conditioned action-value function for grasping. RoboMimic~ survey_ax_2108_03298 studies visual behavior cloning from offline demonstrations. Visual pretraining supplies reusable policy features: R3M~ survey_ax_2203_12601 pretrains an image encoder on human videos for downstream imitation learning. Beyond visual encoding, ACT~ survey_ax_2304_13705 and Diffusion Policy~ survey_ax_2303_04137 model action sequences with a conditional variational autoencoder and conditional diffusion, respectively. Task conditioning extends these policies to multiple behaviors: BC-Z~ survey_ax_2202_02005 and RT-1~ survey_ax_2212_06817 use task descriptions, while VIMA~ survey_ax_2210_03094 combines multimodal prompts with object-centered image tokens. Cross-robot datasets broaden training: RT-1-X~ survey_ax_2310_08864 draws on cross-robot data from Open X-Embodiment, and Octo~ survey_ax_2405_12213 combines heterogeneous image observations with a transformer and a diffusion action head. These policies use scene geometry to predict actions. Transporter Networks~ survey_ax_2010_14406 construct orthographic color-height maps from RGB-D observations to predict spatial pick-and-place actions, using a 2.5D scene representation. PerAct~ survey_ax_2209_05451 represents observations and action locations with 3D voxels, while RVT~ survey_ax_2306_14896 renders virtual views of a reconstructed point cloud and combines their predictions in 3D. Act3D~ survey_ax_2306_17817 lifts image features into a 3D feature field and samples action locations from coarse to fine. These geometric representations also support generative action models: DP3~ survey_ax_2403_03954 conditions action diffusion on compact features encoded from sparse point clouds, whereas 3D Diffuser Actor~ survey_ax_2402_10885 uses spatially located scene tokens and 3D attention to denoise end-effector trajectories. Mamba Policy~ survey_ax_2409_07163 retains point-cloud conditioning and combines selective state-space models with attention in its denoising network. Other methods learn geometric representations for downstream policies. GSRL~ survey_ax_2404_07950 pretrains and freezes a generalizable Gaussian predictor, then supplies its predicted 3D Gaussian scene representation to offline reinforcement-learning algorithms. Structural latent point pretraining~ survey_ax_2605_21258 regularizes point coordinates and features with a point-wise latent variational autoencoder and uses Gaussian rendering supervision; its latent representation is then supplied to an ACT policy. Scene representation, learning objective, and action decoder remain distinct, combinable design choices. Vision-Language-Action Models sec:vision-language-action VLAs adapt large-scale pretrained vision--language backbones to generate robot actions, as in RT-2~ survey_ax_2307_15818 , OpenVLA~ survey_ax_2406_09246 , and RoboFlamingo~ survey_ax_2311_01378 . Earlier policies already used language conditioning and pretrained encoders; VLAs connect broader knowledge of objects, relations, and instructions to action prediction through training on robot trajectories. -VLA~ survey_ax_2608_16885 combines a high-level subtask policy with a flow-matching action expert, using execution memory and selective world-model-guided test-time search for subtask selection. A central choice is how to decode robot actions. RT-2~ survey_ax_2307_15818 and OpenVLA~ survey_ax_2406_09246 discretize continuous actions into tokens for sequence generation. Diffusion- and flow-based approaches, including RDT-1B~ survey_ax_2410_07864 , ~ survey_ax_2410_24164 , ~ survey_ax_2504_16054 , CogACT~ survey_ax_2411_19650 , TinyVLA~ survey_ax_2409_12514 , GR00T N1~ survey_ax_2503_14734 , SmolVLA~ survey_ax_2506_01844 , DexVLA~ survey_ax_2502_05855 , InternVLA-M1~ survey_ax_2510_13778 , LingBot-VLA~ survey_ax_2601_18692 , and Qwen-VLA~ survey_ax_2605_30280 , condition continuous action decoders on visual and language features to generate action sequences. FAST~ survey_ax_2501_09747 compresses action sequences into compact tokens, while OpenVLA-OFT~ survey_ax_2502_19645 combines parallel decoding and action chunking to predict multiple future actions in one forward pass. Vela~ survey_ax_2610_05230 represents future motion with cubic B-splines, using a flow-matching expert to jointly predict control points and a motion-dependent temporal span. title: Graph-Reweighted Behavior Cloning with Human Interventions for Precise Robotic Manipulation
comment: Accepted at CoRL 2026. 25 pages, 16 figures, including appendix. Project page: https://gr-bc.github.io/
summary: Long-horizon precise manipulation produces mixed-quality data for post-training vision-language-action (VLA) models: even successful demonstrations and intervention-assisted rollouts may contain detours, hesitations, failed attempts, and imperfect recoveries. The key challenge is to identify which action chunks actually advance the task, rather than uniformly cloning or discarding imperfect trajectories. We propose Graph-Reweighted Behavior Cloning (GR-BC), an offline iterative post-training framework that builds a task-conditioned goal-reachability graph over demonstrations and iteratively collected rollouts, including both successful and failed episodes with human interventions. Reverse graph search computes minimal remaining steps to task success within the dataset support, and each action chunk is weighted by how much its execution reduces this potential. This consequence-based weighting reuses recoverable segments from failed trajectories, leverages interventions as recovery paths, and down-weights locally regressive chunks even inside successful trajectories. New rollouts are incorporated by appending them to the graph and rerunning search, without training a reward model, action-conditioned critic, or progress predictor. Across four precise manipulation tasks and three VLA backbones, GR-BC improves single-round supervised fine-tuning and reaches 91% success after a few offline iterations, without trajectory comparisons or progress labels. More details and videos are available at: https://gr-bc.github.io

The key challenge is to identify which action chunks actually advance the task, rather than uniformly cloning or discarding imperfect trajectories. We propose Graph-Reweighted Behavior Cloning (GR-BC), an offline iterative post-training framework that builds a task-conditioned goal-reachability graph over demonstrations and iteratively collected rollouts, including both successful and failed episodes with human interventions. Reverse graph search computes minimal remaining steps to task success within the dataset support, and each action chunk is weighted by how much its execution reduces this potential. This consequence-based weighting reuses recoverable segments from failed trajectories, leverages interventions as recovery paths, and down-weights locally regressive chunks even inside successful trajectories. New rollouts are incorporated by appending them to the graph and rerunning search, without training a reward model, action-conditioned critic, or progress predictor. Across four precise manipulation tasks and three VLA backbones, GR-BC improves single-round supervised fine-tuning and reaches 91 success after a few offline iterations, without trajectory comparisons or progress labels. More details and videos are available at Introduction Post-training vision-language-action (VLA) models~ kim2024openvla,zitkovich2023rt,black2024pi_0,black2025pi_,bjorck2025gr00t,zhai2025igniting,wu2026pragmatic,zhang2026prts,yang2025steering,huang2025notvla,liu2026stamo for long-horizon precise manipulation rarely start with ideally clean expert datasets. Demonstrations collected by human experts can contain suboptimal or undesired behaviors~ yin2024offline,mao2026arm,liu2026perfect , such as hesitations, overshoots, alignment detours, or recoveries from an earlier failed attempt. Intervention-assisted rollouts~ kelly2019hg are even more heterogeneous, mixing autonomous failures with delayed expert corrections and recoveries. Conversely, failure rollouts are not uniformly useless as they can also traverse goal-reachable states or contain short trajectory segments that steer the system back toward a viable path. Thus, the core challenge is essentially chunk-level credit assignment: whether an action chunk is worth imitating depends on how much task progress it induces when executed from the current state, rather than the final outcome of the entire trajectory. This motivates our central question: how can we effectively extract these progress-making action chunks from mixed-quality data, especially across iterative human-in-the-loop deployment rounds, to enhance sample efficiency for VLA post-training? Existing post-training and progress estimation approaches struggle to provide this fine-grained signal within the mixed-quality data. Standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) naively treats every action chunk as a positive target, thereby inadvertently cloning undesired behaviors from expert demonstrations or intervention-assisted rollouts~ yin2024offline,liu2025robot . Many progress estimation methods implicitly assume that task progress evolves monotonically along successful trajectories~ chen2025sarm , which hardly holds when trajectories contain correction behaviors or pauses~ yin2024offline,mao2026arm . Although recent reward modeling approaches attempt address this by predicting chunk-level progress, they are inevitably bottlenecked by two limitations: (i) an over-reliance on heavy human or VLM annotations, such as dense progress labels, subtask boundaries, and trajectory comparisons~ chen2025sarm,mao2026arm,feng2026procvlm,liang2026robometer ; and (ii) the out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization gap inherent in large-scale pre-trained reward models, which often fail to provide reliable zero-shot progress signals when confronted with the precise visual nuances of unseen downstream tasks~ lee2026roboreward,tan2025robo,chen2026topreward,wu2026large . While graph-search imitation~ yin2024offline avoids learning a neural progress predictor, it uses graph search primarily to retrieve high-value neighboring actions for imitation, rather than to quantify how much the action chunk actually executed at a state moves the system toward success. Our core insight is that the quality of an action chunk should be measured by its consequence: specifically, whether its execution reduces the minimal remaining steps to task completion. Crucially, this signal naturally penalizes local regressions inside successful trajectories, while simultaneously up-weighting valid progress-making chunks hidden within an overall failed rollouts. To this end, we propose GR-BC, a graph-based framework for iterative offline VLA post-training over long-horizon precise manipulation tasks. GR-BC constructs a task-conditioned goal-reachability graph over demonstrations and intervention-assisted rollouts using multi-view MCR~ jiang2025robots embeddings to retrieve candidate visual neighbors and conservative similarity edges to connect dynamically compatible states. Instead of ranking neighbors or training a progress predictor, GR-BC runs reverse graph search to estimate minimal remaining steps and interpolates this potential to dense training states. The policy is then optimized only on physically executed action chunks, with each chunk's contribution scaled by a precomputed weight proportional to its progress improvement. Because the graph is non-parametric, each offline iteration only appends new rollouts and reruns search, with no reward model, critic, progress predictor, architecture change, or supervised-loss modification. The contributions are: Graph-Retrieved Progress (GRP): We propose a non-parametric progress estimation method that constructs a task-conditioned reachability graph and retrieves minimal remaining steps to success, avoiding reward models, critics, progress labels, or VLM annotations. Graph-Reweighted Behavior Cloning (GR-BC): We introduce a graph-reweighted behavior cloning objective that preserves the standard supervised VLA loss while reweighting each executed action chunk using GRP. This consequence-based reweighting reuses recovery chunks from failed rollouts while suppressing regressive chunks in successful trajectories. Iterative Offline Graph-Guided VLA Adaptation: We validate GR-BC in human-in-the-loop offline iterative training by updating the reachability graph with intervention-assisted rollouts and reusing them in subsequent training rounds, achieving over 90 success on multiple long-horizon precise manipulation tasks with multiple VLA backbones. Related Work sec:related_work Progress Rewards for Robotic Manipulation. Long-horizon precise manipulation often relies on dense progress signals to provide supervision beyond sparse task success. Some methods infer progress from temporal order, goal proximity, or video ranking~ wu2021learning,lee2021generalizable,yang2024rank2reward , while others learn stage- or subtask-aware progress models from segmented demonstrations or language annotations~ chen2025sarm,mu2024drs,kim2025subtask . More recent work uses foundation models or process reward models to estimate visual task progress from language, videos, or VLM judgments~ lee2026roboreward,tan2025robo,hung2025victor,ma2023liv,alakuijala2024video,ma2025vision,zhang2025rewind . ARM~ mao2026arm is closest to our motivation, replacing absolute progress scores with relative advantage labels for progressive, regressive, and stagnant behavior. However, these approaches typically require learned reward models, progress labels, stage annotations, VLM scoring, or temporal-order assumptions. GRP instead retrieves progress directly from graph reachability and reverse search, without learning a reward or progress function. Weighted Behavior Cloning for VLA Post-training. Many RL-based VLA post-training methods improve downstream task performance while preserving the generalization inherited from pretrained VLA backbones through constrained updates~ wagenmaker2025steering,xiao2025self,li2025gr,chen2025conrft,wang2026learning,liu2026perturbot . Within this broader paradigm, weighted behavior cloning improves policy learning from heterogeneous data by assigning higher likelihood weights to actions estimated to be more valuable. Many weighted imitation and offline RL methods derive training weights from estimated values or advantages~ peng2019advantage,nair2020awac,kostrikov2021offline,chen2020bail . Recent robot and VLA post-training methods similarly reweight behavior cloning using reward, advantage, intervention, or off-policy value estimates~ chen2025sarm,mao2026arm,liu2025robot,yang2026aloe,intelligence2025pi,su2026ig . Unlike prior weighted BC methods, GR-BC does not estimate action values, rewards, or advantages. Instead, it uses a non-parametric, graph-derived progress potential to derive weights from the observed reduction in minimal remaining steps, directly measuring the consequence of executed action chunks. title: Hierarchical Residual Policy Learning for Real-World Mobile Manipulation with Sparse Human Guidance
comment: Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026); Project Website: https://hire-moma.github.io/
summary: Mobile Manipulation (MoMa) is a cornerstone of autonomous robotic systems, yet real-world fine-tuning remains a formidable challenge because of high-dimensional action spaces and intricate coupling between heterogeneous modules. In this paper, we propose HiRe-MoMa (Hierarchical Residual Mobile Manipulation), a systematic framework for stable and sample-efficient real-world fine-tuning of complex MoMa systems. At its core, HiRe-MoMa adopts a Hierarchical Residual Architecture that fine-tunes a frozen base policy. A Policy-Agnostic Residual learns additive corrections atop the base policy, while Hierarchical Decoupling splits the residual into mobile-base and manipulator-arm heads with unidirectional conditioning, mitigating gradient interference and aligning corrections with the platform's physical hierarchy. To improve sample efficiency in data-expensive real-world settings, we propose Expert-Guided Value Alignment, which leverages sparse human interventions with under 20% training coverage to reshape the critic's value landscape, effectively guiding autonomous exploration through expert priors. Extensive real-world experiments on the TIAGo++ platform demonstrate that HiRe-MoMa consistently enhances task performance with only around 30 minutes of online interaction, regardless of the base policy architecture. To our knowledge, this is among the first frameworks to enable efficient on-robot fine-tuning for mobile manipulation in the real world, providing a practical paradigm for deploying complex robotic systems in dynamic, human-centric environments. Further details can be found on our project website: https://hire-moma.github.io/
full_text: Corresponding author: jiachen li@gatech.edu Mobile Manipulation (MoMa) is a cornerstone of autonomous robotic systems, yet real-world fine-tuning remains a formidable challenge because of high-dimensional action spaces and intricate coupling between heterogeneous modules. In this paper, we propose HiRe-MoMa ( erarchical sidual bile nipulation), a systematic framework for stable and sample-efficient real-world fine-tuning of complex MoMa systems. At its core, HiRe-MoMa adopts a Hierarchical Residual Architecture that fine-tunes a frozen base policy. A Policy-Agnostic Residual learns additive corrections atop the base policy, while Hierarchical Decoupling splits the residual into mobile-base and manipulator-arm heads with unidirectional conditioning, mitigating gradient interference and aligning corrections with the platform's physical hierarchy. To improve sample efficiency in data-expensive real-world settings, we propose Expert-Guided Value Alignment, which leverages sparse human interventions with under 20 training coverage to reshape the critic’s value landscape, effectively guiding autonomous exploration through expert priors. Extensive real-world experiments on the TIAGo++ platform demonstrate that HiRe-MoMa consistently enhances task performance with only around 30 minutes of online interaction, regardless of the base policy architecture. To our knowledge, this is among the first frameworks to enable efficient on-robot fine-tuning for mobile manipulation in the real world, providing a practical paradigm for deploying complex robotic systems in dynamic, human-centric environments. Further details can be found on our project website . Introduction sec:introduction Mobile manipulation is a key step toward multi-purpose robotic systems that operate in human-centric environments. Performing long-horizon and multi-object tasks, from domestic chores to industrial logistics, requires the coordinated operation of heterogeneous modules such as mobile bases, robotic arms, and sensory heads. Despite its potential, autonomous mobile manipulation remains challenging due to high-dimensional action spaces, tightly coupled inter-module dynamics, and the non-stationarity of real-world deployment. Recent advancements have leveraged Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for semantic reasoning~ shah2025bumble,jiang2026navtrust,zhang2026commcp,yan2025rdd,chakraborty2026toward , generative modeling for robust imitation learning~ jiang2025brs,ghosh2025robust , and simulation-to-real reinforcement learning for skill acquisition~ Hu-RSS-23 . However, a single-shot trained policy often fails to generalize to the stochasticity of diverse real-world deployment scenarios. Post-training or fine-tuning is thus essential to bridge the performance gap. While fine-tuning has seen success in isolated manipulation or locomotion tasks~ amin2025pi, smith2022legged , its application to the coupled, high-dimensional domain of mobile manipulation remains largely unexplored. Real-world fine-tuning, however, is shaped by a series of fundamental trade-offs. Imitation learning (IL), particularly DAgger-based approaches~ ross2011reduction , offers a straightforward optimization objective but is constrained by inherent expert data scarcity and a lack of autonomous exploration, which often leads to limited generalization on out-of-distribution states and compounding errors at deployment. Reinforcement learning (RL) enables broader state-space exploration~ liu2025what but faces significant obstacles when paired with modern generative base policies, whose intractable log-likelihoods preclude standard policy gradient methods~ zhang2025reinflow . Residual RL offers a promising and practical middle ground by learning additive corrections atop frozen base policies for model-agnostic adaptation~ jiang2025transic, ankile2025imitation , yet extending it to mobile manipulation introduces a distinct challenge: inter-module coupling. As shown in~ , a task as routine as grasping becomes difficult in the MoMa context: it requires tight spatiotemporal coordination between the mobile base and the arm, and any misalignment in the base's approach rapidly propagates as a sizable pose error at the manipulator. Without explicit structural priors, the high-dimensional action space and non-stationary inter-module dynamics often hinder convergence and ultimately prevent the precision required for physical interaction. In this paper, we propose HiRe-MoMa ( erarchical sidual bile nipulation), a framework for real-world fine-tuning of mobile manipulation systems, built around three components. First, our Policy-Agnostic Residual Learning paradigm adds a learnable residual atop a frozen base policy, sidestepping the intractable log-likelihoods of generative architectures and allowing the same procedure to refine diverse pre-trained policies. Second, to address this base-arm coupling specific to mobile manipulation, we introduce a Hierarchical Decoupling structure with unidirectional conditioning: the manipulator's residual head is conditioned on the base's correction, reflecting the system's physical hierarchy. Third, an Expert-Guided Value Alignment loss leverages sparse human interventions to reshape the critic's value landscape toward expert-preferred behaviors, improving sample efficiency without overriding RL exploration. HiRe-MoMa is realized as an asynchronous actor-learner system on a single robot: an onboard rollout worker executes the policy while a central learner optimizes the residual on a workstation, enabling on-robot fine-tuning in the real world. Overall, our main contributions are as follows:\\ 1) Systematic Fine-tuning Framework: We present an asynchronous, model-agnostic framework for the real-world fine-tuning of mobile manipulation systems, enabling efficient adaptation in this high-dimensional and coupled robotic domain with 25--40 minutes of online interaction. 2) Hierarchical Residual Architecture: We introduce independent residual policies for distinct modules, coupled with a unidirectional conditioning mechanism to ensure stable and logically coherent coordinated control. 3) Expert-Guided Alignment: We develop an auxiliary human intervention alignment loss that leverages sparse expert guidance ( 20 of collected data) to improve sample efficiency and accelerate convergence. 4) Empirical Validation on Diverse MoMa Tasks: We validate HiRe-MoMa on three real-world TIAGo++ tasks of increasing complexity, demonstrating consistent improvements across two distinct base policy architectures (Diffusion Policy and ACT). Related Work sec:relatedwork Real-World Reinforcement Learning offers a principled path to bridging the sim-to-real gap~ XuC1-RSS-25 , with sample efficiency as the central challenge. The SERL framework~ luo2024serl demonstrated the efficacy of off-policy RL for robot fine-tuning, inspiring subsequent residual correction methods~ chen2025conrft, ankile2025residual . Existing residual and HIL systems~ luo2025precise, chen2025conrft, jiang2025transic, ankile2025imitation, ankile2025residual fine-tune fixed-base arms, where base--arm gradient interference does not arise; HiRe-MoMa instead targets policy-agnostic, on-robot fine-tuning of a whole-body mobile manipulator, without simulation-pre-trained latent action spaces~ hu2025slac . Policy Post-Training of base policies~ chi2025diffusion, zhao2025vlas via RL is hampered by intractable log-likelihoods, motivating surrogate objectives~ zhang2025reinflow, chen2025pi_, wang2024diffusion, pmlr-v267-ma25d or policy-agnostic RL~ mark2024policy, chen2025conrft . Residual RL offers a practical middle ground by learning additive corrections atop frozen policies~ ankile2025residual, gong2025robust,Wang_2026_CVPR,11696068,gao2026guides , with human-in-the-loop variants~ kelly2019hg, hu2025rac,kim2025human further mitigating distributional drift. Yet simple residuals cannot address the cross-module coupling inherent in MoMa: the spatiotemporal dependency between base and arm demands structured decoupling that flat residual methods do not provide. Mobile Manipulation poses unique challenges owing to its high-dimensional action space and tight base-arm coupling~ jiang2025brs, chen2025acdit . Most RL methods still rely on simulation-pre-trained priors~ Hu-RSS-23, zhang2025catch or expensive skill-discovery phases~ hu2025slac, Mendonca2024Continuously to bridge the sim-to-real gap. HiRe-MoMa instead operates directly in the raw action space of any pre-trained policy, modeling hierarchical inter-module dependencies under a sparse success-only reward without manual reward shaping. Human-in-the-Loop corrections serve as safety buffers~ luo2025precise, amin2025pi , imitation data sources~ Liu-RSS-23 , or auxiliary supervision signals~ li2022efficient, wang2025inference, korkmaz2025mile in robot RL. Beyond these roles, interventions implicitly encode expert value preferences~ amin2025pi ; HiRe-MoMa exploits this by treating corrections as functional constraints on the critic’s value surface, directly reshaping the value landscape to reflect expert priorities. A broader discussion of related work on these four topics is provided in~ . Problem Formulation sec:preliminary We study the problem of fine-tuning pre-trained base policies ~ pmlr-v305-black25a, chi2025diffusion, gong2025carp for complex robotic tasks in unstructured real-world environments. While Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) via imitation learning offers a stable convergence path, its efficacy is fundamentally bounded by the coverage and quality of pre-collected demonstrations, which are typically scarce and sub-optimal in practice. Conversely, Reinforcement Learning (RL) enables the agent to extend beyond the constraints of static datasets through active exploration, fostering improved robustness and task proficiency. This online refinement is especially important for high-dimensional systems such as mobile manipulators, where conventional zero-shot transfer leaves a persistent deployment-time gap. We formalize the fine-tuning process as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP), defined by the tuple . represents the underlying hidden environment states, and denotes the high-dimensional continuous action space (e.g., joint velocities or Cartesian poses). The observation space comprises multi-modal sensory inputs, including RGB images and robot proprioception, while the transition dynamics are governed by real-world physical interactions. To minimize reward engineering and remain task-agnostic, we adopt a sparse binary reward function , where denotes task success and otherwise. The objective is to refine the policy to maximize the expected cumulative discounted return: , where is the discount factor. This formulation drives policy refinement toward higher task success rates and improved temporal efficiency under real-world execution. Method sec:method To facilitate efficient fine-tuning for high-dimensional mobile manipulation, we propose HiRe-MoMa ( erarchical sidual bile nipulation), a model-agnostic framework designed for stable real-world adaptation via human-robot interaction ( ). The framework consists of three components: (i) a policy-agnostic residual that learns additive corrections atop a frozen prior without structural assumptions on the base policy; (ii) a hierarchical decoupling mechanism that mitigates optimization interference between heterogeneous modules (e.g., mobile base and manipulator arm) by enforcing a unidirectional dependency aligned with the system's physical hierarchy; (iii) an expert-guided value alignment loss that leverages sparse human interventions to reshape the critic's value landscape, improving sample efficiency under safe real-world exploration. title: SafeDriveVLA: Navigation-Conditioned World Model Dreaming for Conflict-Aware End-to-End Autonomous Driving
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are gaining attention in autonomous driving, inheriting commonsense priors from large language models (LLMs) and widening the navigation interface from a fixed command set to free-form natural-language instructions. However, this open-ended interface exposes a new vulnerability surface: an inattentive driver may issue instructions that are unsafe given the current scene, and a malicious user may issue dangerous ones on purpose. We present the first benchmark suite that evaluates navigation following and conflict awareness together, along with adversarial robustness. Existing VLAs fall short on both: SimLingo completes no language-instructed lane change in closed loop, and all models degrade sharply under conflicting signals. We propose SafeDriveVLA, the first driving VLA that (1) explicitly predicts a three-level navigation-compliance mode to decouple conflict reasoning from action generation, and (2) uses navigation-conditioned world model dreaming to inform this prediction. Unlike prior world models that roll out expert or planned actions, ours dreams of strictly following the navigation signal, showing when following is safe. SafeDriveVLA reaches 88.16 Driving Score (DS) and 68.64% Success Rate (SR) on Bench2Drive, lifts closed-loop language following by 49.3% and reduces collisions under unsafe instructions from 60 to 38 compared to the best SimLingo variant. Video demonstrations are available on our project page.
full_text: 6pt Introduction Autonomous driving has shifted from modular pipelines~ urmson2008autonomous, wei2014behavioral, paden2016survey to end-to-end (E2E) systems~ hu2023planning, jiang2023vad , where the latest generation of E2E models, Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs), further widens the navigation interface from a fixed command set to free-form natural-language instructions~ renz2025simlingo, wang2025alpamayo, zuo2026vega, zhou2025autovla . VLAs are also entering production vehicles: Li Auto has rolled out its VLA driver model to customer cars~ liauto2025i8 , and NVIDIA is bringing its Alpamayo VLA~ wang2025alpamayo to production in the Mercedes-Benz CLA~ lambert2026nvidia . This progression reduces inter-module error accumulation and scales better with large driving datasets, but also removes the explicit safety mechanism that once resolved conflicts between the navigation signal and the local scenarios. Shown in Fig.~ fig:teaser , classical modular stacks routed the navigation signal through a rule-based behavior planner~ wei2014behavioral, fan2018baidu, schwarting2018planning that resolved it against local context, such as traffic lights and pedestrians, before making driving decisions. E2E systems instead internalize this judgment into the neural network, leaving the model to learn from data alone whether to follow or delay a given navigation signal. VLAs amplify this difficulty, as the navigation interface becomes an open-ended language space. In this work, we present the first benchmark suite that evaluates navigation following and conflict awareness together, since a model that ignores every instruction looks safe on a conflict benchmark, while one that follows every instruction looks good on a following benchmark. It covers (i) navigation following (CARLA-F), a closed-loop CARLA benchmark with traffic disabled so every navigation signal should be executed; (ii) navigation-scene conflict (B2D-C and NavSim-C), unsafe instructions or commands triggered at safety-critical events; and (iii) adversarial instructions (B2D-Adv), unsafe under any circumstance. This split mirrors the helpfulness--harmlessness trade-off in LLM alignment~ bai2022training, dai2024safe . Existing VLAs fall short on both: SimLingo completes none of its language-instructed lane changes in closed loop despite an 83 open-loop rate~ renz2025simlingo , and all models degrade drastically under conflicting signals, executing them without grounding in the scene. Next, we propose , to our knowledge, the first driving VLA that (i) explicitly predicts a three-level navigation-compliance mode to decouple conflict reasoning from action generation, and (ii) uses navigation-conditioned world model dreaming to inform this prediction. First, we relabel every expert frame with a mode (strict, cautious, or fallback) for whether the expert executes, cautiously follows, or overrides the signal, and emit this mode token before the action tokens, so conflict reasoning is directly supervised rather than entangled with action generation. Second, unlike prior world models that roll out expert or planned actions, our world model dreams of strictly following the navigation signal, showing the model when following is safe and making it less conservative than with the mode token alone. reaches 88.16 Driving Score (DS) and 68.64 Success Rate (SR) on Bench2Drive, lifts closed-loop language following by 49.3 over the best SimLingo variant, and decreases B2D-C collisions from 60 to 38. Our contributions are: (1) Benchmarks for navigation following and navigation-scene conflict awareness; (2) Design of explicit navigation-compliance modes that decouple conflict reasoning from action generation, and of navigation-conditioned world model dreaming that shows when following is safe; and (3) Evaluation on Bench2Drive and all our benchmarks. DriveBench~ xie2025vlms shows that plausible language outputs can rely on textual cues or general knowledge without reliable visual grounding, motivating evaluation beyond answer fluency. Recent VLAs pursue instruction following through action dreaming~ renz2025simlingo , driver-preference alignment~ wang2026drive , scaled instruction-following data~ zuo2026vega , and related designs~ sima2024drivelm, xing2025openemma, hwangemma, wang2025omnidrive, zengfuturesightdrive, chiimpromptu, fu2025orion, zhou2026opendrivevla, zhou2025autovla . NoRD~ rawal2026nord explores data-efficient driving without dense reasoning annotations. We instead study both sides of this capability, training a VLA to reliably follow safe navigation signals and to recognize when a navigation signal conflicts with the surrounding scene. Early language-driven systems already connect semantic reasoning with driving decisions. DriveGPT4~ xu2024drivegpt4 interprets driving actions and predicts low-level control signals. Dolphins~ ma2024dolphins studies grounded conversational reasoning and reflection, while DriveVLM~ tian2025drivevlm couples scene analysis with hierarchical planning. DriveMLM~ cui2025drivemlm maps multimodal reasoning into explicit behavioral planning states, and RDA-Driver~ huang2024making constrains the correspondence between reasoning traces and planning outputs. These mechanisms address decision representation and consistency; our mode token explicitly indicates whether the requested maneuver should be executed, delayed, or overridden. WorldLens~ liang2026worldlens evaluates visual, geometric, physical, and behavioral fidelity, emphasizing that realistic generation alone does not establish reliable control. The agentic world-modeling taxonomy~ chu2026agentic further emphasizes action-conditioned simulation and decision-centric evaluation. World modeling also extends to structured spatial representations: DynamicCity and DOME~ bian2025dynamiccity, gu2024dome study dynamic semantic occupancy generation and trajectory-controllable occupancy forecasting, respectively, LiDARCrafter~ liang2026lidarcrafter models temporal LiDAR sequences, and U4D~ xu2026u4d incorporates uncertainty into 4D LiDAR generation. Such representations complement image and latent prediction by capturing scene geometry and temporal structure. For instruction-conditioned driving, reliable perception supplies the evidence needed to interpret a maneuver in context: road layout, surrounding agents, and evolving hazards can determine whether the same request remains feasible. Improvements in scene representation therefore support conflict reasoning, although representation quality alone does not determine how a policy should respond to an unsafe request. DriveSafe's risk-detection framework~ artham2026drivesafe identifies scene-grounded hazards and generates safety suggestions, while VLM-AutoDrive~ bhat2026vlmautodrive adapts VLMs to temporally localized collisions and near-collisions. A separate DriveSafe taxonomy~ kumar2026drivesafetaxonomy evaluates unsafe requests to LLM-based driving assistants. title: PAWA: Panoramic Action-conditioned World Modeling for Multiple Agents
summary: A multiplayer world model must predict how the independent actions of several players change a shared environment, including changes outside a player's current field of view. A point-of-view (POV) video captures such changes only after they enter its field of view, whereas panoramic video records the surroundings in every viewing direction and has served as an intermediate representation of the world state in recent world models. Learning this task therefore requires synchronized POV and panoramic videos of interacting players together with their actions, yet no existing dataset provides this combination in Minecraft, an established testbed in which players act independently in a shared, modifiable 3D world. We present PAWA, a dataset and framework for action-conditioned panoramic multiplayer world modeling. The dataset pairs each player's POV video with world-stabilized panoramic video and aligned actions. Its distributed pipeline decouples CPU gameplay capture from GPU rendering, scales beyond 64 simultaneous players, and re-renders each recorded session under new observation configurations without replaying the gameplay. On this dataset, we develop a dual-tower model that jointly predicts POV and panoramic video and couples the two streams through cross-attention that aligns tokens observing the same direction in a shared world frame. We further introduce a quadratic-phase player encoding that provides many more player codes than existing rotary codes at the same embedding dimension. Experiments show that PAWA outperforms state-of-the-art multiplayer world models in POV prediction quality while also producing high-fidelity panoramic predictions. The dataset and collection pipeline are open source to support further research on multiplayer world models.
full_text: We will release both to support future multiplayer world models. Introduction sec:intro In a multiplayer world, several players act independently on a shared environment, and each action can change what every other player sees. A world model for such a world must predict how these combined actions unfold in each player's observations. Many of the consequences arise outside a player's field of view. A teammate places a block behind the player, or an opponent approaches from the side, and the change becomes visible only once the camera turns toward it. A point-of-view (POV) video therefore records the shared world only in part. Panoramic video records the surroundings in every direction at once, and recent world models have adopted it as a representation of the surrounding scene and as spatial memory~ jiang2026panoworld,li2026panoworldmemory . Pairing each player's POV video with a panorama exposes the surroundings of every player to the model, including the regions that no local camera currently observes. Minecraft offers a natural setting, since players act independently in a shared 3D world that every action can modify. It is an established testbed for action-conditioned video world models~ guo2025mineworld,yu2025gamefactory,zhang2025matrixgame,he2025matrixgame2 , and recent multiplayer models synchronize the POV videos of several interacting players~ savva2026solaris,liu2026gammaworld,wu2026multiworld . These multiplayer models learn from perspective observations alone. Other multi-agent world models broaden visual coverage by stitching directional views into panoramas~ zhu2026shareverse or by projecting panoramic recordings into perspective training views~ sun2026prismaworld , yet their generated streams remain perspective videos. Predicting full-sphere panoramic video jointly with each player's POV under the actions of interacting players remains unexplored. Modeling POV and panoramic video together for many players raises three challenges. Existing multiplayer data are recorded by screen capture from live game clients, which yields only the displayed perspective view. Every player also requires its own graphics client, and the recording cost therefore grows with the population. No dataset pairs POV and panoramic video with the actions of interacting players. The same scene direction occupies different image coordinates in a rectilinear POV frame and an equirectangular panorama. Because the POV camera turns with the player's head while the panorama stays fixed to the world, this correspondence changes at every frame. A model that shares parameters across players must keep each observation stream bound to its own actions. Existing rotary player codes admit only equidistant identities in phase planes~ liu2026gammaworld , and the identity pool therefore grows only linearly with the embedding dimension. In this paper, we present (Panoramic Action-conditioned World modeling for multiple Agents), a dataset and framework for action-conditioned panoramic multiplayer world modeling in Minecraft. records gameplay on CPUs without graphics clients, simulating sessions with more than 64 simultaneous players, and renders the saved replays offline on GPUs. Each replay yields a player's POV video, a world-stabilized equirectangular panorama and aligned actions, and can be rendered again with relative depth or along custom camera trajectories without repeating gameplay. These observations serve multiplayer world modeling well beyond panoramic prediction. Coding agents compose interaction scripts from natural-language descriptions, and behavioral checks together with vision-language review retain the scripts whose intended interactions occur (Figure~ fig:collection-overview ). A POV tower and a panorama tower jointly predict the two videos and are repeatedly coupled through bidirectional ray-aligned cross-attention. Each token carries its viewing ray in a shared world frame as a rotary phase, and tokens that observe the same direction thus have zero relative phase regardless of their image coordinates (Figure~ fig:model-overview ). The panorama thus serves as both a prediction target and a source of context for the local view. In the resulting forecasts, a co-player seen in a player's POV appears in the matching direction of the same player's panorama (Figure~ fig:teaser ). Building on classical quadratic-phase codes~ wootters1989optimal , assigns each player a rotary code from a pool of identities in the same phase planes. The identity pool thus grows quadratically rather than linearly with the embedding dimension. Our contributions are threefold. (i) We construct a multiplayer Minecraft dataset of synchronized POV and world-stabilized panoramic videos with aligned actions, whose distributed pipeline scales beyond 64 simultaneous players and re-renders replays with relative depth or custom camera trajectories. (ii) We propose a dual-tower world model that jointly predicts POV and panoramic video, whose ray-aligned cross-attention encodes world-frame viewing rays as rotary phases and thereby assigns identical phases to matching viewing directions in the two projections. (iii) We introduce a quadratic-phase player encoding that enlarges the identity pool from to codes at a fixed embedding dimension, with closed-form correlations between any two codes. Their generated streams remain perspective videos, and their multiplayer data come from live game clients~ savva2026solaris . Like procedural generators that render programmable scenes offline~ greff2022kubric,deitke2022procthor , renders recorded gameplay into aligned POV and panoramic videos, and it predicts both. These models build on 360-degree video diffusion~ wang2024360dvd,zhang2025panodit,xia2025panowan,ji2025campvg, zhou2025holotime , perspective-to-panorama expansion~ ma2024vidpanos,luo2025beyondframe,li2026cubecomposer , and joint perspective and panoramic modeling~ tang2023mvdiffusion,zhang2024panfusion,tan2024imagine360, fang2025viewpoint . Panoramic multiplayer dataset sec:data A panoramic multiplayer world model learns from both projections and the actions of every player within one synchronized interaction. To this end, we construct a dataset that pairs each player's POV video with a world-stabilized panoramic video, aligned actions and camera annotations. Existing multiplayer data such as the Solaris dataset are recorded from live Minecraft clients~ savva2026solaris , which limits each recording to the perspective view displayed during play. Our pipeline instead records programmable interactions on CPUs and renders the saved replays offline on GPUs, which yields POV and panoramic videos, relative depth and custom camera trajectories from a single interaction without repeating the gameplay (Figure~ fig:collection-overview ). Scaling multiplayer data collection. SolarisEngine pairs each Mineflayer controller with a live graphics client~ savva2026solaris , and controller computation and rendering therefore both grow with the player count and must keep pace with the running simulation. removes rendering from gameplay. Its player runtime, built on the open-source Azalea library, executes action scripts written in Rust and simulates interactions among more than 64 simultaneous players while recording per-tick actions, positions, camera orientations and player state. Without graphics clients, independent episodes run in parallel across CPU hosts, and GPU workers render the saved replays on separate hosts, with views and camera paths assigned to workers independently. Capture and rendering thus scale with separate resources, and a large session is recorded once and rendered afterwards. Generating and validating interactions. Interaction scenarios are specified as natural-language descriptions of player behaviors and expected outcomes. Coding agents compose reusable interaction primitives into executable scripts, which may fail to produce their intended interaction, and each scenario is therefore validated on both behavior and appearance. Behavioral quality control (QC) detects inactivity, ineffective movement and abrupt control changes in the recorded actions and states before rendering, and a vision-language model (VLM) then reviews sampled videos against the specified outcomes. Both checks return feedback for the coding agents to revise the scripts. Observing a shared world beyond the local view. Each player's rectilinear POV video is paired with an equirectangular panorama rendered from the same camera origin. The panorama stays oriented to the world as the player's head turns, which gives every frame a stable directional reference and records changes that no local camera observes. All videos share the server clock, and action annotations and camera poses bind each observation to its player (Appendix~ app:data-details ). title: STP-GUI: Spatially-Aware Token Pruning for Efficient Web-GUI Agents
summary: With the rapid development of vision-language models (VLMs), Web-GUI agents have achieved promising performance in interacting with real-world interfaces through screenshot-based grounding. However, high-resolution screenshots and multi-turn histories introduce excessive visual tokens, causing substantial inference overhead. Existing token pruning methods, mainly designed for natural images, often select tokens independently based on importance scores, which can fragment the local visual structures required for recognizing small GUI elements such as buttons, icons, and hyperlinks. In this work, we propose STP-GUI (Spatially-aware Token Pruning for GUI agents), a query-guided token pruning framework that preserves fine-grained instruction-conditioned token scoring while performing spatially coherent window-level selection under aggressive token reduction. A lightweight selector is optimized through policy learning while the VLM backbone remains frozen. Experiments on Online-Mind2Web show that \papername achieves a favorable efficiency-performance tradeoff under low token budgets. At 21% token retention, it preserves 77.7% of full-token performance while reducing inference latency by 31% and FLOPs by 57%. Results on Android in the Wild further suggest that the method transfers to mobile GUI environments.

However, high-resolution screenshots and multi-turn histories introduce excessive visual tokens, causing substantial inference overhead. Existing token pruning methods, mainly designed for natural images, often select tokens independently based on importance scores, which can fragment the local visual structures required for recognizing small GUI elements such as buttons, icons, and hyperlinks. In this work, we propose (Spatially-aware Token Pruning for GUI agents), a query-guided token pruning framework that preserves fine-grained instruction-conditioned token scoring while performing spatially coherent window-level selection under aggressive token reduction. A lightweight selector is optimized through policy learning while the VLM backbone remains frozen. Experiments on Online-Mind2Web show that achieves a favorable efficiency-performance tradeoff under low token budgets. At 21 token retention, it preserves 77.7 of full-token performance while reducing inference latency by 31 and FLOPs by 57 . Results on Android in the Wild further suggest that the method transfers to mobile GUI environments. Introduction sec:intro With the rapid development of vision-language models (VLMs), Web-GUI agents that navigate real websites by grounding actions in screenshots and text instructions have seen growing adoption~ fu2025mano,wang2025ui,bai2025qwen3, bai2025qwen25vltechnicalreport, wang2024qwen2 . This setting requires high-resolution visual inputs to resolve small interactive elements such as hyperlinks, icons, and drop-down menus. The cost is a large visual token sequence: for instance, Qwen3-VL~ bai2025qwen3 encodes a single 1920 1080 screenshot into approximately 2,040 visual tokens. Furthermore, as is a common practice in Web-GUI agent systems~ fu2025mano, qin2025uitarspioneeringautomatedgui,wang2025ui, bai2024digirl , agents receive multiple interaction history---prior screenshots, actions, and observations---at each step, which can easily push the total visual token count beyond 10K. These large prefill token counts severely bottleneck inference, yet users are sensitive to agent response latency. Reducing visual token load is therefore a practical challenge. A straightforward strategy is to prune visual tokens before input the LLM modules, as has been studied for VLM~ shen2025fastvid,shang2025llava, yang2025visionzip . Web-GUI screenshots, however, pose distinct challenges that make standard pruning strategies unreliable. First, informative regions are sparse, localized, and often tiny---a single icon or hyperlink may occupy only a handful of visual tokens---while most of the page consists of blank background, repeated layout blocks, or decorative structure. Second, the spatial continuity of these small regions is essential: losing a few adjacent patches can destroy the visual evidence needed to identify a clickable element. These characteristics make pruning strategies designed for natural images~ liu2026hiprunehierarchicalattentionefficient,xing2024pyramiddrop , where foreground objects are large and continuous, a poor fit for web interfaces. Despite these challenges, prior pruning paradigms in the VLM literature---attention-based selection~ liu2026hiprunehierarchicalattentionefficient,xing2024pyramiddrop,shang2025llava , similarity-based filtering~ cai2025flashvlm,yang2025visionzip,jeddi2025similarity , and learnable summarization~ cha2024honeybee may remain suboptimal for GUI screenshots. Existing pruning methods~ liu2026hiprunehierarchicalattentionefficient,sun2026ivcprunerevealingimplicitvisual involves two related decisions: estimating instruction relevance and organizing the retained evidence. Token-wise selection offers fine-grained relevance ranking, but may retain disconnected fragments of interface elements. Window-wise selection imposes local spatial structure, yet its effectiveness also depends on whether the underlying scores identify useful regions. We therefore study scoring and selection granularity jointly. Our matched-budget comparison shows that pooling Attention scores into windows yields modest improvements, while window-wise selection provides larger gains with the learned STP-GUI scorer. This motivates a lightweight instruction-conditioned selector that estimates token relevance and retains complete spatial windows before LLM processing. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:teaser , we propose STP-GUI (Spatially-aware Token Pruning for GUI agents), a query--guided token pruning method that selects spatially contiguous windows rather than isolated tokens. Concretely, STP-GUI first computes token‑wise importance scores using a lightweight query--conditioned scoring module, aggregates the scores within windows, and then uses a Plackett--Luce policy during training to learn which windows to retain. At inference time, windows are selected greedily by score rank under a fixed token budget, while the VLM backbone remains frozen throughout. This design preserves fine‑grained token scoring while reducing spatial fragmentation of the retained set, thereby helping the model preserve local evidence around GUI elements such as buttons, icons, and label‑field pairs. Experiments on Online-Mind2Web (300 tasks across 136 live websites)~ xue2025illusion show that STP-GUI is particularly competitive at low retention budgets. By evaluating on Android in the Wild (AitW)~ rawles2023androidwildlargescaledataset , we further show that the same design transfers beyond web screenshots to mobile GUI settings. At 21 token retention, it achieves the strongest success rate among the compared methods reported at their evaluated operating points while reducing inference latency by 31 and FLOPs by 57 relative to the dense baseline. Our main contributions are summarized as: We identify a previously overlooked failure mode of GUI-agent token pruning: coupling importance estimation and selection granularity causes spatial fragmentation of action-relevant visual evidence. We introduce STP-GUI, a granularity-decoupled selection paradigm that scores tokens precisely while selecting contiguous windows to preserve spatial coherence. We formulate GUI visual token retention as a budget-constrained discrete selection problem and design a lightweight query-conditioned selector trained with policy learning, while keeping the VLM backbone frozen. Experiments on Online-Mind2Web show that STP-GUI provides a favorable tradeoff between accuracy and efficiency under token pruning, reducing inference latency by 31 and FLOPs by 57 . Results on AitW also show the generalization for mobile GUI environments. Related Work Web-GUI Agents. Early GUI agents relied on modular pipelines combining text extraction, reasoning, and memory components~ hurst2024gpt-4o,xie2024osworld , which can be brittle under changing environments~ xia2024agentless . Recent VLM-based agents instead directly ground actions from screenshots and achieve stronger generalization on benchmarks such as Mind2Web and AitW~ wang2024cogvlm,hong2024cogagent,chen2025guicourse . Meanwhile, mobile GUI agents further improve grounding through specialized training pipelines~ tang2025magicgui . However, regardless of agent architecture, high-resolution visual inputs introduce substantial token overhead, making efficient visual token selection an important problem for deployment. Token Pruning in VLMs. Token pruning reduces the inference cost of VLMs by removing redundant visual tokens. Existing approaches can be broadly categorized into training-based and training-free methods~ bolya2022token . Training-based methods, such as ATP-LLaVA~ ye2025atp , learn adaptive pruning policies or ratios, while STP-GUI instead freezes the VLM backbone and optimizes a lightweight query-conditioned selector for spatially coherent pruning. Training-free methods mainly rely on importance-based scoring (e.g., FastV~ chen2024image , SparseVLM~ zhang2024sparsevlm , MustDrop~ liu2024multi , PDrop~ xing2024pyramiddrop ) or redundancy-based filtering (e.g., DART~ wen2025stop , DivPrune~ alvar2025divprune ). However, these methods are primarily designed for natural images and select tokens independently, which may fragment the spatial evidence required for GUI grounding. STP-GUI addresses this limitation by decoupling token relevance estimation from evidence retention granularity, enabling spatially coherent token selection under constrained budgets. Visual Grounding for GUI Agents. Recent works improve GUI grounding through richer supervision or region-aware representations. For example, Gao et al.~ gao2024enhancing enhance vision-language alignment with region-level supervision, YORO~ ho2022yoro develops efficient visual grounding models, and R-VLM~ park2025rvlm introduces region-aware visual representations for GUI grounding. Different from these approaches, STP-GUI addresses visual token reduction for a frozen GUI agent rather than modifying the grounding backbone. Its selector uses action-level supervision and/or full-token model feedback, without requiring token-retention masks or UI-element bounding boxes. We refer to as the keep ratio, i.e., the fraction of visual tokens retained after pruning. For multi-turn GUI agent interaction where input history concatenated with current observation yields multiple image frames, STP-GUI applies the window selection mechanism frame-wise under a uniform keep ratio . This ensures that each temporal visual step retains a spatially contiguous and coherent local representation before entering the LLM. Given visual tokens and an instruction, a lightweight scorer produces token-level relevance scores. These scores are aggregated within non-overlapping spatial windows. During training, windows are sampled under a fixed budget and the selector is optimized using action-level feedback from the frozen VLM. At inference, the highest-scoring windows are retained deterministically. title: Where Should the Gaussians Go? Reusable Label-Aware Allocation for Budget-Constrained Gaussian Splatting of Cinematic CT
summary: Anatomical labels help 3D Gaussian splatting preserve vessels in cinematic renderings of CT, but the representation is still found by optimising each patient's scene, where densification decides where Gaussians go, while real-time displays cap their number. We address one part of this process: deciding where a fixed budget of B Gaussians should be placed. We propose a reusable, labelaware allocation front end that maps a patient's CT, labels and transfer function to a density over 2mm cells and draws exactly B positions from it without per-patient optimisation; the other Gaussian attributes are still fitted per patient. The front end is learned once from per-patient optimised scenes and implemented as a population-trained neural prior and an interpretable seven-parameter visibility-aware closed form (VACF). With identical attribute fitting on 20 held-out patients at 10K-100K Gaussians, both raise vessel-masked PSNR over uniform allocation by 4.5-7.1dB and over pruning a dense voxel-aligned model by 1.6-3.3dB. The neural prior does not differ significantly from per-patient optimised allocation at any budget, and VACF is within 0.6dB of it on vessels; on 19 external patients the neural prior again matches it on vessels and VACF is within 0.7dB. As an initialisation for position optimisation, VACF allocation beats per-patient densification on vessels at 10K Gaussians and, at 25K, reaches a higher vessel PSNR after 118s of optimisation than densification after 248s. Under altered rendering presets, VACF transfers to new colours and lighting but not to a label-free transfer function, whereas the neural prior shows the opposite pattern.
