Gaussian splatting cinematic rendering anatomical labels volume visualisation liver vessels mixed reality Introduction sec:intro Cinematic rendering simulates the transport of light through a CT volume classified by a transfer function (TF). It conveys depth, shape and the spatial relations of vessels and lesions better than conventional direct volume rendering and is increasingly used for surgical planning, patient communication and education eid2017cinematic,dappa2016cinematic , but path tracing takes far longer than interactive frame rates allow on mobile and head-mounted hardware. 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) kerbl2023gaussian removes this barrier at display time: a set of anisotropic Gaussians fitted to path-traced images rasterises at hundreds of frames per second. Label-aware Gaussian splatting (LAGS) lags showed that anatomical labels are valuable in this process: using them during optimisation preserves fine structures such as vessels, and the resulting scenes can be explored on a standalone headset. The Gaussian representation itself, however, is still found by optimising each patient's scene. Starting from an initial set of Gaussians, densification and pruning decide, over tens of thousands of iterations on path-traced views, where Gaussians are needed and how many there are, and this search is repeated for every patient and every TF lags,clipgs . The resulting count is a by-product of thresholds, whereas the devices that motivate the approach impose a fixed budget on the number of Gaussians that can be stored, streamed, sorted and blended per frame. Feed-forward models such as Render-FM renderfm avoid per-patient optimisation but place one Gaussian per foreground voxel, so their count follows the size of the organ (50K--800K Gaussians in Render-FM). Neither approach answers where a fixed number of Gaussians should go. We address this one part of the process. Our premise is that where a scene needs its Gaussians is largely predictable from the anatomy and the rendering setup, so that it can be learned once from optimised scenes of other patients and reused. We propose a label-aware allocation front end: from a patient's CT, labels and TF it computes a density over 2\,mm cells and draws exactly Gaussian positions from it, in seconds and without per-patient optimisation (Fig.~ fig:problem ). The front end takes over the placement decisions that densification makes; it does not estimate colour, opacity or shape. Every complete scene reported in this paper still has these attributes fitted to path-traced views of the patient (about 2\,min on a GPU), optionally together with the positions; we do not generate complete 3DGS scenes in one forward pass. We implement the front end in two ways that share their supervision and objective and differ in model class. Both are trained to reproduce oracle densities, the per-cell counts of Gaussians in per-patient optimised scenes of training patients. A population-trained neural prior, a 3D U-Net on ten cell-level inputs, can represent any dependence of these densities on the inputs. A visibility-aware closed form ( ) has seven parameters: six weights for the label fractions and TF gradient of a cell, and an exponent on the visibility of the cell from the viewing sphere. It is inspectable and its failure modes can be stated in advance. We evaluate both under a protocol in which all methods share the same attribute fitting and differ only in where the Gaussians are, and let the results establish their respective strengths. Our contributions are: A reusable, label-aware allocation front end for budget-constrained Gaussian splatting of cinematic CT, which separates the placement of Gaussians from the fitting of their attributes, together with an equal-budget evaluation protocol that isolates the effect of placement. Two implementations learned once from per-patient optimised scenes: a population-trained neural prior and an interpretable visibility-aware closed form. Evidence on held-out and external patients. At equal budgets, both raise anatomical rendering quality far above uniform placement and above pruning a dense voxel-aligned model; the neural prior does not differ significantly from the per-patient optimised allocation, on 20 held-out patients and on 19 external patients from another centre. As an initialisation, the closed-form allocation lets position optimisation surpass per-patient densification on vessels at 10K Gaussians, and at 25K reach a higher vessel PSNR in less than half the optimisation time. Rendering presets show the limits of each implementation: the closed form fails when appearance no longer follows the labels, and the neural prior fails when the TF changes the contrast it was trained on. Supporting analysis. Per-patient optimised allocations at 25K--200K Gaussians differ about as much as two optimisation seeds do, as a simple power-law model predicts, which supports drawing different budgets from one density per patient; and the main systematic difference between optimised allocations and anatomy-only rules is the visibility of each cell. Scope of comparisons. All baselines are our own implementations under the common protocol. The dense voxel-aligned baseline adopts Render-FM's placement (one Gaussian per foreground cell) but is fitted per patient; it is not the Render-FM network. We do not evaluate the official LAGS pipeline: our per-patient models use generic absolute-gradient densification absgs , and label-aware training as in LAGS is complementary to, and could start from, our allocation. Related work sec:related Gaussian splatting for medical volumes. LAGS lags introduced label-aware densification and rasterisation for path-traced medical volumes with a mixed-reality viewer; its budget study (50K--200K Gaussians; Table~IV of ) reported gains of 2.7--9.2\,dB over vanilla 3DGS at equal counts, attributed to a better distribution of Gaussians, which motivates the present work. ClipGS and XClipGS add interactive clipping clipgs,xclipgs ; DDGS-CT targets X-ray rendering from CT ddgsct . All of these optimise each scene. Render-FM renderfm is a feed-forward model trained on 991 TotalSegmentator CTs that predicts one 6D Gaussian per foreground voxel from the CT, masks and TF, without per-patient optimisation but without control of the count. Expressive kernels (6DGS, 7DGS, Universal Beta Splatting) reduce counts as a side effect of the kernel 6dgs,7dgs,ubs ; allocation is complementary to the kernel. Compact Gaussians and budget control. For natural scenes, compactness is pursued by pruning with importance scores such as LightGaussian's global significance lightgaussian , by growth under a budget as in Taming 3DGS taming , by Markov-chain relocation mcmc , by densification on absolute gradients absgs and by codebook compression compact3dgs . All operate per scene by optimisation. We use significance pruning of a dense voxel-aligned model as a baseline, and budget-capped growth to build per-patient references. Feed-forward Gaussian prediction. Generalisable models predict Gaussians from images or volumes in one pass pixelsplat,renderfm ; they typically tie Gaussians to pixels or voxels. Our front end decides positions under a budget and could precede such a decoder; in this work, attributes are fitted per patient. Optimal point density and visibility. The allocation model of Section~ sec:model is a finite-cell form of asymptotic quantisation theory, in which the optimal density of quantisation points is a power of the source density zador,gersho . Importance-driven and visibility-driven volume rendering viola2005importance,correa2011visibility use related notions of how visible a structure is, but to classify or emphasise structures, not to represent a volume with a fixed number of primitives. title: Reflect After Failure: Brain-Inspired Self-Evolving Agents for Embodied Spatial Intelligence
summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have made substantial progress in spatial reasoning, and self-evolving agents further extend these capabilities to embodied environments by learning from interactions. However, current self-evolution remains particularly challenging in embodied spatial tasks, complex and multi-step decisions from partial visual evidence making it difficult to determine why an execution fails. The failure may stem from misperception, insufficient exploration, or incorrect planning, yet execution feedback alone rarely reveals which component is responsible. As a result, simply accumulating interaction experience can reinforce ineffective strategies. To address this, we propose HiMeco, a brain-inspired self-evolving agent for embodied spatial intelligence, inspired by metacognitive monitoring and hippocampal memory consolidation. Through Hippocampal-Metacognitive Reflection, HiMeco diagnoses failures in perception-exploration-planning (PEP), then compares execution attempts to derive reusable strategies and guidance for avoiding recurring errors. It also abstracts interaction programs into parameterized skills, using evidence contracts and execution-based validation to determine their retention and reuse. These strategies and skills guide subsequent interactions, with memory updated only between rounds and model parameters kept frozen. HiMeco achieves state-of-the-art performance on ESI-Bench, and it also improves accuracy on EmbSpatial-Bench by 3.94 percentage points without evolution.

Introduction Embodied agents operating in complex physical environments require robust spatial intelligence, the ability to not only perceive visible geometry but also reason about hidden structures and topologies majumdar2024openeqa,yang2025thinking,gong2026space10,feng2026seeing . While Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated remarkable zero-shot reasoning capabilities, their spatial understanding remains fundamentally constrained by passive observation yang2025thinking,gong2026space10,hong2026esibench . In real-world scenarios riddled with non-line-of-sight (NLOS) occlusions and unobservable physical dynamics, passive VLMs struggle to perform deep spatial reasoning without actively interacting with the environment to uncover latent topologies feng2026seeing,majumdar2024openeqa,hong2026esibench . Existing research on enhancing spatial reasoning in VLMs broadly falls into two paradigms based on physical feedback availability: static perception cheng2024spatialrgpt,song2025robospatial,zhu2025llava3d and dynamic interaction ziliotto2025tango,hong2026esibench . The former, whether through offline optimization (e.g., SFT or RL) or static prior injection from expert modules (e.g., 3D/depth estimation and prompt engineering), treats the environment as a passive and fixed observation space. Lacking closed-loop interaction, it relies heavily on explicit in-view visual cues, suffering from cognitive blind spots under NLOS occlusions and hidden topologies feng2026seeing,hong2026esibench . In contrast, the dynamic interaction paradigm incorporates physical environment feedback into planning, enabling agents to actively resolve local ambiguities ziliotto2025tango,kim2025flare . However, extending self-evolving agent to embodied spatial tasks introduces a critical bottleneck. Prior work on self-evolving agent often focused on tasks where the causes of failure are relatively easy to identify. While in embodied spatial tasks, agents must make complex multi-step decisions based on partial and dynamically acquired visual evidence in continuous 3D environments subject to physical noise. These conditions make failures difficult to diagnose, while feedback across interaction rounds offers limited guidance on how to revise the underlying strategies li2024eai,duan2025aha,qi2026armor,ju2026embodiskill . This ambiguity hinders agents from reliably assessing which strategies are effective and identifying productive directions for further adaptation. As a result, agents may reinforce flawed experiences and update strategies in the wrong direction, causing errors to accumulate over successive evolution rounds ju2026embodiskill . Remarkably, animals can efficiently distill effective strategies from experience to solve embodied spatial tasks in unfamiliar environments. This adaptive ability of biological brains is supported in part by interactions between the hippocampus and prefrontal metacognitive circuits liao2024learning,jensen2024recurrent,fleming2026integrative . In contrast, existing embodied spatial intelligence, whether static (e.g., via parameter updates or external tools) or dynamic self-evolving systems, struggle to deliver accurate spatial reasoning during active exploration yang2025thinking,feng2026seeing,hong2026esibench . Because they cannot determine whether failures stem from noisy perception, suboptimal exploration, or improper planning li2024eai,ju2026embodiskill . This makes it difficult to translate interaction feedback and accumulated experience into consistent behavioral improvements, leaving errors unresolved across successive interactions ju2026embodiskill,zhang2026sma,tian2026nesy . These limitations motivate Hippocampal-Metacognitive Reflection, which couples failure diagnosis with memory consolidation to guide future interactions. Inspired by these neurobiological functions, we hope to achieve a brain-inspired self-evolving agent equipped with multi-turn Hippocampal-Metacognitive reflection for resource-efficient and adaptive embodied spatial intelligence. Translating this brain-inspired concept into practice presents two challenges. The first is adaptive semantic abstraction: deciding what to retain from repeated interactions and how broadly it should apply zhang2026sma,shu2026remem,xu2026multigranularity . Across interaction and evolution rounds, a parameter-frozen agent must turn individual attempts into reusable strategies and executable skills. Overly specific knowledge transfers poorly, while overly general knowledge loses the detail needed for reliable execution wang2025awm,zhang2026sma . The second is reliable failure attribution li2024eai,ju2026embodiskill . An incorrect answer alone does not reveal whether the agent misinterpreted its observations, explored insufficiently, or executed a flawed plan. Without this distinction, the agent may retain unreliable procedures or reinforce ineffective strategies. To address these challenges, we propose , a brain-inspired self-evolving agent for embodied spatial reasoning. It consolidates interaction experience into a strategy bank and a library of parameterized executable skills . Evidence contracts and invocation-based validation govern which skills are retained, promoted, or suspended across evolution rounds. A perception-exploration-planning (PEP) diagnostic module uses execution traces, task outcomes, and privileged simulator metadata to assess failures across these three dimensions after execution. These diagnostics guide candidate comparison and reflection, yielding reusable strategies and negative constraints for subsequent interactions. Model parameters remain frozen, and both memories are updated only between rounds. alternates between online inference and offline evolution. During inference, the frozen VLM generates programs conditioned on retrieved experiences and skills, while evidence contracts check the observations and intermediate outputs used for reasoning. Memory remains fixed throughout each interaction round. At the round boundary, diagnostic feedback guides comparative reflection and experience consolidation, while execution outcomes support skill abstraction and lifecycle updates. The resulting memories guide subsequent interactions without modifying model parameters. This separation allows the agent to accumulate experience across rounds while evaluating each attempt against a fixed memory snapshot. title: Feed-Forward Multi-View Feature Coding for 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) methods enable efficient reconstruction of 3D scenes from sparse multi-view images in a single forward pass, without scene-specific optimization. However, existing feed-forward scene-coding pipelines first generate a complete Gaussian representation and then encode its geometry and appearance attributes separately, often involving non-differentiable operations. The resulting 'generate-then-compress' pipeline requires complex attribute-specific codec designs and limits rate-distortion performance by restricting the exploitation of cross-attribute redundancy. We propose multi-view feature coding for Gaussian splatting (MFGS), an end-to-end feed-forward framework for scene coding. Instead of compressing an explicit Gaussian representation, MFGS extracts multi-view features from the input images and encodes them into a compact bitstream. Through end-to-end rate-distortion training, MFGS learns compact multi-view features that jointly represent geometry and appearance, enabling the receiver to predict Gaussian attributes from the decoded features. We further introduce importance-guided Gaussian selection to accommodate different rendering budgets, allowing the receiver to adjust the number of Gaussians used for rendering from the same bitstream. Across RE10K, ACID, and DL3DV, MFGS achieves 99.76-99.86% bitrate savings over the generate-then-compress pipeline, as measured by BD-rate, while reducing total GMACs by 52-55% and providing an approximately 12 times end-to-end speedup.

Introduction sec:intro 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl20233d enables high-quality novel-view synthesis with real-time rendering, but its large explicit representations incur substantial storage and transmission costs. Optimization-based 3DGS compression methods~ hac2024,hacpp2025,contextgs2024,compgs2024,rdogaussian2024 , which optimize Gaussian representations for each scene, achieve strong rate--distortion performance at the cost of time-consuming iterative optimization. This limits their applicability to live applications that require rapid reconstruction and transmission of newly captured scenes. Feed-forward methods~ pixelsplat2023,mvsplat2024,depthsplat2024,monosplat2025,transplat2025 address this limitation by reconstructing Gaussian representations directly from sparse input views in a single pass. Scene transmission then follows the `generate-then-compress' pipeline in , which encodes the predicted Gaussian attributes through specialized coding paths. For example, FCGS~ fcgs2025 , a representative feed-forward 3DGS compression model, uses G-PCC~ schwarz2019emerging for positions and learned coding for the remaining attributes. This separation complicates the architecture and limits joint compression of shared geometry and appearance information, while non-differentiable operations hinder end-to-end rate--distortion training. FCGS also requires repeated spatial and channel context evaluations over per-Gaussian latents and sequential decoding across context groups, increasing coding latency. r 0.5 Relative bitrate and complexity of versus FCGS (generate-then-compress), using the same generator architecture ( ). Our base model, , encodes multi-view features and predicts all Gaussian attributes from the decoded features at the receiver ( ). Each feature plane has the same 3D tensor structure as an image, allowing us to use an established learned image codec. The shared coding path simplifies the architecture and exploits redundancy between geometry and appearance. Together with end-to-end joint rate--distortion training, this design improves rate--distortion performance while reducing computation, memory usage, and runtime relative to the generate-then-compress baseline ( ). Receiver devices vary in computational capacity, while interactive viewing requires rendering within a per-frame time budget. To accommodate these constraints, our adaptive model, , combines importance-guided bit allocation with receiver-side Gaussian selection. At each rate point, the receiver can adjust the number of rendered Gaussians from a single bitstream to match its rendering capacity. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce the framework as an alternative to generate-then-compress for feed-forward 3D scene coding. By encoding multi-view features and reconstructing Gaussians at the receiver, the framework unifies attribute-specific coding paths, enabling joint compression of geometry and appearance and end-to-end rate--distortion optimization. We instantiate the proposed framework in the model and demonstrate substantial bitrate savings together with lower computation, peak GPU memory, and runtime than the generate-then-compress baseline across RE10K, ACID, and DL3DV. The joint reduction in bitrate and processing time supports the potential of multi-view feature coding for 3D live streaming. We extend the baseline with the model, enabling receiver-side adjustment of the number of rendered Gaussians from a single bitstream. Experiments demonstrate limited quality degradation across rendering budgets, allowing a shared bitstream to serve receivers with different rendering capacities. Related Work sec:related Optimization-based 3DGS compression Optimization-based 3DGS compression methods optimize a compact Gaussian representation separately for each scene. HAC~ hac2024 models the relationship between unstructured anchors and a structured hash grid, while HAC++~ hacpp2025 further captures dependencies among attributes within each anchor. ContextGS~ contextgs2024 introduces a hierarchical autoregressive context model across anchor levels. CompGS~ compgs2024 applies K-means-based vector quantization while optimizing the Gaussian parameters, whereas RDO-Gaussian~ rdogaussian2024 combines pruning and entropy-constrained vector quantization under a rate--distortion objective. These methods achieve strong compression performance but require scene-specific optimization, limiting their use in live applications. Feed-forward 3DGS generation Feed-forward 3DGS methods predict explicit Gaussian primitives from input multi-view images without per-scene optimization. pixelSplat~ pixelsplat2023 models Gaussian depth using a probabilistic parameterization, while MVSplat~ mvsplat2024 estimates depth using plane-sweep cost volumes. DepthSplat~ depthsplat2024 further combines multi-view cost volumes with features from a pretrained monocular depth model. MonoSplat~ monosplat2025 adapts monocular depth features into multi-view representations, whereas TranSplat~ transplat2025 combines confidence-guided feature matching with monocular depth priors. ZPressor~ zpressor2025 aggregates information from support views into a compact anchor-view latent representation, improving scalability to dense input views. Feed-forward 3DGS compression FCGS~ fcgs2025 encodes an existing Gaussian representation without scene-specific fine-tuning using a multi-path entropy module and inter- and intra-Gaussian context models. The MPEG-GSC test model TMCV~ mpeggsc2025 also provides coding tools for explicit Gaussian parameters. These codecs retain the generated Gaussians as the coded representation, so coding operates on explicit geometry and appearance attributes. In contrast, our approach moves coding before Gaussian prediction and jointly compresses the shared information in an image-like multi-view feature representation. Gaussian pruning Gaussian pruning reduces the number of primitives, thereby lowering storage and rasterization costs. LightGaussian~ lightgaussian2023 ranks Gaussians using a global significance score computed over the training views and removes the least significant primitives. It then recovers rendering quality through SH distillation with pseudo views and applies vector quantization. PUP-3DGS~ pup3dgs2024 uses a second-order approximation of reconstruction sensitivity with respect to the spatial parameters of each Gaussian and applies a multi-round prune--refine procedure. EcoSplat~ ecosplat2025 introduces a two-stage training scheme for feed-forward 3DGS. It first learns pixel-aligned Gaussian prediction and then ranks and adjusts the predicted primitives according to a target primitive count. Learned image compression Learned image compression uses neural analysis and synthesis transforms, quantized latent representations, and entropy models trained under a rate--distortion objective. The scale hyperprior model~ balle2018variational predicts spatially varying scale parameters for the latent distribution. Joint autoregressive and hierarchical priors~ minnen2018joint combine a hierarchical prior with causal autoregressive context to improve entropy modeling. Attention-based image compression~ cheng2020learned uses discretized Gaussian mixture likelihoods to model the latent distribution. AuxT~ li2025disentangled introduces wavelet-based linear shortcuts that support feature decorrelation and energy modulation, accelerating the training of nonlinear transforms. title: GeoThinker-$F$: Endogenous Predictive World Representations for Fast Spatial Intelligence
summary: Existing geometry-aware Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) increasingly rely on external 3D encoders to provide structural priors, but executing these additional encoder paths at inference introduces substantial latency and computational overhead. We propose GeoThinker-$F$, an efficient framework that internalizes spatiotemporal perception by transforming causal MLLM hidden states into predictive latent world representations. Our key insight is that intermediate semantic representations contain sufficient information to predict useful representations of current geometry and future semantics, without requiring an exact reproduction of features from a dedicated 3D encoder. To realize this idea, GeoThinker-$F$ adopts a decoupled two-stage training strategy. In the first stage, the MLLM backbone is frozen while lightweight Latent Frame Prediction (LFP) heads learn from an offline 3D geometry expert and next-frame semantic targets. In the second stage, the external expert is removed, and the model is jointly optimized to generate and selectively integrate its self-predicted priors through a specialized Spatial-Grounded Temporal (SGT) Fusion module. Extensive evaluations show that GeoThinker-$F$ eliminates runtime dependence on external 3D geometry encoders while maintaining competitive performance across diverse spatial intelligence benchmarks. It achieves up to a $3.6\times$ inference speedup, reducing latency from $1.45\,\mathrm{s}$ to $0.40\,\mathrm{s}$ while retaining strong spatial reasoning performance.

Introduction Spatial intelligence has emerged as a central capability for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), with broad applications in 3D scene understanding~ cai2025scaling(sensenova),yang2025cambrian,cao2026vggt(caoyang), cao2023coda , embodied AI~ zhou2025roborefer,xu20253d , and autonomous decision-making~ li2025recogdrive . To bridge the gap between 2D semantic perception and 3D structural understanding, recent geometry-aware frameworks~ zheng2025learning(vgllm),fan2025vlm(vlm3r),chen2025reasoning(gsreasoner),li2026thinking(geothinker) increasingly leverage priors from external 3D geometry foundation models~ wang2025vggt,wang2025pi3,wang2025continuous(cut3r) , either by integrating their features into the inference pipeline or distilling their representations during training. By jointly processing multiple frames, these geometry models provide fine-grained structural cues that complement the semantic representations of conventional visual encoders for reliable spatial relation understanding across views. However, methods that retain a dedicated 3D geometry encoder at inference incur substantial computation, memory consumption, and synchronization latency, limiting deployment in latency-sensitive settings. Training-time distillation~ chen2025think(3dthinker) avoids this dependency by absorbing geometric supervision into the MLLM parameters, but does not provide a dense, frame-aligned geometry interface for explicit routing across intermediate layers at inference. Dual-encoder architectures~ li2026thinking(geothinker) retain such an explicit feature interface, but at the cost of executing an external geometry branch. Our key insight is that intermediate semantic representations contain sufficient information to predict useful latent representations of current geometry and future semantics, without exactly reproducing features from a dedicated 3D encoder. This raises a natural question: Can an MLLM generate geometric and temporal priors from its own hidden states, thereby eliminating runtime dependence on external geometry models? To eliminate this runtime overhead, we introduce , an efficient framework that internalizes predictive latent world representations within the MLLM. Rather than executing a dedicated 3D geometry encoder at inference, learns to transform intermediate hidden states into complementary representations of current geometry and future semantics. We realize this design through a decoupled two-stage training strategy. In Stage 1 (LFP pretraining), the MLLM backbone is frozen, while only lightweight Latent Frame Prediction~ yang2025cambrian (LFP) MLP heads attached to intermediate layers are trained using latent geometry features from an offline 3D expert and next-frame semantic features as prediction targets. In Stage 2 (self-driven tuning), the external geometry expert is removed, and the self-predicted representations are selectively integrated into intermediate MLLM layers through a Spatial-Grounded Temporal (SGT) Fusion module for spatial reasoning. At inference, generates both representations endogenously within its own latent space, eliminating runtime dependence on external geometry encoders. Together, these components shift geometry-aware spatial reasoning from runtime external feature extraction toward endogenous latent prediction. On the Qwen3-VL-8B~ Qwen3-VL backbone, the complete system, combined with spatial token compression, reduces inference latency from to , yielding a speedup while achieving a VSI-Bench score of . Across six spatial intelligence benchmarks, further reaches an average score of , demonstrating strong cross-benchmark performance without executing an external geometry encoder at inference. By jointly predicting representations of current geometry and future semantics, integrates spatial structure and short-horizon temporal evolution within the MLLM latent space, providing an efficient alternative to runtime multi-encoder architectures. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: Endogenous Predictive Latent Modeling: We propose , an efficient framework that predicts complementary representations of current geometry and future semantics from causal intermediate MLLM states. Through decoupled two-stage training, an external 3D geometry model is used only as an offline teacher, eliminating the need to execute a dedicated geometry encoder at inference. Specialized Spatiotemporal Fusion: We introduce Spatial-Grounded Temporal (SGT) Fusion, which employs separate geometry and temporal branches to selectively integrate the self-predicted representations. A layer-interleaved injection strategy further separates the two feature streams across intermediate MLLM layers, reducing interference during spatial reasoning and preserving their complementary spatial cues. Inference Efficiency and Cross-Benchmark Performance: Under controlled training data, achieves performance comparable to the dual-encoder baseline GeoThinker while removing its runtime geometry branch. Across six spatial intelligence benchmarks, reaches an average score of . When combined with spatial token compression, it reduces inference latency from to on Qwen3-VL-8B, yielding a speedup in end-to-end execution time. Related Work Semantics-Driven Spatial Reasoning MLLMs~ yang2025qwen3technicalreport,team2023gemini,openai_gpt5_systemcard have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in general visual comprehension across both static images and video sequences. Nevertheless, recent evaluations~ yang2025thinking(vsi) highlight a persistent deficiency in dependable spatial reasoning, positioning spatial intelligence as a critical hurdle in achieving human-level multi-modal reasoning. To address this limitation, existing literature has investigated several distinct methodologies. One prominent direction involves the integration of explicit 3D information into the model pipeline. For instance, Video-3D LLM~ zheng2025video(video3dllm) enriches video tokens with frame-wise 3D spatial coordinates back-projected from RGB-D data to capture location-sensitive representations. Conversely, another line of work emphasizes implicit geometric regularization within the latent space. RoSS3D~ wang2025ross3d leverages cross-view and bird's-eye-view (BEV) reconstruction targets alongside denoising-style objectives to foster geometry-consistent feature spaces. Parallel to architectural modifications, expanding training data has emerged as a highly potent strategy. Cambrian-S~ yang2025cambrian curates the VSI-590K dataset to investigate the boundaries of data scaling in spatial contexts. Similarly, SenseNova-SI~ cai2025scaling(sensenova) introduces the massive SenseNova-SI-8M dataset, achieving substantial performance leaps on both VSI-Bench and the EASI leaderboard~ cai2025holistic without sacrificing general multimodal proficiency. Complementing these approaches, reasoning-centric optimization seeks to fully unlock the inherent cognitive power of the underlying LLM. SpatialLadder~ li2025spatialladder reinforces complex, multi-step spatial reasoning by utilizing reinforcement learning paired with verifiable reward signals. While these approaches avoid persistent external encoders and preserve standard inference efficiency, they typically acquire spatial structure indirectly through training data, auxiliary objectives, or reasoning supervision, rather than generating dedicated geometry representations at inference. Our work instead uses a pretrained geometry encoder as a training-time teacher, enabling the MLLM to predict geometry-derived structural priors internally without introducing an additional encoder at runtime. A prevalent paradigm introduces explicit architectural additions to stream these geometric features directly into the MLLM pipeline. VG-LLM~ zheng2025learning(vgllm) employs direct patch-level feature addition to construct geometry-augmented visual tokens at the input layer. VLM-3R~ fan2025vlm(vlm3r) concatenates enriched 3D features with camera parameters, subsequently leveraging a cross-attention layer to allow visual tokens to query the geometric context. G VLM~ hu2025g2vlm introduces a Mixture-of-Transformer-Experts (MoT) style architecture that bifurcates processing into dedicated geometric and semantic expert modules, optimizing joint 3D reconstruction and high-level reasoning through shared self-attention layers. Complementary to explicit streaming pipelines, another prominent direction utilizes feature distillation or semantic alignment to bypass the runtime overhead of external models. title: DynThinker: Unifying Static 3D and Dynamic 4D Spatial Reasoning
summary: Achieving general spatial intelligence requires a unified understanding of both static 3D and dynamic 4D. However, we find that existing models struggle to excel at both: 3D post-training can weaken dynamic understanding, while 4D-specialized models often lack strong static 3D reasoning. Our analysis reveals that this spatial--dynamic interference is highly non-uniform across parameter groups, with the balance between static and dynamic capabilities particularly sensitive to changes in late-layer MLPs. To address this interference, we propose DynThinker, a unified framework for jointly strengthening static and dynamic spatial reasoning. Decoupled Exponential Moving Average (D-EMA) applies configurable group-wise averaging to constrain drift in interference-sensitive pretrained parameters while preserving flexibility for capability enhancement. Spatial-Dynamic Fusion (SDF) complements D-EMA by selectively integrating spatial and temporal priors from a dynamic geometry encoder into intermediate VLM representations under semantic guidance. Across ten metrics spanning nine static 3D and dynamic 4D benchmarks, DynThinker achieves the highest average score among all evaluated models. Notably, DynThinker achieves 56.0 on ReVSI, 67.2 on DSR-Bench, and 51.2 and 40.1 under the sample-wise and group-wise evaluation protocols of DSI-Bench, respectively, setting new state-of-the-art results among the compared open-source models across all four evaluations within a unified model.

Introduction sec:intro Spatial intelligence has emerged as a central capability for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), enabling them to understand and reason about both static 3D structure and dynamic 4D environments, supporting applications ranging from scene understanding~ yang2025thinking, cao2026vggt(caoyang) to embodied interaction~ lin2025evo,li2025spatialforcing,yang2026visual . Recent post-training methods have substantially improved static 3D reasoning~ tong2024cambrian(cambrian-1),zhang2025flatland(spar),yin2025spatial(mindcube),li2025viewspatial , while parallel efforts have extended spatial reasoning to dynamic 4D environments~ zhou2025vlm4d,zhou2025DSR-GSM,zhang2025dsi,li2025sti . Yet these directions remain largely specialized: 3D-oriented models often lack dynamic understanding, whereas 4D-oriented models remain limited in static 3D reasoning. This gap motivates a unified model capable of strong spatial reasoning across both static and dynamic environments. However, unified spatial reasoning is challenging, as improving one capability can come at the expense of the other. We find that 3D-focused spatial post-training can interfere with pretrained dynamic competence: improvements in static 3D reasoning are accompanied by substantial degradation on dynamic 4D benchmarks~ zhou2025vlm4d . This trade-off leads to imbalanced capability profiles shown in Figure~ fig:teaser , revealing spatial--dynamic interference that hinders joint capability improvement. Existing capability-preservation strategies provide only partial remedies. Data replay requires auxiliary data and careful mixing, regularization can limit adaptation, and parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA~ hu2022lora may restrict update capacity. The central challenge is therefore to preserve existing dynamic competence while allowing sufficient flexibility to strengthen static 3D reasoning, without relying on replay data or additional regularization objectives. To better understand this interference, we analyze 3D-specialized VLMs through checkpoint interpolation and parameter-group restoration. We find that the interference is highly non-uniform across parameter groups, with the balance between static and dynamic capabilities particularly sensitive to changes in late-layer MLPs, as shown in Figure~ fig:motivation . Restoring these parameters to their pretrained values substantially recovers dynamic performance, while partially reversing the gains in static 3D reasoning. This opposing response indicates that the tension between static 3D enhancement and dynamic capability preservation is particularly pronounced in late-layer MLPs. Motivated by these observations, we propose , a unified spatial reasoning framework that addresses spatial--dynamic interference through complementary designs. First, Decoupled Exponential Moving Average (D-EMA) mitigates interference through configurable group-wise temporal averaging, allowing stronger consolidation for interference-sensitive parameters while preserving flexibility for capability enhancement. The decay is adjusted according to the number of EMA updates, ensuring consistency across training schedules. Second, Spatial-Dynamic Fusion (SDF) complements parameter preservation with joint spatial--dynamic perception by selectively integrating spatial and temporal priors from a dynamic geometry encoder into intermediate VLM representations. Guided by the VLM's semantic context, SDF adaptively modulates contribution of each prior stream, enabling model to capture both static geometric structure and temporal evolution. Extensive experiments demonstrate strong and balanced performance across static 3D and dynamic 4D reasoning. Across ten metrics, achieves the highest average score of 60.5, surpassing the proprietary frontier model GPT-5.6 Sol at 59.5, while also attaining state-of-the-art results among the compared open-source models on ReVSI, DSR-Bench, and DSI-Bench. Ablation studies further confirm the complementary roles of D-EMA and SDF in mitigating spatial--dynamic interference while strengthening spatial reasoning, showing that spatial specialization need not come at the expense of dynamic capabilities. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: Diagnosing Spatial--Dynamic Interference. We identify a spatial--dynamic interference in which 3D-focused post-training strengthens static reasoning while degrading dynamic competence inherited from pretraining, posing a key challenge to unified spatial reasoning. A Unified Framework for Spatial Reasoning. To overcome this interference and bridge static 3D and dynamic 4D reasoning, we propose , a unified framework that strengthens both capabilities within a single VLM. D-EMA mitigates interference during adaptation, while SDF adaptively integrates spatial and temporal priors for enhancement. Strong and Scalable 3D--4D Performance. achieves strong and balanced performance across ten static 3D and dynamic 4D metrics, attaining state-of-the-art results among compared open-source models on ReVSI, DSR-Bench, and DSI-Bench. Related Work sec:related_work Static and Dynamic Spatial Intelligence Progress toward real-world spatial intelligence requires vision–language models (VLMs) to reason about both static spatial structure and dynamic changes over time. Early work explores image-based spatial reasoning, with SpatialVLM learning qualitative and metric spatial relations from automatically generated image--question pairs~ chen2024spatialvlm . Beyond individual images, benchmarks such as VSI-Bench and MindCube require models to integrate observations across multiple views and reason about 3D scene layout, spatial relationships, and metric properties~ yang2025thinking,yin2025spatial(mindcube),yang2025mmsi . Recent work has extended spatial intelligence toward dynamic 4D settings, with benchmarks spanning complementary data sources and reasoning targets that together motivate unified reasoning across static 3D and dynamic 4D. VLM4D combines real and synthetic videos to assess motion, viewpoint changes, and temporal continuity~ zhou2025vlm4d , while DSI-Bench focuses on disentangling observer motion from object motion~ zhang2025dsi . DSR-Bench instead builds on real-world videos to evaluate evolving 3D relations and multi-object interactions~ zhou2025DSR-GSM , and MLLM4D-Bench uses scenarios derived from stereo videos to probe spatial and temporal reasoning~ yin2026mllm4d . Building on these efforts, we study how to jointly strengthen static and dynamic spatial capabilities during post-training. Geometry Integration in Vision--Language Models To equip VLMs with stronger 3D and 4D reasoning, methods augment semantic visual features with explicit geometric cues~ wang2026feed . Geometry encoders include VGGT, which recovers 3D scene structure from multiple views~ wang2025vggt , and V-DPM, which extends geometric reconstruction to dynamic scenes with 3D motion estimation~ sucar2026v(VDPM) . Existing methods incorporate geometric knowledge into VLMs through input-level feature fusion~ zheng2025learning(vgllm) , distillation~ li2025spatialforcing , and intermediate-layer integration~ li2026thinking . For static and dynamic spatial reasoning, DSR-GSM uses ~ wang2026pi3 to capture both scene geometry and motion, together with stacked Q-Formers to select question-relevant features for VLM integration~ zhou2025DSR-GSM . GeoSR improves geometric evidence use through geometry-unleashing masking and geometry-guided fusion, while employing separate models for static and dynamic reasoning~ zhang2026geosr . Building on GeoThinker’s semantic-guided intermediate-layer integration~ li2026thinking , we introduce Spatial-Dynamic Fusion (SDF) to fuse complementary spatial and dynamic priors within a single VLM, adaptively balancing their contributions. Capability Preservation during Post-Training Specialized post-training can improve target performance while degrading previously acquired capabilities, a phenomenon observed in language models and other adaptation settings, including embodied models~ kotha2024forgetting,hancock2026actions . Weight averaging provides one approach to balancing adaptation and capability retention: WiSE-FT interpolates pretrained and fine-tuned checkpoints to improve robustness~ wortsman2022wiseft , while SWA~ izmailov2018averaging and EMA~ moralesbrotons2024ema aggregate parameter states within a training run to improve generalization. Prior work has examined how EMA hyperparameters should adapt to training scale, such as batch size~ busbridge2023scaleema . In spatial post-training, however, we find that capability interference is unevenly distributed across parameter groups, calling for more targeted control over the balance between static and dynamic capabilities. Motivated by this observation, D-EMA applies configurable group-wise averaging horizons, normalized by training duration, to mitigate interference while retaining sufficient flexibility for capability enhancement across training scales. Diagnosing Spatial--Dynamic Interference sec:motivation Static--dynamic trade-off. To understand why existing specialization struggles to achieve unified spatial reasoning, we first examine how 3D-focused post-training reshapes the balance between static and dynamic capabilities in a pretrained VLM. As shown in Figure~ fig:motivation (A), interpolating between the Qwen3-VL-8B~ qwen3vl2025 model and its 3D-specialized counterpart GeoThinker~ li2026thinking reveals opposing trends: performance on VSI-Bench steadily improves, while performance on VLM4D consistently declines. Notably, static 3D performance begins to saturate at intermediate interpolation coefficients, whereas dynamic 4D performance continues to decline toward the 3D-specialized checkpoint. This opposing trajectory reveals spatial--dynamic interference during post-training: improving static 3D reasoning can progressively erode dynamic competence inherited from pretraining. Parameter-group sensitivity. This observation raises a central question: which parameters drive this interference, and can dynamic competence be preserved without constraining static 3D adaptation? To answer this, we conduct a parameter-group sensitivity analysis by selectively restoring different modules and layer ranges in the 3D-specialized model toward their pretrained values and measuring the resulting changes in static and dynamic performance. title: VITAL: From Visual Motion to Precise Action
comment: Technical Report; 37 pages, 14 figures, 19 tables; Project Page at https://worldbench.github.io/vital GitHub at https://github.com/worldbench/VITAL
summary: World-action models aim to turn visual anticipation into driving decisions, yet typically train action experts on trajectory representations defined independently of visual dynamics. This motivates deriving action targets directly from visual motion. We first examine a simpler setting in which trajectories are reconstructed from recorded future images. Even without the need for future prediction, reconstruction captures the dominant maneuver but leaves centimeter-scale errors. We therefore introduce VITAL (Vision-Induced Tokens for Action Learning), an action tokenizer that couples a visually derived motion scaffold with a compact residual encoding the trajectory error left by that scaffold. This representation makes visual motion the principal prediction target and gives small metric corrections a separate, normalized learning scale. Using flow matching, the action expert jointly predicts both components from the current image, ego state, and navigation command, without generating future images at inference. The same residual coordinates support bounded reinforcement post-training that refines execution while keeping the predicted visual scaffold fixed. With only one action denoising step, VITAL achieves 90.8 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 navtest, within 0.13 points of its ten-step score at 3.29x the end-to-end inference speed. Without retraining, it achieves 91.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 navtest and 38.6 on navhard. Project page: https://worldbench.github.io/vital

Yet even with recorded future images, our study recovers the dominant maneuver while leaving local metric errors. ~ jointly addresses visual grounding and execution precision: visual motion defines the principal action target, and a paired residual encodes its remaining trajectory error. fig:vital_teaser Introduction sec:introduction Learning to anticipate a driving scene should also help a vehicle decide how to move. World-action models pursue this connection by coupling visual prediction with trajectory generation~ xia2026drivelaw,zhao2026simwam,yuan2026suv . A common design couples video and action experts in a mixture of transformers, allowing action tokens to attend to visual features before decoding an ego trajectory~ zhao2026simwam,li2026metis,yuan2026suv . As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:vital_teaser , the promise is to learn how to act from a model that anticipates how the world moves. Yet exchanging information does not necessarily give the two experts a shared prediction target. Attention~ vaswani2017attention connects their features, while the video expert learns to predict scene evolution and the action expert often learns a code defined only by trajectory coordinates. The two experts describe the same physical motion through separately constructed representations. We therefore ask whether action targets can be derived directly from observed visual motion. Recent advances in robot control suggest that this connection can be learned at the tokenizer level. RepWAM~ wang2026repwam learns latent actions from transitions between semantically aligned visual representations, and LingBot-VA 2.0~ zhang2026native adopts this strategy for joint pretraining of video and action. Their gains in control precision make visual motion a promising source of action targets. Motion-token and continuous-motion learning offer complementary evidence for connecting videos to control~ chen2025moto,yang2026como . However, these tokenizers reconstruct transitions in visual feature space. It remains unclear how much of the metric detail needed for driving can be recovered from visual motion alone, even before a planner has to predict that motion from the observations available at deployment. We therefore remove future prediction from the problem altogether. As shown in Appendix~ app: method_reconstruction , in a simpler task than world-action modeling, the model receives recorded current and future images and reconstructs the corresponding ego trajectory. Even with the future already in view, a precision gap remains. As shown in Fig.~ fig:vital_visual_precision , reconstruction leaves 123.6\,mm average displacement error (ADE) and 221.6\,mm final displacement error (FDE) across all NAVSIM validation scenes~ dauner2024navsim . Looking more closely at the recovered motion, we find that its HF fraction, the mean share of velocity energy at high frequencies across and , is only 0.1 . What emerges is a smooth motion scaffold. It captures the maneuver but still misses metric detail that matters near road boundaries, where small deviations can make an otherwise plausible trajectory noncompliant. r 0.45 Visual reconstruction and residual precision. .6em ~vision only, .6em ~ , .6em ~residual. HF denotes the mean high-frequency velocity energy fraction. fig:vital_visual_precision This finding suggests preserving the motion that vision captures while giving the missing detail a representation of its own. We introduce , short for Vision-Induced Tokens for Action Learning, an action tokenizer built around this separation. A visual motion code decodes into the trajectory scaffold. A second code, the paired metric residual, encodes the difference between that scaffold and the demonstrated trajectory. Normalization gives these small corrections their own learning scale alongside the dominant motion. Decoding both codes restores the missing trajectory detail. As shown in Fig.~ fig:vital_visual_precision , supplying recorded images and the residual encoded from ground truth reduces reconstruction ADE and FDE to 0.3\,mm and 0.5\,mm and raises PDMS from 92.1 to 94.7. The residual's HF fraction reaches 61.4 , revealing faster local variations in the component that restores metric precision. The resulting representation retains both the visual motion scaffold and the finer corrections needed to reconstruct the demonstrated trajectory. Precise reconstruction is useful for planning only if the representation can be predicted before the future is observed, consistent with recent analyses of action tokenization beyond reconstruction fidelity~ chen2026proact . We train the action expert with flow matching to generate both codes jointly from the current image, ego state, and navigation command. One flow step then produces a trajectory without generating future images. Separating the metric correction also opens a route to policy improvement~ johannink2019residual . After imitation learning, we freeze the action generator and decoder and learn bounded updates in the residual coordinates. At deployment, a single deterministic correction refines local execution while keeping the predicted visual scaffold fixed. The gains extend from reconstruction to planning. On NAVSIM, strengthens visual conditioning. With equal action training budgets, it gains 5.1 PDMS points in one step over an autoencoder trained only on trajectories. Residual refinement brings the final policy to 90.8 PDMS in one step, within 0.1 points of ten steps at the inference speed, including image encoding. Our contributions bridge visual motion, precise action learning, and efficient policy refinement. 1.4em .6em .5em 3pt 3pt 0pt 0pt We propose , an action tokenizer that pairs visual motion with a normalized metric residual to preserve both visual grounding and fine trajectory precision for autonomous driving. We propose residual reinforcement learning that improves planning through a single correction, without additional denoising, candidate search, or reward evaluation at inference. We achieve 90.8 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 with a single flow evaluation. Without retraining, the same policy reaches 91.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 and 38.6 EPDMS on reactive navhard. Related Work sec:related_work World-action models The survey of 3D and 4D world modeling organizes video-, occupancy-, and LiDAR-based approaches and their evaluation protocols~ kong2025worldsurvey . Quo Vadis, World Modeling? broadens this view to agent-centric proxies that provide dynamics, spatial, execution, memory, skill, and reward feedback~ yang2026quovadis . Together, these perspectives distinguish scene prediction from the information a policy needs to select and improve executable actions. World-action models connect visual prediction to control by using generated futures or their latent representations to inform action generation. Drive-WM evaluates candidate plans through generated multiview videos~ wang2024driving , while MaskGWM combines video generation with masked reconstruction to learn generalizable driving dynamics~ ni2025maskgwm . DriveLaW injects video-generator latents into a trajectory planner~ xia2026drivelaw , and SUV lets the action expert attend to predicted appearance, semantics, relative depth, and instance dynamics~ yuan2026suv . Metis and SimWAM use attention masks to support joint video-action training while avoiding future-video generation during action inference~ li2026metis,zhao2026simwam . Latent world models also support driving without reconstructing full future videos. LAW predicts action-conditioned future features to improve scene representations~ li2025law , while World4Drive incorporates intention-aware physical latent modeling~ zheng2025world4drive . Latent-WAM combines geometry-informed scene compression with dynamic latent prediction~ wang2026latentwam . A separate use of future prediction is to evaluate plans: WoTE forecasts BEV states for online trajectory evaluation~ li2025wote , and DA-WAM predicts an action-specific future latent for each candidate and uses it for scoring~ zhong2026dawam . WorldLens evaluates driving world models across generation, reconstruction, action-following, downstream tasks, and human preference~ liang2026worldlens . The associated workshop study, Is Your Driving World Model an All-Around Player?, examines six driving world models across 24 evaluation dimensions within the same WorldLens framework~ kong2026allaround . These evaluations show that visual realism alone does not establish geometric or behavioral fidelity. This motivates assessing the control interface separately: our recorded-future reconstruction study isolates retained action precision, while conditional prediction and NAVSIM scores test whether that representation supports planning from current observations. Broader surveys place both directions within agentic world modeling and vision-language-action driving systems~ chu2026agentic,hu2025vlasurvey . LCVN studies language-conditioned navigation through latent imagination or joint observation-action prediction, while UniWM couples future prediction with memory-augmented planning~ dong2026lcvn,dong2026uniwm . OneVL uses language and future-video supervision to learn compact reasoning tokens, discarding auxiliary decoders during planning inference~ lu2026onevl . Beyond video, DynamicCity generates dynamic occupancy, while LiDARCrafter and U4D model controllable or uncertainty-aware LiDAR sequences~ bian2025dynamiccity,liang2026lidarcrafter,xu2026u4d . OmniLiDAR extends diffusion-based scan generation across weather, sensor configurations, and acquisition platforms through a shared range-image representation and domain-conditioned modeling~ liu2026omnilidar . These scene-generation interfaces provide a broader context for our focus on visually grounded, metric action targets. Related strategies appear in robotic manipulation. Prediction with Action couples visual and action prediction through joint denoising~ guo2024prediction , and UWM uses independent video and action diffusion timesteps within one transformer to support policy and dynamics modeling~ zhu2025uwm . WorldVLA studies autoregressive action-world modeling~ cen2025worldvla ; VideoVLA and DreamZero leverage pretrained video generators to jointly predict actions and visual outcomes~ shen2025videovla,ye2026dreamzero . Video Prediction Policy uses predictive visual representations with inverse dynamics~ hu2024video , while DreamVLA forecasts compact dynamic, spatial, and semantic knowledge for action prediction~ zhang2025dreamvla . V-JEPA 2-AC plans through an action-conditioned predictor in visual feature space~ assran2025vjepa2 . Gen2Act transfers information from generated human videos to manipulation~ bharadhwaj2024gen2act , and World Guidance predicts compact conditions derived from future observations alongside actions~ su2026world . constructs the action target from recorded visual motion and explicitly encodes the metric trajectory error left unresolved by that representation. Future images supply training supervision and target-construction inputs; deployment predicts the paired action codes from current context without generating future images or scoring trajectory candidates. Representation alignment and latent actions REPA aligns diffusion-model features with pretrained visual representations~ yu2024representation . For driving, Drive-JEPA learns predictive video representations for planning~ wang2026drive , ReWorld supervises intermediate video and action representations through prediction, alignment, and geometric discrimination~ xia2026reworld , and RAP introduces 3D geometric supervision through rasterization~ feng2026rap .
